# Overview



This page introduces **DeSCOPE** (*Decoding Single-Cell Omics of Perturbation Responses*) — a single-cell perturbation prediction framework for scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, and general cell-level perturbation modeling. By the end of this page, you will understand what problem DeSCOPE solves, how its codebase is organized, and where to go next in your learning journey.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L13-L24), [src/descope/__init__.py](src/descope/__init__.py#L39-L55)

## What Problem Does DeSCOPE Solve?

In perturbation biology experiments (e.g., Perturb-seq), scientists knock out or knock down a gene and measure how thousands of other genes respond. Because experiments are expensive, a natural question arises: *can we computationally predict the post-perturbation cell state instead of measuring it?*

DeSCOPE answers this with a **conditional Variational Autoencoder (cVAE)**. The key inputs are:

- The **control cell's expression profile** (what the cell looked like before perturbation)
- The **perturbed gene's embedding**, derived from the protein language model **ESM2**

The output is a predicted expression vector for the perturbed cell. The same framework applies to two modalities: gene expression (RNA) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L19-L24), [src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L117-L128)

![DeSCOPE framework overview](https://github.com/Peg-Wu/DeSCOPE/blob/main/assets/main.png?raw=true)

## Architecture at a Glance

The model is intentionally compact: everything is a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) block orchestrated in a VAE pattern. Three components matter:

1. **PertGeneEncoder** — projects the ESM2 gene embedding into the model's hidden space.
2. **VariationalEncoder** (two instances) — a *prior* encoder that sees only the control cell + perturbation, and a *posterior* encoder that additionally sees the true post-perturbation expression during training. Both output a mean and log-variance, from which a latent vector is sampled via the reparameterization trick.
3. **VariationalDecoder** — reconstructs the full expression vector from the latent sample plus the perturbation embedding, ending with a `softplus` activation so predictions stay non-negative.

During training, the loss combines reconstruction error (MSE) and a KL divergence between posterior and prior. During inference, only the **prior** path is used — the model has never seen the true perturbed expression, which is exactly the prediction we want.

Sources: [src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L15-L98), [src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L138-L169), [src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L264-L282)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs
        A["Control cell profile<br/>(ctrl_cell_expr)"]
        B["Perturbed gene<br/>ESM2 embedding"]
        C["Post-perturbation profile<br/>(labels, training only)"]
    end

    B --> PGE["PertGeneEncoder<br/>(MLP → hidden_size)"]

    subgraph VAE["Conditional VAE Core"]
        PR["Prior Encoder<br/>ctrl + pert → (μ, logσ²)"]
        PO["Posterior Encoder<br/>labels + pert → (μ, logσ²)<br/>training only"]
        Z(("Latent z<br/>reparameterize"))
        DEC["VariationalDecoder<br/>(z + pert → genes)"]
    end

    A --> PR
    PGE --> PR
    C --> PO
    PGE --> PO
    PR --> Z
    PO --> Z
    PGE --> DEC
    Z --> DEC

    DEC --> OUT["Softplus output<br/>predicted expression"]
    OUT --> LOSS["Loss = α·MSE + α·KL<br/>(training)"]
```

> [!TIP]
> The RNA and ATAC model classes (`DeSCOPEForRNA`, `DeSCOPEForATAC`) share an identical VAE architecture — the codebase keeps them as separate classes specifically so each modality can be tuned independently. If you read one forward pass, you have read both (see the NOTE comments at [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L117-L118)).

Sources: [src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L199-L222), [src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L117-L136)

## Repository Layout

The codebase follows a thin, flat structure — one module per pipeline stage, plus a `models/` package:

```
DeSCOPE/
├── src/descope/              # Installable Python package
│   ├── arguments.py          # Data / Model / Training argument groups
│   ├── dataset.py            # HuggingFace dataset wrappers (RNA & ATAC)
│   ├── tokenizer.py          # AnnData → HuggingFace dataset conversion
│   ├── trainer.py            # DeSCOPETrainer (Accelerate-based)
│   ├── inference.py          # Prediction & evaluation orchestration
│   ├── logging.py            # Verbosity control
│   ├── utils.py              # Preprocessing helpers + metrics
│   └── models/
│       ├── configuration_descope.py   # DeSCOPEConfig
│       ├── modeling_descope.py        # cVAE components & model classes
│       ├── baselines.py               # Simple baseline models
│       └── utils.py                   # MLP builder, KL loss, output types
├── tutorials/                # Runnable end-to-end examples
│   ├── ATAC_Gene/            # scATAC perturbation pipeline
│   ├── RNA_Gene/             # scRNA genetic perturbation pipeline
│   └── RNA_Drug/             # Drug perturbation (Sciplex3, Tahoe-100M)
└── docs/                     # This documentation (Sphinx)
```

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L5-L6), [src/descope/__init__.py](src/descope/__init__.py#L1-L36)

## Key Components and Their Roles

| Module | Key Classes / Functions | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `models/modeling_descope.py` | `DeSCOPEForRNA`, `DeSCOPEForATAC` | The cVAE models; each exposes `forward()` (training) and `inference()` (prediction) |
| `models/configuration_descope.py` | `DeSCOPEConfig` | All hyperparameters (hidden size, layer counts, input length) |
| `tokenizer.py` | `TokenizerForRNA`, `TokenizerForATAC`, `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_*` | Converts Scanpy `AnnData` objects into HuggingFace `datasets` |
| `dataset.py` | `HFDatasetForRNA`, `HFDatasetForATAC` | Dataset wrappers that fetch model-ready tensors |
| `trainer.py` | `DeSCOPETrainer` | Training loop with checkpointing, early stopping, Accelerate/DeepSpeed support |
| `inference.py` | `InferenceForRNA`, `InferenceForATAC` | Runs prediction and computes perturbation metrics |
| `utils.py` | `preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata`, `pearson_delta_on_topk_de`, `direction_match_on_topk_de` | Data preprocessing and evaluation metrics |

Sources: [src/descope/__init__.py](src/descope/__init__.py#L10-L22), [src/descope/__init__.py](src/descope/__init__.py#L24-L36), [src/descope/trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L35-L59)

The API deliberately mirrors the **HuggingFace Transformers** conventions (`PreTrainedModel` + config classes), so if you have used transformers before, DeSCOPE will feel familiar: construct a `DeSCOPEConfig`, instantiate a model, wrap it in a trainer. The package is published on PyPI as **`descopex`**, requires Python ≥ 3.10, and depends on PyTorch, `cell-eval` (metrics), and `wppkg` (trainer infrastructure); DeepSpeed is optional for large-scale distributed training.

Sources: [src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L1-L12), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L8-L26), [README.md](README.md#L71-L92)

## The End-to-End Workflow

Every tutorial in the repository follows the same three-stage pipeline, regardless of modality:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Raw data<br/>.h5ad (AnnData)"] --> B["Tokenize<br/>AnnData → HuggingFace dataset"]
    B --> C["Train<br/>DeSCOPETrainer + Accelerate"]
    C --> D["Inference<br/>predict perturbed profiles"]
    D --> E["Evaluate<br/>Pearson delta, direction match<br/>via cell-eval"]
```

1. **Tokenize** — notebooks like `tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb` read `.h5ad` files and produce HuggingFace datasets aligned to a fixed gene vocabulary.
2. **Train** — scripts like `train.py` (driven by `train_descope.sh`) configure `DeSCOPETrainer` through the three argument groups.
3. **Evaluate** — the inference module predicts perturbed states and scores them against ground truth using top-k differentially-expressed gene metrics.

Sources: [src/descope/__init__.py](src/descope/__init__.py#L16-L22), [tutorials/RNA_Gene](tutorials/RNA_Gene/README.md), [src/descope/trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L49-L59)

> [!TIP]
> Before training, input data must be preprocessed with the helpers in `utils.py` — e.g., `preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata` normalizes RNA perturbation data, and ATAC data must be preprocessed consistently with the EpiAgent convention (`preprocess_atac_perturbation_adata_consistent_with_epiagent`). Skipping this step is the most common source of shape-mismatch errors for newcomers.

Sources: [src/descope/__init__.py](src/descope/__init__.py#L28-L31)

## Supported Modalities and Entry Points

| | **RNA (gene expression)** | **ATAC (chromatin accessibility)** |
|---|---|---|
| Model | `DeSCOPEForRNA` | `DeSCOPEForATAC` |
| Config / Arguments | `DeSCOPEModelArguments`, `DeSCOPEDataArguments` | Same, modality flag decides |
| Tokenizer | `TokenizerForRNA` | `TokenizerForATAC` |
| Dataset | `HFDatasetForRNA` | `HFDatasetForATAC` |
| Inference | `InferenceForRNA` | `InferenceForATAC` |
| Tutorial | `tutorials/RNA_Gene`, `tutorials/RNA_Drug` | `tutorials/ATAC_Gene` |
| Example datasets | K562_GWPS, RPE1, Norman, HEPG2, JURCAT… | Human-scATAC-Corpus (cell-by-cCRE matrices) |

Sources: [src/descope/__init__.py](src/descope/__init__.py#L10-L22), [README.md](README.md#L94-L115)

## Installation in One Breath

The full procedure lives in the Quick Start guide, but the shape of it is: create a Python ≥ 3.10 conda environment, install PyTorch (≥ 2.6 recommended), optionally DeepSpeed, then `pip install descopex` (or install from source with `pip install -e .`). Verify with:

```python
import descope
descope.welcome()
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L27-L92)

# Quick Start



This page gets you from zero to your first single-cell perturbation prediction with **DeSCOPE** in under an hour. You will install the package, verify the environment, run a complete prediction-and-evaluation workflow using the public API, and preview the end-to-end Tokenize → Train → Evaluate pipeline. No prior experience with the codebase is assumed — only basic Python and familiarity with running Jupyter notebooks.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L13-L25)

## What is DeSCOPE? (30-Second Orientation)

DeSCOPE (**Dec**oding **S**ingle-Cell **O**mics of **P**erturbation R**e**sponses) is a framework for predicting how individual cells respond to genetic perturbations. It supports both **scRNA-seq** and **scATAC-seq** modalities and is built on a **conditional Variational Autoencoder (cVAE)**, where each perturbed gene is represented by an embedding derived from **ESM2** (a protein language model). In plain terms: you give DeSCOPE a batch of untreated control cells plus the identity of the gene you plan to perturb, and it generates what those cells' expression profiles would look like after the perturbation.

![DeSCOPE framework overview](https://github.com/Peg-Wu/DeSCOPE/blob/main/assets/main.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L19-L25)

## Installation

DeSCOPE ships on PyPI under the name `descopex` and requires **Python ≥ 3.10**. The install follows four steps: create an isolated environment, install PyTorch first (so you get the correct CUDA build for your machine), optionally install DeepSpeed, then install the package itself.

```bash
# Step 1: Create and activate a Python 3.10 environment
conda create -n descope python=3.10
conda activate descope

# Step 2: Install PyTorch for your CUDA version (torch ≥ 2.6 recommended)
# Example for CUDA 12.6:
pip install torch==2.7.1 torchvision==0.22.1 torchaudio==2.7.1 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126

# Step 3 (optional, for multi-GPU training): install DeepSpeed
pip install deepspeed

# Step 4: Install DeSCOPE
pip install descopex
# ...or from source:
git clone https://github.com/Peg-Wu/DeSCOPE.git
cd DeSCOPE
pip install -e .
```

The summary table below collects the four steps and their purpose:

| Step | Action | Why It Matters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Environment | `conda create -n descope python=3.10` | Isolates dependencies; Python ≥ 3.10 is a hard requirement |
| 2. PyTorch | `pip install torch==...` (per your CUDA) | Must match your GPU driver; old versions are unsupported |
| 3. DeepSpeed *(optional)* | `pip install deepspeed` | Only needed if you plan distributed/large-scale training |
| 4. DeSCOPE | `pip install descopex` | Pulls the core runtime dependencies automatically |

Installing `descopex` automatically pulls its pinned runtime stack — `torch`, `wppkg==0.1.4`, `cell-eval==0.6.6` (the evaluation backend), and `pdex==0.1.28` — so there is nothing else to wire up manually.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L27-L85), [docs/source/Installation.md](/docs/source/Installation.md#L1-L57), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L19-L26)

## Verify Your Installation

Before touching any data, confirm the package resolves correctly. The library exposes a one-line health check that prints the version banner, repository links, and author contacts:

```python
import descope
descope.welcome()
```

If the ASCII-art banner prints without import errors, your environment is ready. Note that simply importing `descope` also surfaces the entire public API — models (`DeSCOPEForRNA`, `DeSCOPEForATAC`, `DeSCOPEConfig`), tokenizers (`TokenizerForRNA`, `TokenizerForATAC`), inference tools (`InferenceForRNA`, `InferenceForATAC`), and the `DeSCOPETrainer` are all exported at the top level.

Sources: [src/descope/__init__.py](/src/descope/__init__.py#L1-L36), [src/descope/__init__.py](/src/descope/__init__.py#L39-L71)

## Your First Perturbation Prediction

The fastest way to see DeSCOPE work end-to-end is the inference API. The library ships runnable notebooks in `tutorials/RNA_Gene/test.ipynb` and `tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb` that demonstrate the full flow in three cells: **initialize → predict → evaluate**. Here is the RNA workflow (the ATAC variant is identical, swapping in `InferenceForATAC`):

```python
import torch
from descope.inference import InferenceForRNA

# 1. Initialize the inference tool
infer = InferenceForRNA(
    test_csv_template_fp="Test_Info_HEPG2.csv",   # CSV listing perturbations to simulate
    adata="HEPG2.h5ad",                            # AnnData containing control + perturbed cells
    pretrained_model_name_or_path="./trainer_output/HEPG2/last_model",
    pert_col="target_gene",                        # obs column holding perturbation labels
    ctrl_name="non-targeting",                     # label of the control population
    target_sum=1e4,
    skip_raw_counts_check=True,
)

# 2. Run the generation loop (always keep use_generated_control_cells=False)
infer.inference(
    gene_embs_file="ESM2_pert_features.pt",        # precomputed ESM2 embeddings per gene
    device=torch.device("cuda:0"),
    batch_size=256,
    use_generated_control_cells=False,
)

# 3. Evaluate predictions against ground truth
metrics_to_calculate = ["pearson_delta", "overlap_at_50", "mae", "discrimination_score_l1"]
results, agg_results, evaluator = infer.compute_metrics(
    adata_pred=infer.adata_pred,
    adata_real=infer.adata_test_ground_truth,
    metrics_to_calculate=metrics_to_calculate,
    control_pert=infer.ctrl_name,
    pert_col=infer.pert_col,
)
```

Under the hood, step 2 samples control cells in batches, pairs each with the ESM2 embedding of the target gene, runs the model's `inference()` forward pass, and accumulates exactly `n_cells` predictions per perturbation before assembling a predicted `AnnData` in `infer.adata_pred` [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L286-L348). Step 3 delegates to the bundled `cell-eval` library through the `CellEvalMixin` that every inference class inherits [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L70-L158).

The constructor arguments you will most often touch:

| Parameter | Default | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `test_csv_template_fp` | required | CSV specifying which perturbations to generate; must contain `target_gene` and `n_cells` columns |
| `adata` | required | Path to a `.h5ad` file (or an `AnnData` object) that includes your control cells |
| `pretrained_model_name_or_path` | required | Directory of a trained checkpoint (loaded via `from_pretrained`) |
| `pert_col` | `"perturbation"` | Column in `adata.obs` that labels each cell's perturbation |
| `ctrl_name` | `"control"` | Label identifying the control population inside `pert_col` |
| `target_sum` / `skip_raw_counts_check` | RNA-specific | Normalization target and count-format validation toggle for scRNA inputs |

Sources: [tutorials/RNA_Gene/test.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/test.ipynb#L10-L120), [src/descope/inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L199-L241)

> [!TIP]
> The test CSV template is validated at construction time: it **must** contain the columns `target_gene` and `n_cells`, or initialization raises a `ValueError` listing the missing columns. `n_cells` controls how many simulated cells are generated per perturbation, matching real dataset scale.

> [!TIP]
> Never set `use_generated_control_cells=True` — the constructor actively asserts against it. Final predictions always splice in the **real** control cells rather than model-generated ones, which keeps evaluation stable [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L295-L300).

## The End-to-End Tutorial Pipeline (5-Minute Tour)

While the inference API lets you evaluate a pretrained checkpoint immediately, the full DeSCOPE workflow for training your own model follows a fixed three-stage pattern, mirrored identically in all three tutorial folders (`tutorials/RNA_Gene/`, `tutorials/ATAC_Gene/`). Each stage has a dedicated artifact: notebooks handle tokenization and evaluation, and a shell script drives training.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Raw data (.h5ad)"] --> B["Stage 1: Tokenize<br/>tokenize.ipynb<br/>AnnData → HuggingFace Dataset (Arrow)"]
    B --> C["Stage 2: Train<br/>sh train_descope.sh<br/>accelerate launch train.py"]
    C --> D["Checkpoint<br/>results/descope/trainer_output/..."]
    D --> E["Stage 3: Evaluate<br/>test.ipynb<br/>InferenceForRNA / InferenceForATAC + cell-eval metrics"]
    E --> F["Predicted AnnData +<br/>metric reports"]
```

The three commands you would actually run:

```bash
# Stage 1 — open and run tokenize.ipynb to convert .h5ad into a tokenized HF dataset

# Stage 2 — train (edit paths inside the script first)
sh train_descope.sh       # standard training
sh train_descope_loo.sh   # leave-one-out variant (held-out perturbation protocol)

# Stage 3 — open and run test.ipynb for inference + metrics
```

Each training script is organized into three commented parameter blocks — `MODELPARAMS` (architecture: hidden size, layer counts), `DATAPARAMS` (dataset directory, control label, ESM2 embedding file), and `TRAINPARAMS` (epochs, batch size, learning rate, mixed precision) — then launched through Hugging Face `accelerate` with a local `accelerate_config.yaml`, so a single machine or a multi-GPU cluster uses the same entrypoint.

Sources: [tutorials/RNA_Gene/README.md](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/README.md#L1-L25), [tutorials/ATAC_Gene/README.md](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/README.md#L1-L25), [tutorials/RNA_Gene/train_descope.sh](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/train_descope.sh#L1-L58)

## Pick a Starter Dataset

Every tutorial needs an `.h5ad` perturbation dataset and a matching ESM2 gene-embedding file. The repository's Datasets Zoo curates public scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq resources with direct download links. For a first run, start **small**: the table below is ordered roughly by download size, and `HEPG2` (5.2 GB) is the exact dataset used in the bundled `test.ipynb` example.

| Dataset | Size | Source (Paper) | Notes for Beginners |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| HEPG2 | 5.2 GB | Nadig et al., 2025 | Smallest scRNA option; used in the official test notebook |
| RPE1 | 8.1 GB | Replogle et al., 2022 | Classic genome-wide Perturb-seq benchmark |
| JURKAT | 8.7 GB | Nadig et al., 2025 | T-cell line dataset |
| K562_ESSENTIAL | 9.9 GB | Replogle et al., 2022 | Default dataset in `train_descope.sh` |
| Norman_K562 | — | Norman et al., 2019 | combinatorial-perturbation benchmark |
| K562_GWPS | 61.3 GB | Replogle et al., 2022 | Full genome-wide screen — download last |
| PC-9 | — | DeSCOPE authors | In-house dataset (Zenodo) |
| Human-scATAC-Corpus | — | — | Cell-by-cCRE matrices for the ATAC modality |

One important shortcut: the **ESM2 gene embeddings** that inference requires (the `gene_embs_file` argument) can be obtained alongside the H1 dataset from the [Virtual Cell Challenge 2025](https://virtualcellchallenge.org/) — the README explicitly calls this out, so you do not need to run ESM2 yourself to get started.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L94-L114)

## Architecture at a Glance

A minimal mental model will make every later page easier to read. DeSCOPE treats perturbation prediction as **conditional generation**: control cells flow through an encoder into a probabilistic latent space, and the decoder reconstructs expression *conditioned on* the target gene's ESM2 embedding. Training optimizes an ELBO objective (reconstruction + KL divergence), which is why you see both `alpha_mse_loss` and `alpha_kl_loss` in the training script.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Control cells<br/>(gene expression / cCRE matrix)"] --> B["Variational Encoder"]
    B --> C["Latent space z<br/>(mean & variance)"]
    D["ESM2 embedding<br/>of target gene"] --> E["PertGene Encoder"]
    E --> F["Condition vector"]
    C --> G["Decoder"]
    F --> G
    G --> H["Predicted perturbed<br/>expression profile"]
```

Two concrete model classes implement this design — `DeSCOPEForRNA` and `DeSCOPEForATAC` — and both are Hugging Face `PreTrainedModel` subclasses, which is why checkpoints load with a familiar `from_pretrained(...)` call in the inference classes.

Sources: [src/descope/inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L18-L30), [tutorials/RNA_Gene/train_descope.sh](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/train_descope.sh#L10-L48), [README.md](/README.md#L23-L24)

## Repository Layout

Familiarizing yourself with the directory structure maps each Quick Start step to its source of truth:

```
DeSCOPE/
├── src/descope/            # The installable package (imported as `descope`)
│   ├── __init__.py         #   Public API exports + welcome()
│   ├── tokenizer.py        #   Stage 1: AnnData → HF Dataset tokenizers
│   ├── trainer.py          #   Stage 2: DeSCOPETrainer (accelerate-based)
│   ├── inference.py        #   Stage 3: InferenceForRNA / InferenceForATAC
│   ├── models/             #   cVAE architectures + configs
│   ├── dataset.py          #   HFDatasetForRNA / HFDatasetForATAC
│   ├── arguments.py        #   Data/Model/Training argument groups
│   └── utils.py            #   Metrics, preprocessing, embedding loaders
├── tutorials/
│   ├── RNA_Gene/           #   tokenize.ipynb, train_descope.sh, test.ipynb
│   ├── ATAC_Gene/          #   Same three-stage pattern for scATAC
│   └── RNA_Drug/           #   Drug perturbation case studies
└── docs/source/            #   Read the Docs pages (you are here)
```

Sources: [src/descope/__init__.py](/src/descope/__init__.py#L10-L22), [tutorials/RNA_Gene](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/README.md#L1-L25)

# Datasets Zoo and Downloads



This page is your map to every dataset DeSCOPE consumes and every companion file you must download alongside them. DeSCOPE predicts single-cell perturbation responses from two major modalities — scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq — plus a drug-perturbation branch built on the massive Tahoe-100M corpus. Here you will learn what each dataset is, where to fetch it, how much disk space to budget, and exactly where to place the files so the library's data pipeline can find them.

![main](https://github.com/Peg-Wu/DeSCOPE/blob/main/assets/main.png?raw=true)

## The Zoo at a Glance

Before diving into individual datasets, it helps to understand the overall shape of the data flow. Every entry in the zoo follows the same lifecycle: you download raw **`.h5ad`** (AnnData) files from a public repository, organize them in a local directory, tokenize them into Hugging Face Arrow datasets, and finally hand them to the training system:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Public Sources<br/>Figshare / GEO / Zenodo / GCS"] -->|"download .h5ad"| B["Raw Data Directory<br/>data/RNA/{CellLine}/{CellLine}.h5ad<br/>data/ATAC/{CellLine}/{CellLine}.h5ad"]
    C["Virtual Cell Challenge 2025"] -->|"ESM2_pert_features.pt"| D["Gene Embeddings<br/>{gene: tensor}"]
    B --> E["tokenize.ipynb<br/>(AnnData → Arrow)"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["HuggingFace Dataset<br/>labels, pert_gene, celltype"]
    F --> G["HFDatasetForRNA /<br/>HFDatasetForATAC"]
    G --> H["DeSCOPE Trainer"]
```

The one companion asset every path depends on is the **ESM2 gene embedding file** (`ESM2_pert_features.pt`), which we cover in its own section below. Note that no dataset in this zoo is distributed *inside* the repository itself — DeSCOPE only ships the vocabulary pickles and pretrained drug models it authored; all perturbation data lives on external hosts such as Figshare, NCBI GEO, Zenodo, and Google Cloud Storage.

Sources: [Datasets.md](docs/source/Datasets.md#L1-L21), [README.md](README.md#L94-L114), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L37-L71)

## scRNA-seq Perturbation Datasets

The core of the zoo is a collection of seven CRISPR-based gene perturbation datasets, spanning both perturb-seq style screens and targeted knockout studies. Each entry lists its source paper, on-disk size (where reported), and direct download link:

| Paper | Dataset | Size | Host | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [Replogle et al., 2022](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(22)00597-9) | K562_GWPS | 61.3 GB | [Figshare](https://plus.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/35775507) | Genome-wide perturbation screen — the largest download |
| [Replogle et al., 2022](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(22)00597-9) | K562_ESSENTIAL | 9.9 GB | [Figshare](https://plus.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/35773219) | Essential-gene subset |
| [Replogle et al., 2022](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(22)00597-9) | RPE1 | 8.1 GB | [Figshare](https://plus.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/35775606) | — |
| [Nadig et al., 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-025-02169-3) | HEPG2 | 5.2 GB | [NCBI GEO (GSE264667)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/download/?acc=GSE264667&format=file&file=GSE264667%5Fhepg2%5Fraw%5Fsinglecell%5F01%2Eh5ad) | Direct `.h5ad` link |
| [Nadig et al., 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-025-02169-3) | JURKAT | 8.7 GB | [NCBI GEO (GSE264667)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/download/?acc=GSE264667&format=file&file=GSE264667%5Fjurkat%5Fraw%5Fsinglecell%5F01%2Eh5ad) | Direct `.h5ad` link |
| [Norman et al., 2019](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aax4438) | Norman_K562 | — | [NCBI GEO (GSE133344)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE133344) | GEO accession page; includes multi-gene combinations |
| Ours (DeSCOPE team) | PC-9 | — | [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/21622013) | Authored by the DeSCOPE team |

In addition to the tabular entries, the **H1** dataset comes from the [Virtual Cell Challenge 2025](https://virtualcellchallenge.org/) ([direct download](https://storage.googleapis.com/vcc_data_prod/datasets/state/competition_support_set.zip)). H1 is a special case in the RNA_Gene tutorial: it is the only cell line that uses `pert_col="target_gene"` and `target_sum=5e4` instead of the library defaults.

> [!TIP]
> **Critical insight**: the Virtual Cell Challenge support-set ZIP is also where the project recommends obtaining the **ESM2 gene embeddings** — a single download gives you both the H1 dataset and the embedding file every training run requires.

Sources: [Datasets.md](docs/source/Datasets.md#L3-L16), [README.md](README.md#L96-L109), [tokenize.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L20-L36)

## scATAC-seq Data

For the chromatin-accessibility modality, DeSCOPE consumes cell-by-cCRE (or cell-by-peak) matrices sourced from the **[Human-scATAC-Corpus](https://health.tsinghua.edu.cn/human-scatac-corpus/download.php)** hosted by Tsinghua University. Unlike the scRNA-seq catalog, this is a corpus-level resource: you select and download the cell lines you need, then organize them into per-cell-line `.h5ad` files yourself.

The ATAC tutorials operate on five cell lines — `K562`, `K562_1`, `K562_2`, `MCF7`, and `GM12878` — and apply a `topk_ccres=50000` filter, meaning only the 50,000 most relevant cCREs are retained per cell line. Budget your download and disk space accordingly: accessibility matrices are sparse but wide.

Sources: [Datasets.md](docs/source/Datasets.md#L18-L21), [README.md](README.md#L112-L114), [tokenize.ipynb](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L20-L36), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L110-L136)

## Essential Companion Asset: ESM2 Gene Embeddings

Every dataset class in DeSCOPE expects a PyTorch file named **`ESM2_pert_features.pt`** (the default path is `./ESM2_pert_features.pt`). This file is a dictionary mapping gene names to ESM2-derived embedding tensors: `{gene_name: torch.Tensor}`. The model uses these embeddings to condition its predictions on *which* gene was perturbed — without this file, training cannot start.

The loading logic in `load_gene_embs` has two behaviors worth knowing as a beginner:

1. **Missing genes become zero vectors** — if a perturbation in your data has no entry in the embedding file, it is silently embedded as zeros.
2. **Multi-gene perturbations are averaged** — perturbations like `"GeneA+GeneB"` (the required concatenation convention for combinatorial knockouts) are embedded as the mean of their constituent gene embeddings, zeros included.

| Aspect | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| File name | `ESM2_pert_features.pt` |
| Format | `{gene_name: torch.Tensor}` dictionary, loadable via `torch.load` |
| Default lookup path | `./ESM2_pert_features.pt` (working directory) |
| Recommended source | [Virtual Cell Challenge 2025](https://virtualcellchallenge.org/) support-set ZIP |
| Used by | All dataset classes (legacy and HuggingFace-based) |

> [!TIP]
> **Critical insight**: when running the leave-one-out (`DeSCOPE_LOO`) pretraining across multiple cell lines, the names of control cells in `obs[pert_col]` must be **identical across all `.h5ad` files** — the tutorial notebooks flag this as the single most common setup mistake, and the tokenizer cannot merge datasets with inconsistent control labels.

Sources: [Datasets.md](docs/source/Datasets.md#L15-L16), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L204-L208), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L378-L399), [tokenize.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L4-L11)

## Where Your Downloads Go: Expected File Layout

The tutorial notebooks make no assumptions about a magic install directory — they reference explicit paths like `/fse/home/wupengpeng/perturbation_data_origin/RNA/{CellLine}/{CellLine}.h5ad`, which are the *authors'* machine paths. You should mirror this structure locally and edit the notebook paths to match your own layout:

```
your_data_root/
├── RNA/
│   ├── H1/
│   │   ├── H1.h5ad
│   │   └── Test_Info_H1.csv
│   ├── K562_ESSENTIAL/
│   │   ├── K562_ESSENTIAL.h5ad
│   │   └── Test_Info_K562_ESSENTIAL.csv
│   ├── JURKAT/ ...
│   ├── RPE1/ ...
│   └── HEPG2/ ...
├── ATAC/
│   ├── K562/
│   │   ├── K562.h5ad
│   │   └── Test_Info_K562.csv
│   ├── K562_1/ ...  K562_2/ ...  MCF7/ ...  GM12878/ ...
└── ESM2_pert_features.pt
```

Two conventions in this layout matter for correctness:

- **`Test_Info_{CellLine}.csv`** files list the held-out perturbation gene names per cell line. They are fed into `load_gene_names_engine` as `perts_to_exclude` during tokenization, implementing the evaluation split. The loader accepts either a single-column gene list or a CSV with a `target_gene` header.
- **Metadata column conventions differ by modality.** The table below summarizes what your `.h5ad` files must contain so the tokenizers and dataset classes can find perturbation labels and control cells:

| Modality | Perturbation column (`pert_col`) | Control label (`ctrl_name`) | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| scRNA-seq (most cell lines) | `"gene"` | `"non-targeting"` | H1 uses `"target_gene"` instead |
| scRNA-seq (H1 only) | `"target_gene"` | `"non-targeting"` | Also uses `target_sum=5e4` |
| scATAC-seq | `"perturbation"` | `"control"` | top-k cCRE filtering applied downstream |
| Multi-gene knockouts | symbols joined by `+` | — | e.g., `"GeneA+GeneB"` |

Sources: [tokenize.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L20-L80), [tokenize.ipynb](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L20-L110), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L330-L375), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L109-L165)

## Who Consumes These Files: The Dataset Classes

DeSCOPE ships **two generations** of dataset classes. The legacy family reads `.h5ad` files directly and is explicitly marked `# Slow | Deprecated`; the current family consumes the Arrow-format datasets produced by tokenization and is marked `# Fast`. As a beginner, target the `HF*` classes — the legacy classes remain in the codebase mainly for reference and backward compatibility.

| Class | Generation | Input | `MAIN_INPUT_NAME` | Preprocessing |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `BaseDataset` | Slow (deprecated) | `.h5ad` path or `AnnData` | — (abstract) | subclass-defined |
| `DatasetForATAC` | Slow (deprecated) | `.h5ad` / `AnnData` | `ctrl_cell_tf_idf` | EpiAgent-consistent cCRE filtering |
| `DatasetForRNA` | Slow (deprecated) | `.h5ad` / `AnnData` | `ctrl_cell_expr` | raw-count checks + normalization |
| `HFBaseDataset` | Fast | `datasets.Dataset` (Arrow) | — (abstract) | expects pre-tokenized features |
| `HFDatasetForATAC` | Fast | Arrow dataset | `ctrl_cell_tf_idf` | none (done at tokenization) |
| `HFDatasetForRNA` | Fast | Arrow dataset | `ctrl_cell_expr` | none (done at tokenization) |

The Fast classes validate your Arrow dataset strictly: it **must** contain the features `labels`, `pert_gene`, and `celltype`, or construction fails with an explicit error listing the missing features. At training time, each `__getitem__` call assembles a sample by pairing the perturbed cell with a randomly drawn control cell of the same cell type, and injects the corresponding ESM2 embedding for the perturbed gene.

Sources: [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L22-L106), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L109-L165), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L200-L335)

## Drug Perturbation Assets: Tahoe-100M and Sci-Plex3

The drug branch of the zoo works differently: instead of downloading one raw `.h5ad` per cell line, you work with the enormous **Tahoe-100M** corpus (approximately **60,000 genes**) and the **Sci-Plex3** evaluation set. To make Tahoe-100M tractable, the team pre-filtered genes by highly variable genes (HVGs) and frequency analysis — the preprocessing scripts live at `tahoe100m_pretrain/HVGs/calc_hvgs.py` and `calc_freq.ipynb`.

Three pretrained DeSCOPE checkpoints (each trained 10 epochs, batch size 1024) are hosted on Hugging Face, and each pairs with a gene-vocabulary pickle that **is** shipped in this repository:

| Pretrained Model | Gene Vocabulary (in-repo) | Hugging Face Repository |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `descope-tahoe100m-2k-hvgs` | `tahoe100m_pretrain/HVGs/merged_2k_hvgs.pkl` | [wpp02/descope-tahoe100m-2k-hvgs](https://huggingface.co/wpp02/descope-tahoe100m-2k-hvgs) |
| `descope-tahoe100m-5k-hvgs` | `tahoe100m_pretrain/HVGs/merged_5k_hvgs.pkl` | [wpp02/descope-tahoe100m-5k-hvgs](https://huggingface.co/wpp02/descope-tahoe100m-5k-hvgs) |
| `descope-tahoe100m-12059-hvgs` | `tahoe100m_pretrain/HVGs/merged_12059_hvgs.pkl` | [wpp02/descope-tahoe100m-12059-hvgs](https://huggingface.co/wpp02/descope-tahoe100m-12059-hvgs) |

Choose the vocabulary size based on your compute budget — larger vocabularies cover more genes (the 12059-HVG model covers **482 of the 2,000** genes evaluated on Sci-Plex3). The recommended strategy is **pretraining on Tahoe-100M once, then fine-tuning on downstream datasets**, which avoids repeating expensive preprocessing and tokenization; the zero-shot fine-tune-free workflow is also supported. Repository assets also include `tahoe100m_drug_dose_embed.pt` (drug-dose embeddings) and `tahoe_100m_all_genes.pkl`.

![scrna_drug_perturbation_performance](https://github.com/Peg-Wu/DeSCOPE/blob/main/tutorials/RNA_Drug/scrna_drug_perturbation_performance.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](tutorials/RNA_Drug/README.md#L1-L40), [repo structure: tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain)

## Suggested Reading Path

You now know what to download and where to put it. Here is the recommended progression through the documentation:

1. **[Quick Start](2-quick-start)** — if you have not yet installed `descopex` and verified your environment.
2. **[Tutorial Pipeline: Tokenize, Train, Evaluate](4-tutorial-pipeline-tokenize-train-evaluate)** — the end-to-end walkthrough that turns the `.h5ad` files you just downloaded into Arrow datasets and trained checkpoints.
3. **[Tokenization: AnnData to HuggingFace Datasets](12-tokenization-anndata-to-huggingface-datasets)** — the deep dive into the exact conversion step this page only sketched.
4. **[Drug Perturbation Case Studies: Sciplex3, Tahoe-100M](5-drug-perturbation-case-studies-sciplex3-tahoe-100m)** — once your drug assets are in place, follow the complete pretrain → fine-tune/zero-shot workflows.


# Tutorial Pipeline: Tokenize, Train, Evaluate



This page walks you through DeSCOPE's hands-on tutorial pipeline end to end: converting raw `.h5ad` single-cell data into Hugging Face datasets, training a model (either the standard DeSCOPE or the leave-one-out DeSCOPE_LOO variant), and running inference plus metric computation on unseen perturbations. Everything here is driven by the runnable artifacts in `tutorials/ATAC_Gene/` and `tutorials/RNA_Gene/` — the third folder, `tutorials/RNA_Drug/`, is a larger-scale case study covered separately in [Drug Perturbation Case Studies: Sciplex3, Tahoe-100M](5-drug-perturbation-case-studies-sciplex3-tahoe-100m).

Sources: [Tutorials.md](/docs/source/Tutorials.md#L1-L8), [README.md](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/README.md#L1-L25), [README.md](/tutorials/RNA_Drug/README.md#L1-L8)

## Pipeline at a Glance

Both gene-perturbation tutorials share an identical three-stage execution flow, differing only in which modality-specific classes they import. Stage 1 converts AnnData into Arrow-format Hugging Face datasets, Stage 2 trains the conditional VAE, and Stage 3 generates predicted cells and scores them against real data. The entire workflow is chained by file paths: each stage consumes the output directory of the previous one.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Stage1["Stage 1 · tokenize.ipynb"]
        A[".h5ad raw data"] -->|"tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_*"| B["HuggingFace Dataset<br/>(Arrow, on disk)"]
    end
    subgraph Stage2["Stage 2 · train_descope.sh / train_descope_loo.sh"]
        B -->|"load_from_disk"| C["HFDatasetForRNA / ForATAC"]
        C --> D["DeSCOPETrainer"]
        D --> E["./trainer_output/.../last_model"]
    end
    subgraph Stage3["Stage 3 · test.ipynb"]
        E --> F["InferenceForRNA / ForATAC"]
        T["Test_Info CSV template"] --> F
        F --> G["adata_pred"]
        G --> H["CellEval metrics +<br/>extra metrics"]
    end
```

Sources: [README.md](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/README.md#L7-L24), [train.py](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L20-L72), [test.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb#L12-L46)

Each tutorial folder contains the same set of files, so once you understand one modality you can transfer that knowledge directly:

```
tutorials/ATAC_Gene/           tutorials/RNA_Gene/
├── README.md                  ├── README.md
├── accelerate_config.yaml     ├── accelerate_config.yaml
├── tokenize.ipynb             ├── tokenize.ipynb
├── train.py                   ├── train.py
├── train_descope.sh           ├── train_descope.sh
├── train_descope_loo.sh       ├── train_descope_loo.sh
└── test.ipynb                 └── test.ipynb
```

Sources: [README.md](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/README.md#L1-L25), [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L1-L123)

The only differences between the two variants are the modality-specific API names, which follow a strict one-to-one mapping:

| Pipeline Role | RNA_Gene API | ATAC_Gene API |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| One-shot tokenization | `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_rna` | `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_atac` |
| LOO pretrain tokenization | `TokenizerForRNA` | `TokenizerForATAC` |
| Dataset wrapper in training | `HFDatasetForRNA` | `HFDatasetForATAC` |
| Model class | `DeSCOPEForRNA` | `DeSCOPEForATAC` |
| Inference engine | `InferenceForRNA` | `InferenceForATAC` |
| Default control label | `non-targeting` | `control` |

Sources: [train.py](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/train.py#L4-L17), [train.py](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L4-L17), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L146-L157), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L381-L424)

## The Test CSV Template: The Pipeline's Contract

Before touching any notebook, you must prepare a test CSV template (named `Test_Info_{cellline}.csv` in the tutorials) that declares which unseen genes to predict and how many cells to generate per gene. This file is surprisingly load-bearing: it is consumed at *two* ends of the pipeline — during tokenization to exclude test perturbations from the training set, and during inference to drive cell generation. It must contain exactly two columns, `target_gene` and `n_cells`, and the control label does not need to appear (the inference pipeline always uses real, experimentally observed control cells rather than synthetic ones).

| Column | Meaning | Example values |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `target_gene` | Perturbation genes held out from training; multi-gene knockouts are joined with `+` (e.g., `GeneA+GeneB`); a `non-targeting`/`control` entry is optional and ignored if present | `PRCP`, `MED13`, `non-targeting` |
| `n_cells` | Number of cells to generate for that target gene | `4331`, `2787` |

Sources: [Tutorials.md](/docs/source/Tutorials.md#L10-L33), [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L4-L21), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L216-L219)

> [!TIP]
> Notice how `perts_to_exclude=load_gene_names_engine(f".../Test_Info_{c}.csv")` appears in the tokenization cell of both tutorials. This is the mechanism that makes genes truly "unseen": the same CSV that defines your evaluation targets also filters them out of the training data, guaranteeing the leave-one-out protocol is leak-free.

Sources: [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L30-L51), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L14-L45)

## Stage 1: Tokenize AnnData into Hugging Face Datasets

Run `tokenize.ipynb` to transform raw `.h5ad` files into tokenized Arrow datasets. Conceptually, tokenization performs a **before → after** transformation on your data:

| | Before (raw AnnData) | After (tokenized HF Dataset) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Storage format | `.h5ad` file, expression matrix in `.X`, labels in `.obs[pert_col]` | Arrow dataset on disk via `save_to_disk` |
| Columns | Gene × cell matrix + metadata | Three columns: `"labels"` (expression vector), `"pert_gene"` (perturbation label or control), `"celltype"` |
| Perturbation set | Everything observed, including test genes | Test genes excluded via `perts_to_exclude` |
| Feature space | Whatever the file contains | Unified: top-`50000` variable cCREs (ATAC) or the finetune file's gene set (RNA) |

Sources: [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L93-L107), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L187-L222), [README.md](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/README.md#L9-L11)

The notebook has two sections that matter: **`1. DeSCOPE`** tokenizes each cell line individually for fine-tuning, while **`2. DeSCOPE_LOO`** tokenizes the *remaining* cell lines jointly for pretraining. If you only plan to run standard DeSCOPE, Section 1 alone suffices; DeSCOPE_LOO requires both. In Section 2, a `TokenizerForRNA`/`TokenizerForATAC` object is first initialized on the held-out cell line — this freezes its feature space and perturbation vocabulary — and then `.tokenize()` is called on every other cell line, aligning each one to that frozen space before saving to `loo_{cellline}` directories.

Sources: [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L30-L87), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L331-L358), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L467-L501)

Key tokenization parameters you will actually edit:

| Parameter | Where used | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `perts_to_exclude` | Section 1 | Removes the CSV's test genes from training data |
| `topk_ccres=50000` | ATAC only | Keeps the 50,000 most variable cCREs as the input feature space |
| `target_sum` | RNA only | Per-cell normalization target (e.g., `1e4`; `5e4` for the H1 cell line) |
| `pert_col` / `ctrl_name` | Both | Column holding perturbation labels; the control label (RNA defaults to `non-targeting`, ATAC to `control`) |
| `skip_raw_counts_check` | RNA only | Bypasses the integer-counts assertion; set `True` only if you are certain inputs are raw counts |
| `duplicated_features_handling` | RNA LOO only | Strategy for duplicate gene symbols, e.g., `DuplicatedFeatureHandling.max_pooling` |
| `apply_pert_gene_filter=False` | Section 2 | Keeps *all* perturbations in pretraining cell lines rather than only those in the finetune set |

Sources: [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L30-L87), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L238-L272), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L413-L435), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L578-L579)

Two data-hygiene rules are emphasized directly in the notebook's Tips cell. First, when tokenizing pretraining cell lines for LOO, **control cell names must be identical across all `.h5ad` files**, because DeSCOPE_LOO merges those datasets and needs one consistent control label. Second, multi-gene knockouts must concatenate gene symbols with a plus sign, e.g. `'GeneA+GeneB'`.

Sources: [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L4-L21), [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L4-L25), [Tutorials.md](/docs/source/Tutorials.md#L32-L33)

## Stage 2: Train with the DeSCOPE Trainer

Training is launched from bash — never by running `train.py` directly — because the scripts invoke `accelerate launch` with a distributed configuration. `train_descope.sh` runs a single standard training job, while `train_descope_loo.sh` runs a **two-phase protocol**: pretrain on all cell lines except the held-out one, then finetune on the held-out line by loading the pretrain checkpoint via `--pretrained_model_name_or_path`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph LOO["train_descope_loo.sh"]
        P["Phase 1 · Pretrain<br/>tokenized data: loo_GM12878/<br/>(all cell lines except held-out)"] --> CKPT["pretrain_output_dir/last_model"]
        CKPT -->|"--pretrained_model_name_or_path"| F["Phase 2 · Finetune<br/>tokenized data: GM12878/<br/>(held-out cell line only)"]
        F --> OUT["finetune_output_dir/last_model"]
    end
    S["train_descope.sh<br/>(single phase, one cell line)"] -.-> OUT
```

Sources: [train_descope.sh](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L52-L59), [train_descope_loo.sh](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope_loo.sh#L43-L97)

Inside `train.py`, the flow is always the same three steps regardless of modality: parse the three argument dataclasses, build the dataset wrapper, then hand everything to `DeSCOPETrainer`. The dataset loading has a built-in convenience — it first tries `load_from_disk` on the directory as a whole, and on `FileNotFoundError` falls back to concatenating the per-cell-line subdirectories beneath it, which is exactly how the LOO pretrain directory is laid out. A small but important line is `HFDatasetForATAC.INVOLVE_CONTROL_TO_CONTROL = True`, which includes control-to-control pairs in training. Finally, when training from scratch, the model's `input_length` and embedding size are **inferred from the data itself** (`train_ds[0]["labels"].shape[-1]` and `pert_gene_emb` shape), so tokenization output and model dimensions can never disagree.

Sources: [train.py](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L20-L64), [train.py](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/train.py#L20-L64), [train.py](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L66-L72)

Every flag in the shell scripts maps to one of three argument groups parsed by `HfArgumentParser`:

| Parameter Group | Data Arguments | Model Arguments | Training Arguments |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Purpose | Where data lives | Architecture shape | Optimization loop |
| Key fields | `tokenized_datasets_dir`, `keep_in_memory`, `ctrl_name`, `gene_embs_file` | `hidden_act`, `hidden_size`, `hidden_dropout`, `pert_gene_encoder_layers`, `variational_encoder_layers`, `variational_decoder_layers`, `add_layernorm` | `seed`, `num_train_epochs`, `per_device_train_batch_size`, `learning_rate`, `lr_scheduler_type`, `alpha_mse_loss`, `alpha_kl_loss`, `pretrained_model_name_or_path` |
| Tutorial defaults | Paths set at script top | `gelu`, `672`, `0`, `1`, `4`, `4`, `True` | `42`, `20`, `64`, `1e-4`, `cosine`, `1.0`, `1.0`, unset (scratch) / pretrain dir (LOO finetune) |

Sources: [arguments.py](/src/descope/arguments.py#L5-L85), [train_descope.sh](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L6-L50)

The `alpha_mse_loss` and `alpha_kl_loss` fields are DeSCOPE-specific extensions of a standard `TrainingArguments` class: they weight the MSE reconstruction term and the KL divergence term of the ELBO objective (both default `1.0` in the tutorials). Two other settings worth knowing as a beginner: `checkpointing_steps=epoch-10` saves a checkpoint every 10 epochs, and `--mixed_precision=bf16` plus the `dataloader_*` flags are pure throughput knobs that don't change model semantics.

Sources: [arguments.py](/src/descope/arguments.py#L5-L15), [train_descope.sh](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L32-L50), [train_descope_loo.sh](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope_loo.sh#L20-L42)

Distributed behavior comes from `accelerate_config.yaml`, which is deliberately minimal — its only decision is `distributed_type: MULTI_GPU` or `DEEPSPEED` (if you choose MULTI_GPU, do not pass a DeepSpeed config file). The launcher combines this file with `--num_processes=1` and the three parameter blocks into one training invocation.

Sources: [accelerate_config.yaml](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/accelerate_config.yaml#L1-L3), [train_descope.sh](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L52-L59)

## Stage 3: Inference and Evaluation with test.ipynb

`test.ipynb` is organized as five sequential steps, and its outputs are everything you need for reporting: per-perturbation metrics, aggregate metrics, and a predicted AnnData on disk. First, initialize the inference engine by pointing it at three things — the test CSV template, the original `.h5ad` (the source of real control cells), and the trained checkpoint (`./trainer_output/GM12878/last_model`). Initialization immediately validates the CSV (`target_gene`/`n_cells` columns are mandatory and a missing-column error is raised otherwise), splits the ground truth into control and test subsets, and loads the model weights.

Sources: [test.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb#L12-L24), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L199-L247), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L249-L256)

Second, call `infer.inference(...)`. The loop samples real control cells in batches, pairs each batch with the ESM2 embedding of the target gene from `gene_embs_file`, and decodes `n_cells` predicted cells per target gene — dropping any batch that contains NaN outputs. For RNA data you'll additionally pass `target_sum` and `skip_raw_counts_check` at initialization, mirroring tokenization.

Sources: [test.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb#L41-L46), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L286-L348), [test.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/test.ipynb#L14-L24)

> [!TIP]
> The notebook screams this in bold for a reason: always keep `use_generated_control_cells=False`. The code enforces it with a hard assertion — generated controls exist only for internal debugging, and using them in evaluation causes result instability. Final metrics must always compare predictions against *real, experimentally observed* control cells, which the pipeline substitutes into the output automatically.

Sources: [test.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb#L25-L46), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L295-L300), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L364-L368)

Third, compute metrics via `infer.compute_metrics(...)`, which wraps the cell-eval library. Browse `infer.all_metrics` to see the full catalog, pick your subset, and receive a `(results, agg_results, evaluator)` tuple — per-perturbation scores, aggregate scores, and a live evaluator object.

| Metric Category | Examples from the tutorial | What it measures |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Distributional | `pearson_delta`, `mae`, `discrimination_score_l1` | Agreement between predicted and real expression profiles |
| DE-overlap | `overlap_at_50/100/200/500`, `overlap_at_N` | Overlap of top differentially-expressed genes vs. ground truth |
| Extra (DeSCOPE-added) | `pearson`, `pearson_delta_on_topk_de`, `direction_match_on_topk_de` | Correlation and up/down-regulation direction on top-k DE genes |

Sources: [test.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb#L47-L95), [Tutorials.md](/docs/source/Tutorials.md#L35-L105), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L70-L97), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L160-L196)

Fourth, run the extra metrics through `infer.extra_metrics_func`, e.g., `direction_match_on_topk_de` with `separate_up_down_regulated=True` returns separate up- and down-regulated direction-match scores. Fifth, aggregate per-perturbation results into a pandas DataFrame, join the extra metrics by mapping on the `perturbation` column, and export `results_for_each_perturbation.csv`; finally, save the predicted AnnData via `infer.write_h5ad(...)` as `descope_preds.h5ad`.

Sources: [test.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb#L96-L210), [test.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb#L211-L221), [Tutorials.md](/docs/source/Tutorials.md#L107-L176)

## Troubleshooting Common Pitfalls

| Symptom | Root Cause | Fix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `Missing required columns in test csv template: [...]` | CSV lacks `target_gene` or `n_cells` | Re-export the CSV with exactly those two columns |
| LOO pretraining merges data incorrectly | Control cell labels differ across `.h5ad` files | Rename controls to one consistent label before Section 2 of tokenization |
| Hard assertion crash during `infer.inference` | `use_generated_control_cells=True` | Keep `False` for all evaluations; generated controls are debug-only |
| `Detected NaN, drop current batch.` in logs | Numerical instability in a decoded batch | Expected behavior — the batch is regenerated automatically; no action needed |
| Test genes appear "seen" during training | `perts_to_exclude` not wired to `Test_Info_*.csv` | Pass `load_gene_names_engine(...)` output as `perts_to_exclude` in Section 1 |
| RNA tokenization asserts non-integer values | Input is already normalized, not raw counts | Set `skip_raw_counts_check=True` only if you have verified your data yourself |

Sources: [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L249-L256), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L295-L300), [inference.py](/src/descope/inference.py#L331-L333), [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L4-L21), [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L8-L9)

## Where to Go Next

You have now run the full tokenize → train → evaluate loop for gene perturbation prediction. Natural next steps, following the documentation catalog: if you want the drug-perturbation workflow with pretrained Tahoe-100M checkpoints, continue to [Drug Perturbation Case Studies: Sciplex3, Tahoe-100M](5-drug-perturbation-case-studies-sciplex3-tahoe-100m). To understand what happened inside each stage, read [Tokenization: AnnData to HuggingFace Datasets](12-tokenization-anndata-to-huggingface-datasets), [Trainer and Accelerate Integration](15-trainer-and-accelerate-integration), [Inference Pipeline Design](19-inference-pipeline-design), and for evaluation theory, [Perturbation Metrics via Cell-Eval](20-perturbation-metrics-via-cell-eval) plus [Leave-One-Out Evaluation Protocol](21-leave-one-out-evaluation-protocol). If you need a refresher on where to download the datasets used here, revisit [Datasets Zoo and Downloads](3-datasets-zoo-and-downloads).

# Drug Perturbation Case Studies: Sciplex3, Tahoe-100M



This page walks through DeSCOPE's flagship drug perturbation workflow: pretraining on the full Tahoe-100M dataset (~50 billion cells across ~60,000 genes, hundreds of drugs, dozens of cancer cell lines), then transferring that model to the Sci-Plex3 benchmark via either **zero-shot inference** or **fine-tuning**. The workflow lives in `tutorials/RNA_Drug/` and exercises nearly every subsystem in the library — molecular drug encodings, chunked tokenization, accelerate-based training, and cell-eval-backed evaluation — making it the best end-to-end reference for intermediate developers.

## Case Study Workflow at a Glance

The tutorial is organized as two sequential phases. Phase 1 builds a general-purpose drug perturbation model from Tahoe-100M; Phase 2 evaluates that model on Sci-Plex3, a chemically *disjoint* dataset, which is what makes the zero-shot result meaningful. The entire pipeline hinges on one architectural idea: a perturbation is encoded as a **Uni-Mol2 molecular embedding of the drug's SMILES concatenated with a scalar normalized dose**, so the model can, in principle, respond to any drug expressible as SMILES — not just the ones seen in training.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph P1["Phase 1 · Tahoe-100M Pretraining"]
        A["Metadata download<br/>(drug / cell-line / gene / obs)"] --> B["Uni-Mol2 1.1B<br/>SMILES → 1536-dim CLS"]
        B --> C["Append normalized dose<br/>→ 1537-dim drug_dose_embed.pt"]
        D["HVGs/calc_hvgs.py + calc_freq.ipynb<br/>gene vocabulary selection"] --> E["2_tokenize.ipynb<br/>normalize_total(1e4) + log1p<br/>20-chunk tokenization"]
        C --> F["3_train.py<br/>DeSCOPETrainer<br/>10 epochs · batch 1024"]
        E --> F
    end
    F --> G[("HuggingFace Hub<br/>2k / 5k / 12059 HVGs")]
    subgraph P2["Phase 2 · Sci-Plex3 Evaluation"]
        G --> H["zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb<br/>feature alignment · dose calibration<br/>ground truth · drug embeddings"]
        H --> I{"Strategy"}
        I -->|"zero-shot"| J["2_inference.ipynb<br/>InferenceForRNA"]
        I -->|"fine-tune"| K["fine-tune/<br/>2_train.py → 3_inference.ipynb"]
    end
    J --> L["cell-eval metrics<br/>restricted to reliable genes"]
    K --> L
```

The repository layout mirrors this flow exactly:

```
tutorials/RNA_Drug/
├── sciplex3_evaluation/
│   ├── fine-tune/          # 1_prepare → 2_train.py → 3_inference (+ accelerate config, shell script)
│   └── zero-shot/          # 1_prepare.ipynb → 2_inference.ipynb
├── tahoe100m_pretrain/
│   ├── 1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb   # Uni-Mol2 drug/dose vectors
│   ├── 2_tokenize.ipynb                  # AnnData → HF datasets, chunked
│   ├── 3_train.py                        # full-dataset pretraining
│   ├── 4_test.ipynb
│   ├── HVGs/                             # per-plate 5k HVGs + merged 2k/5k/12059 vocabularies
│   ├── tahoe100m_drug_dose_embed.pt      # committed drug-dose embedding artifact
│   └── tahoe_100m_all_genes.pkl
└── scrna_drug_perturbation_performance.png
```

Sources: [README.md](tutorials/RNA_Drug/README.md#L1-L4), [README.md](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/README.md#L1-L2), [README.md](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/README.md#L1-L1)

## Pretrained Models and Gene Vocabularies

Tahoe-100M contains roughly **60,000 genes**, which is computationally prohibitive to model directly. The authors therefore built gene vocabularies via highly-variable-gene (HVG) selection and gene-frequency analysis (`HVGs/calc_hvgs.py`, `HVGs/calc_freq.ipynb`), and released three pretrained checkpoints — one per vocabulary size — so you can trade gene coverage against memory/compute. All three were trained for 10 epochs at batch size 1024.

| Pretrained Model | Gene Vocabulary File | Hugging Face Repo |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `descope-tahoe100m-2k-hvgs` | `tahoe100m_pretrain/HVGs/merged_2k_hvgs.pkl` | `wpp02/descope-tahoe100m-2k-hvgs` |
| `descope-tahoe100m-5k-hvgs` | `tahoe100m_pretrain/HVGs/merged_5k_hvgs.pkl` | `wpp02/descope-tahoe100m-5k-hvgs` |
| `descope-tahoe100m-12059-hvgs` | `tahoe100m_pretrain/HVGs/merged_12059_hvgs.pkl` | `wpp02/descope-tahoe100m-12059-hvgs` |

The vocabulary files are not just training artifacts — they are the **interface between the two datasets**. Sci-Plex3 preparation downloads a checkpoint, reads its `.pkl` vocabulary, and uses it to align genes before any model runs. Choose the vocabulary whose overlap with your downstream data is highest.

Sources: [README.md](tutorials/RNA_Drug/README.md#L8-L23)

## Phase 1: Tahoe-100M Pretraining

### Step 1 — Molecular Drug Embeddings via Uni-Mol2

Notebook `1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb` proceeds in three stages. First, it pulls four Tahoe-100M metadata parquet files from the Hub: `obs_metadata.parquet` (drug + dose per cell), `drug_metadata.parquet` (SMILES + target), `cell_line_metadata.parquet`, and `gene_metadata.parquet`. Second, it builds a drug-name → canonical-SMILES map over **378 drugs** — with one manual fix: control cells are labeled `DMSO_TF` in `obs_metadata`, but that "drug" is absent from `drug_metadata`, so its SMILES `"CSC(C)=O"` is inserted by hand. Third, it runs `unimol_tools.UniMolRepr` (the **Uni-Mol2 1.1B** model) on the SMILES list and extracts the CLS-token representation — a 1536-dim vector per drug.

The final stage turns a drug embedding into a *drug-dose* embedding. Tahoe-100M has exactly four dose levels — 0.0 μM (DMSO controls), 0.05 μM, 0.5 μM, 5.0 μM — and each dose is **max-normalized by 5.0** before being appended as a scalar to the embedding's last dimension:

```python
norm_dose = float(d / max_dose)
results[f"{drug}_{norm_dose}"] = torch.cat([embed, torch.tensor([norm_dose], dtype=torch.float32)])
```

Two guard clauses enforce semantics: non-control drugs skip dose 0, and `DMSO_TF` skips all non-zero doses. The result — `tahoe100m_drug_dose_embed.pt` — is a dictionary keyed by `"{drug}_{norm_dose}"` with 1537-dim tensors, exactly the format `HFDatasetForRNA` and `InferenceForRNA` expect from their `gene_embs_file` argument.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    S["Drug SMILES<br/>(378 Tahoe drugs + manual DMSO_TF)"] --> U["Uni-Mol2 v2 · 1.1B<br/>cls_repr"]
    U --> E["1536-dim vector"]
    D["Dose ∈ {0.0, 0.05, 0.5, 5.0} μM"] --> N["dose / 5.0 (max-normalize)"]
    N --> X["1-dim scalar"]
    E --> CAT["torch.cat → 1537-dim"]
    X --> CAT
    CAT --> V["drug_dose_embed.pt<br/>key: '{drug}_{norm_dose}'"]
    V --> M["consumed as gene_embs_file<br/>(training + inference)"]
```

Sources: [1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb#L77-L91), [1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb#L1208-L1218), [1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb#L1253-L1269), [1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb#L1276-L1284), [1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/1_extract_drug_embeddings.ipynb#L1335-L1352)

### Step 2 — Chunked Tokenization

Notebook `2_tokenize.ipynb` converts plate-level `.h5ad` files into HuggingFace datasets. The critical preprocessing function, `generate_condition_col_for_tahoe100m`, parses the `drugname_drugconc` column (a stringified tuple of drug name and dose), strips whitespace on `obs["drug"]`, **drops two problematic drugs** (`Sacubitril/Valsartan`, `Verteporfin`), and normalizes doses to the same `dose / 5.0` scale as Step 1, producing a `condition` column of the form `"{drug}_{norm_dose}"`. This means the tokenized dataset's perturbation keys and the drug-dose embedding dictionary share an identical naming convention — a silent but load-bearing contract.

Because Tahoe-100M plates are enormous, each AnnData is split into 20 row-chunks (bump `n_chunks` if chunk `.X` doesn't fit in dense memory), and per chunk the notebook manually applies `sc.pp.normalize_total(target_sum=1e4)` followed by `sc.pp.log1p`, filters columns down to the chosen vocabulary (e.g., `merged_2k_hvgs.pkl`), and calls the library tokenizer:

```python
tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_rna(
    adata=adata_chunk,
    cell_line_col="cell_line",
    target_sum=1e4,
    pert_col="condition",
    ctrl_name="DMSO_TF_0.0",
    save_dir=f".../Tahoe_100M/2k_hvgs/{plate}_chunk{i}"
)
```

Note the control name `DMSO_TF_0.0` — dose 0.0 marks the vehicle control, and this string becomes the reference condition the model trains against.

Sources: [2_tokenize.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/2_tokenize.ipynb#L36-L58), [2_tokenize.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/2_tokenize.ipynb#L83-L112)

### Step 3 — Training Script Anatomy

`3_train.py` is deliberately thin — it composes library primitives rather than implementing logic. It parses the three standard argument groups (`DeSCOPEDataArguments`, `DeSCOPEModelArguments`, `DeSCOPETrainingArguments`) via `HfArgumentParser`, then loads tokenized data in one of two ways: either the save directory is a single `load_from_disk` dataset, or — as produced by Step 2's per-plate, per-chunk outputs — each subdirectory is loaded and stitched together with `concatenate_datasets`. The `HFDatasetForRNA` wrapper then attaches the control name and the drug-dose embedding file at tensor-construction time.

A detail worth noticing: when training from scratch, the `DeSCOPEConfig` is *derived from the data itself* rather than hardcoded — `input_pert_gene_embedding_size` comes from `train_ds[0]["pert_gene_emb"].shape[-1]` (1537 here) and `input_length` from `train_ds[0]["labels"].shape[-1]` (the vocabulary size). This is what makes the same script work unchanged across the 2k/5k/12059 vocabularies. If `pretrained_model_name_or_path` is set instead, `DeSCOPEForRNA.from_pretrained` bypasses config construction — which is precisely the hook the fine-tuning phase exploits. Training is handed to `DeSCOPETrainer` together with `train_ds.collate_fn` and an accelerate config (`accelerate_config.yaml`, `train_descope.sh`).

Sources: [3_train.py](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/3_train.py#L22-L53), [3_train.py](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/3_train.py#L55-L91)

## Phase 2: Sci-Plex3 Evaluation

### Zero-Shot Preparation

The zero-shot track (`sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/`) demonstrates transfer to a dataset DeSCOPE never saw. Sci-Plex3 data comes from Hetzel et al. (2022) — `sciplex_complete_middle_subset.h5ad` from the chemCPA collection — and preparation in `1_prepare.ipynb` runs four ordered transformations:

1. **Normalization check.** `guess_is_lognorm(adata)` decides whether `normalize_total` + `log1p` should run; if applied, `target_sum` must equal **1e4** because that is what Tahoe-100M was pretrained with.
2. **Feature alignment.** `UniformFeatureForAnnData` (with `DuplicatedFeatureHandling.mean_pooling`) reorders/extends the AnnData's genes to exactly match the pretrained vocabulary — retaining overlapping genes, zero-padding missing ones. Before aligning, the notebook computes *gene coverage* — for the 12059-HVG model, only **482 of Sci-Plex3's 2,000 genes** overlap the vocabulary — and persists that intersection as `reliably_genes.pkl`. These are the "reliably predicted genes" that every later metric will be restricted to.
3. **Dose unit calibration.** Sci-Plex3 doses are in nM, Tahoe-100M in μM. The notebook sets control-cell dose explicitly to 0, converts nM → μM (`/1000`), then applies the same max-normalization (`/5`) used in pretraining, and builds a `drug_and_dose` condition column (`"{condition}_{dose_norm}"`).
4. **Ground truth + drug embeddings.** Per cell type, ground-truth AnnData files are written by concatenating OOD-split perturbed cells with control cells from the test split, alongside a `test_info_{celltype}.csv` template (rows: condition, cell count — matching the biolord convention). Finally, Uni-Mol2 embeddings are extracted for Sci-Plex3's own SMILES list, doses appended under the identical concat-and-key scheme, and saved as `drug_dose_embed.pt`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["sciplex3_biolord.h5ad<br/>(raw + SMILES + dose in nM)"] --> B["guess_is_lognorm<br/>normalize_total(1e4) + log1p"]
    B --> C["UniformFeatureForAnnData<br/>align to pretrained vocab<br/>pad missing genes w/ 0"]
    C --> D["reliably_genes.pkl<br/>(482/2000 @ 12059-HVGs)"]
    C --> E["dose: nM→μM, /5<br/>control dose := 0<br/>drug_and_dose column"]
    E --> F["per-cell-type ground truth<br/>OOD perturbed + test controls<br/>+ test_info CSV"]
    E --> G["Uni-Mol2 on Sci-Plex3 SMILES<br/>→ drug_dose_embed.pt"]
    F --> H["InferenceForRNA"]
    G --> H
```

Sources: [1_prepare.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L41-L44), [1_prepare.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L62-L77), [1_prepare.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L84-L127), [1_prepare.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L134-L198), [1_prepare.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L206-L244)

### Zero-Shot Inference and Metrics

`2_inference.ipynb` instantiates `InferenceForRNA` with the downloaded checkpoint directory, the ground-truth AnnData, the `test_csv_template` produced in preparation, `pert_col="drug_and_dose"`, `ctrl_name="control_0.0"`, `target_sum=1e4`, and `skip_raw_counts_check=False` (data is already log-normalized, so double normalization must be avoided). The single inference call passes the drug-dose embedding file and a batch size of 256:

```python
infer.inference(
    gene_embs_file="./drug_dose_embed.pt",
    device=torch.device("cuda:0"),
    batch_size=256,
    use_generated_control_cells=False
)
```

> [!TIP]
> **Always set `use_generated_control_cells=False` in perturbation evaluation** — the notebook flags this with double exclamation marks. Predictions are compared against *real* control cells, so letting the model hallucinate its own controls would contaminate every downstream metric.

Metric computation happens in two layers. First, the **built-in cell-eval metrics**: predictions and ground truth are subset to `reliably_genes.pkl`, then `infer.compute_metrics(...)` runs the selected list (Pearson on deltas, MSE/MAE and their delta variants, discrimination score, DE overlap/precision at N∈{50,100,200,500}, direction match, Spearman LFC on significant DE genes, PR-AUC/ROC-AUC) with Wilcoxon DE testing and results written to an output directory. Second, **extra metrics** from `infer.extra_metrics_func`: overall Pearson, Pearson delta on top-k DE genes (`topk=20`), and up/down-regulated direction match on top-k DE genes (`topk=100`).

| Layer | Function | Metrics | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Built-in | `infer.compute_metrics` | `pearson_delta`, `mse(_delta)`, `mae(_delta)`, `discrimination_score_l1`, `overlap_at_N`, `precision_at_N`, `de_direction_match`, `de_spearman_lfc_sig`, `pr_auc`, `roc_auc` | Computed on reliable genes only; Wilcoxon DE; results to `cell-eval-outdir/{celltype}` |
| Extra | `infer.extra_metrics_func.*` | `pearson`, `pearson_delta_on_topk_de` (k=20), `direction_match_on_topk_de` (k=100, split up/down) | Uses `evaluator.anndata_pair` and `real_de.csv` from the built-in run |

Sources: [2_inference.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/2_inference.ipynb#L20-L70), [2_inference.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/2_inference.ipynb#L89-L148), [2_inference.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/2_inference.ipynb#L155-L200)

### Fine-Tuning Alternative

If zero-shot quality is insufficient, the `sciplex3_evaluation/fine-tune/` directory (`1_prepare.ipynb` → `2_train.py` → `3_inference.ipynb`, plus `accelerate_config.yaml` and `train_descope.sh`) adapts the pretrained checkpoint to Sci-Plex3. The mechanism is already present in Phase 1's training script: passing `pretrained_model_name_or_path` switches `3_train.py` from scratch-training to `DeSCOPEForRNA.from_pretrained`, so fine-tuning reuses the identical script path with a Sci-Plex3 tokenized dataset. The tutorial README recommends this **pretrain + fine-tune** strategy as the default, precisely to avoid re-tokenizing Tahoe-100M redundantly; the alternative **DeSCOPE_LOO** leave-one-out strategy offers stronger task-specific adaptation but at a substantially higher compute cost.

Sources: [README.md](tutorials/RNA_Drug/README.md#L27-L31), [3_train.py](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/3_train.py#L75-L81)

## Cross-Dataset Consistency Invariants

The entire transfer workflow depends on a handful of numeric and string conventions being identical across both datasets. Violating any of them produces silently wrong results rather than errors:

| Invariant | Tahoe-100M (pretraining) | Sci-Plex3 (evaluation) | Enforced By |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Library size target | `normalize_total(target_sum=1e4)` + `log1p` | same (checked via `guess_is_lognorm`) | tokenizer / inference `target_sum` arg |
| Dose normalization | `dose / 5.0` (max 5 μM) | `dose / 1000 / 5` (nM → μM → norm) | condition-column builders |
| Control condition string | `DMSO_TF_0.0` | `control_0.0` | `ctrl_name` argument, dose-0 guard clauses |
| Control SMILES | manually added `CSC(C)=O` | from dataset's `SMILES` column | drug embedding dicts |
| Perturbation key format | `"{drug}_{norm_dose}"` | `"{drug}_{dose_norm}"` | `pert_col` + `gene_embs_file` keys |
| Gene ordering | merged HVG `.pkl` vocabulary | zero-padded alignment to same `.pkl` | `UniformFeatureForAnnData` |
| Metric gene subset | — | intersection AnnData ∩ vocab (`reliably_genes.pkl`) | subsetting before `compute_metrics` |

Sources: [2_tokenize.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/2_tokenize.ipynb#L36-L112), [1_prepare.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L62-L158), [2_inference.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/2_inference.ipynb#L20-L40)

## Performance Summary

The published result uses the 12059-HVG pretrained model on Sci-Plex3. Two interpretive notes from the authors matter when reading the figure: the model's metrics are calculated only on its 482 in-vocabulary genes out of Sci-Plex3's 2,000, and the zero-shot checkpoint shows notably high DE overlap — a known artifact of perturbation tasks, since **DE overlap on the validation set typically trends downward continuously during training**.

![scrna_drug_perturbation_performance](https://github.com/Peg-Wu/DeSCOPE/blob/main/tutorials/RNA_Drug/scrna_drug_perturbation_performance.png?raw=true)

> [!TIP]
> When benchmarking against this figure, replicate the gene-subsetting step exactly — metrics computed on all 2,000 genes instead of the 482 reliable genes are not comparable, because zero-padded genes contribute trivially easy predictions.

Sources: [README.md](tutorials/RNA_Drug/README.md#L33-L40)
