| Weighted MSE reduction (when `mse_weights` given) | `(w * e).sum(dim=-1).mean()` | `(w * e).mean()` |
| Dataset partner | `HFDatasetForATAC` (`MAIN_INPUT_NAME="ctrl_cell_tf_idf"`) | `HFDatasetForRNA` (`MAIN_INPUT_NAME="ctrl_cell_expr"`) |
| Inference partner | `InferenceForATAC` | `InferenceForRNA` |
| Default control label | `"control"` | `"non-targeting"` |

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L120-L160), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L202-L246), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L324-L334), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L381-L424)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    PG["pert_gene_emb<br/>(ESM2, 5120-d)"] --> ENCA["PertGeneEncoder<br/>configurable MLP — ATAC"]
    PG --> ENCR["Linear + LayerNorm<br/>hard-coded — RNA"]
    ENCA --> CATA["concat[ctrl, pert]"]
    ENCR --> CATR["concat[ctrl, pert]"]
    IN_A["ctrl_cell_tf_idf<br/>(ATAC, input_length)"] --> CATA
    IN_R["ctrl_cell_expr<br/>(RNA, input_length)"] --> CATR
    CATA --> CORE["Identical CVAE core:<br/>prior + posterior VariationalEncoders,<br/>VariationalDecoder, softplus, ELBO"]
    CATR --> CORE
```

The two `forward` methods read as mirrored pseudocode: embed the perturbation, condition the prior on (control, perturbation), condition the posterior on (ground-truth labels, perturbation), decode `(z, perturbation)`, apply `softplus`, then compose `alpha_mse_loss * mse + alpha_kl_loss * kl`. The KL term is computed identically in both classes inside `torch.amp.autocast(enabled=False)` on `.float()` tensors — a numerical-stability guard against bf16 mixed precision. The same mirroring holds for the `@torch.no_grad()` `inference` methods, where the posterior branch is dropped and samples are drawn from the prior directly.

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L138-L176), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L224-L262), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L162-L169), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L178-L196)

> [!TIP]
> When `mse_weights` is `None`, both variants reduce identically to a flat element-wise `.mean()` — but with weights enabled, ATAC sums across the gene axis before averaging over the batch, while RNA takes a global mean. The two reductions yield different loss magnitudes for identical inputs, so weighted-MSE checkpoints are **not** numerically comparable across variants without rescaling `alpha_mse_loss`.

## The PertGeneEncoder Divergence: Nominal, Not Architectural

The most visible code difference deserves scrutiny because it looks like an architecture change but behaves as one only under non-default hyperparameters. ATAC delegates to `PertGeneEncoder`, whose `build_mlp` call emits a single `Linear(5120, 672)` followed by `LayerNorm` when `n_layers=1` and `add_layernorm=True` — which is exactly what RNA hard-codes as a bare `nn.Sequential`. Under the tutorial defaults (`pert_gene_encoder_layers=1`, `add_layernorm=True`), the two encoders are functionally interchangeable; the practical difference is that ATAC's version responds to CLI overrides while RNA's is frozen at depth 1 regardless of config.

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L15-L33), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L209-L213), [utils.py](src/descope/models/utils.py#L119-L122), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L10-L17)

> [!TIP]
> If you raise `--pert_gene_encoder_layers` or disable `--add_layernorm` in the RNA tutorial, only the ATAC-style encoder would honor it — RNA's `nn.Sequential` ignores these flags by construction. Keep this in mind when writing ablation sweeps that must apply symmetrically to both modalities.

## The Modality Boundary: An Input-Naming Contract

The variant split is anchored by a naming contract enforced in the data layer. Each dataset subclass must define `MAIN_INPUT_NAME` — `HFDatasetForATAC` returns batches keyed by `ctrl_cell_tf_idf`, `HFDatasetForRNA` by `ctrl_cell_expr` — and the HF base dataset injects randomly sampled control cells from the same cell type under exactly that key (`batch[self.MAIN_INPUT_NAME] = ...`). Because the trainer passes batches straight into `model(**batch)`, the tensor names must match the model's `forward` keyword arguments; renaming one side without the other silently breaks training. The modality semantics behind these names are fixed upstream at tokenization: the ATAC entry point applies `preprocess_atac_perturbation_adata_consistent_with_epiagent` (top-`k` cCRE selection, TF-IDF scale) while the RNA entry point applies `preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata` (normalize-total to `target_sum=1e4`).

Sources: [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L175-L200), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L295-L313), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L324-L334), [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L146-L222), [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L225-L305)

## Training and Inference Pairing Matrix

Each modality follows the same four-stage pipeline — tokenize → dataset wrapper → model class → inference engine — with one class per stage per modality. The tutorial `train.py` scripts differ only in the imports and in the default `ctrl_name` (`control` for ATAC, `non-targeting` for RNA); both build `DeSCOPEConfig` dynamically from the first batch (`input_length = labels.shape[-1]`, `input_pert_gene_embedding_size = pert_gene_emb.shape[-1]`), so the same scripts adapt to any feature-space width without code edits. On the inference side, both `InferenceForATAC` and `InferenceForRNA` implement the same `load_model` / `preprocess_adata` hooks via `from_pretrained`; note that ATAC even derives its cCRE count from `model.config.input_length` at evaluation time, re-using the config as the single feature-space registry.

| Pipeline stage | ATAC variant | RNA variant |
|---|---|---|
| Tokenization | `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_atac` | `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_rna` |
| Training dataset | `HFDatasetForATAC` | `HFDatasetForRNA` |
| Model class | `DeSCOPEForATAC` | `DeSCOPEForRNA` |
| Inference engine | `InferenceForATAC` | `InferenceForRNA` |
| Tutorial directory | `tutorials/ATAC_Gene/` | `tutorials/RNA_Gene/` |

Sources: [train.py](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L5-L9), [train.py](tutorials/RNA_Gene/train.py#L5-L9), [train.py](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L52-L77), [train.py](tutorials/RNA_Gene/train.py#L52-L77), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L381-L424), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L6-L7), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/RNA_Gene/train_descope.sh#L6-L7)

## Maintenance Implications of the Twin-Class Pattern

Because the forward/inference bodies are duplicated rather than factorized, any behavioral change — say, altering the softplus output or the KL formulation — must be applied to both classes simultaneously to keep the modalities in sync; this is precisely the risk the two inline `NOTE` comments flag for future maintainers. The duplication buys independent evolution: hyperparameters, preprocessing, and loss weighting can drift per modality without a shared class accreting `if modality == ...` branches. If you plan to add a third modality, this twin-class template — config reuse, `MAIN_INPUT_NAME` contract, mirrored output dataclass, and paired tokenizer/inference classes — is the pattern to replicate, as detailed in [Extending DeSCOPE to New Modalities](24-extending-descope-to-new-modalities).

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L117-L118), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L199-L200), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L201-L283)

## Where to Go Next

The variant classes are thin modality shells around components documented in depth elsewhere: the Gaussian machinery lives in [Prior and Posterior Variational Encoders](9-prior-and-posterior-variational-encoders), the softplus output design in [Decoder and Softplus Output Design](10-decoder-and-softplus-output-design), and the ELBO composition (MSE + KL, including the `mse_weights` path) in [ELBO Loss: MSE and KL Composition](16-elbo-loss-mse-and-kl-composition). For the data half of the contract, see [Tokenization: AnnData to HuggingFace Datasets](12-tokenization-anndata-to-huggingface-datasets) and [Feature Alignment and Vocabulary Handling](14-feature-alignment-and-vocabulary-handling); for how these classes are exercised after training, continue to [Inference Pipeline Design](19-inference-pipeline-design). Configuration defaults are catalogued in [Model Configuration Reference](7-model-configuration-reference).


# Tokenization: AnnData to HuggingFace Datasets



This page explains how DeSCOPE converts single-cell perturbation data from the AnnData ecosystem into HuggingFace `datasets.Dataset` objects ready for training. It covers the core conversion primitive, modality-specific preprocessing (scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq), the two `Tokenizer` classes used in multi-dataset pretraining workflows, and how the resulting datasets are consumed by the training loader. By the end, you will understand the exact on-disk schema produced by tokenization and how to prepare your own `.h5ad` files correctly.

## What "Tokenization" Means in DeSCOPE

If you arrive from Geneformer or scGPT, calibrate your expectations first: DeSCOPE's "tokenization" performs **no vocabulary encoding and no rank-based token sequences**. Here, tokenization means packaging an AnnData object into a HuggingFace `datasets.Dataset` whose rows correspond to cells and whose columns form a fixed, loader-friendly schema. Each output row carries three features: `"labels"` (the cell's full expression vector as a list of floats), `"pert_gene"` (the perturbation label, e.g., a gene name or `"non-targeting"` for controls), and `"celltype"` (the cell line or cell type name). Normalization stays in expression space — `labels` holds log-normalized values, not integer token IDs.

This schema is a **strict contract** downstream: `HFBaseDataset._check_hf_dataset_features` raises a `ValueError` if any of `["labels", "pert_gene", "celltype"]` is missing from the dataset it loads, so any custom tokenization must produce exactly these columns. The perturbation label also connects to the ESM2 embedding lookup (`load_gene_embs`), where multi-gene perturbations must be joined with `+` (e.g., `"GeneA+GeneB"`) to be decomposed and mean-pooled into an embedding.

| Feature | Content | Type | Role at training time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `labels` | Expression vector per cell (dense) | list of floats → torch | Prediction target (perturbed profile) |
| `pert_gene` | Perturbation identifier or control label | string | ESM2 embedding lookup + control masking |
| `celltype` | Cell line / cell type name | string | Within-celltype control pairing |

Sources: [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L58-L143), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L95-L106), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L225-L235), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L438-L447)

## End-to-End Pipeline Architecture

The two public functional wrappers — `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_rna` and `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_atac` — compose the same five stages: load (accepting either a `.h5ad` path or an in-memory AnnData), modality-specific preprocessing, perturbation filtering, chunked HF Dataset construction, and `save_to_disk`. Both are exported from the package root alongside the class-based tokenizers, making them the intended entry points for single-dataset (fine-tuning) tokenization.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input: .h5ad path or AnnData"] --> B{Modality?}
    B -->|"scRNA-seq"| C["preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata:<br/>drop NaN perturbations,<br/>normalize_total(target_sum) + log1p"]
    B -->|"scATAC-seq"| D["preprocess_atac_..._consistent_with_epiagent:<br/>format check (1,355,445 cCREs, float dtype),<br/>top-k cCRE selection"]
    C --> E["_filter_perturbations:<br/>include/exclude lists,<br/>control condition always preserved"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset:<br/>build labels / pert_gene / celltype dicts"]
    F --> G["Chunked Dataset.from_dict<br/>+ concatenate_datasets"]
    G --> H["save_to_disk(save_dir)"]
```

The wrappers differ in their preprocessing hooks and defaults: the RNA path defaults to `pert_col="gene"`, `ctrl_name="non-targeting"`, and `target_sum=1e4` normalization, while the ATAC path defaults to `pert_col="perturbation"`, `ctrl_name="control"`, and a `topk_ccres=50000` peak selection. Both default to `save_dir="./tokenized_dataset"` and return the in-memory dataset in addition to persisting it.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L146-L222), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L225-L305), [__init__.py](/src/descope/__init__.py#L16-L20)

## Core Conversion: Chunked AnnData to Dataset

All pipelines funnel into `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset`, the single conversion primitive. It begins with parameter validation: `cell_line_name` and `cell_line_col` are mutually exclusive and one must be provided — either stamp every cell with one string, read per-cell labels from an `.obs` column, or pass a list matching `adata.n_obs`. The function then zips three parallel sequences into per-cell dictionaries: the expression row (calling `.toarray()` if `adata.X` is sparse), the whitespace-stripped perturbation labels, and the celltype assignments.

Memory management comes from the chunking loop: per-cell dicts are grouped into slices of `chunk_size` (default `20000`), each slice is merged column-wise by `_merge_list_of_dicts` (a `defaultdict(list)` transpose), converted with `Dataset.from_dict`, and the resulting chunk datasets are stitched together with `concatenate_datasets`. The chunk boundary is purely a construction-granularity control — the final object is one unified `datasets.Dataset` with Arrow-backed storage.

> [!TIP]
> Notice that the chunking only controls how HF `Dataset` objects are constructed; the per-cell dict list at [tokenizer.py L127-L134](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L127-L134) is materialized in memory first. For very large AnnData, the dominant memory cost is the sparse→dense `.toarray()` conversion, not the chunk loop — plan RAM for a fully dense expression matrix.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L108-L134), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L135-L143), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L50-L55)

## Perturbation Filtering Semantics

`_filter_perturbations` implements the include/exclude policy shared by every tokenization path (it is even imported by `dataset.py` for runtime filtering). The include and exclude lists are mutually exclusive — specifying both raises immediately — and specifying neither keeps all perturbations. Two safety behaviors matter in practice: the control condition is **always preserved** (it is force-appended to an include list and stripped from an exclude list), and perturbation labels are `.str.strip()`-ed before matching, so stray whitespace in `.obs` cannot silently drop cells. This is why the tutorial notebooks can pass `perts_to_exclude=load_gene_names_engine(...)` to hold out test perturbations without risking loss of the `non-targeting` baseline.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L19-L47), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L12)

## Modality-Specific Preprocessing

Preprocessing diverges sharply by modality because RNA and ATAC demand different mathematical invariants. For **scRNA-seq**, `preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata` first drops cells with missing perturbation labels, then applies library-size normalization (`sc.pp.normalize_total` with `target_sum`) followed by `log1p`. A subtlety lives in `skip_raw_counts_check`: with the default `False`, a heuristic (`guess_is_lognorm` from `wppkg`) inspects the data and *skips* normalization if it already appears log-normalized; setting `True` bypasses the check and unconditionally normalizes — safe only when you are certain the input holds raw integer counts, hence the notebook's warning.

For **scATAC-seq**, `preprocess_atac_perturbation_adata_consistent_with_epiagent` enforces compatibility with the EpiAgent feature space: a hard assertion that the matrix has exactly **1,355,445 cCRE columns** with continuous (float) values, i.e., global TF-IDF must already have been applied upstream. It then retains the top-`topk_ccres` peaks by total column-sum signal using a *stable* descending sort (`np.argsort(..., kind="stable")[::-1]`) — the stability guarantee makes top-k selection deterministic under ties — and finally removes cells with NaN perturbations.

| Aspect | scRNA-seq (`preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata`) | scATAC-seq (`preprocess_atac_..._consistent_with_epiagent`) |
|---|---|---|
| Input assumption | Raw counts (or already log-normalized) | EpiAgent-format: 1,355,445 cCREs, TF-IDF floats |
| Value transform | `normalize_total(target_sum)` + `log1p` | None (TF-IDF applied upstream) |
| Feature selection | None (alignment handled by `UniformFeatureForAnnData`) | Top-k by column-sum, stable sort |
| Cell filtering | Drop NaN perturbation labels | Drop NaN perturbation labels |
| Guardrail | `guess_is_lognorm` heuristic / `skip_raw_counts_check` | Hard shape + dtype `ValueError` |

Sources: [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L571-L637), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L467-L489), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L491-L520), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L523-L568)

## The Tokenizer Classes: Fine-Tune-Anchored Alignment

`TokenizerForRNA` and `TokenizerForATAC` serve the multi-dataset pretraining workflow (e.g., leave-one-out cell-type transfer). Their design rests on an **anchor principle**: the constructor takes one *fine-tune* cell line whose feature space and perturbation universe become the reference for every *pretrain* dataset tokenized afterward. `TokenizerForATAC.__init__` extracts `topk_ccres_list` (the processed `.var_names`) and `pert_genes_list` from the fine-tune AnnData; `TokenizerForRNA.__init__` analogously extracts `input_genes_list` and `pert_genes_list` (after dropping null-perturbation cells, and optionally re-keying `.var_names` from a `gene_names_col` for symbol harmonization).

Each `tokenize()` call then iterates over lists of pretrain datasets (with a `tqdm` progress bar and a length-consistency assertion), and per dataset: reads the h5ad, aligns its features to the anchor's gene/cCRE list via `UniformFeatureForAnnData`, filters cells, converts with the core primitive, and persists to a **per-dataset subdirectory** `save_dir/cell_line_name` — producing one HF Dataset folder per pretraining cell line, which is exactly the layout the training script expects.

Alignment deserves close attention. `UniformFeatureForAnnData` reindexes the matrix to the target feature names: features absent from the input are **zero-padded**, extra features are dropped, and duplicate feature names are resolved through the `DuplicatedFeatureHandling` strategy (sparse input is densified, and integer matrices are promoted to `float32` if mean pooling is selected, preventing silent truncation).

| Strategy | Behavior | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `max_pooling` (default) | Keep the duplicate with highest average expression | Duplicated gene symbols with one dominant assay probe |
| `mean_pooling` | Replace duplicates with their mean expression across cells | Collapse probes into consensus signal |

Ordering matters in `TokenizerForRNA._tokenize`, governed by `normalize_before_align_features`. When `True`, normalization runs *before* alignment (aligning log-normalized values); when `False` (default), alignment runs on raw counts first and normalization *after* — which is mathematically preferable because `normalize_total` should distribute library size across the final feature set, not a superseteing one. Critically, the perturbation column is **cached before** any transformation (`pert_genes` read from the file or AnnData up front) and re-assigned to `obs[pert_col]` after alignment, since `.var`-level reindexing could otherwise orphan row metadata. After alignment, cells are filtered against `pert_genes_list` when `apply_pert_gene_filter=True`; when `False`, all non-null perturbations are kept (the tutorial uses `False` for pretraining to maximize perturbation diversity).

> [!TIP]
> The ATAC tokenizer takes a stricter route than RNA: instead of zero-padding via `UniformFeatureForAnnData`, it subsets columns directly (`cell_line_pt[:, self.topk_ccres_list]` at [tokenizer.py L381](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L381)) and runs `check_adata_format_consistent_with_epiagent` first. This implicitly requires pretrain ATAC data to share the EpiAgent cCRE universe with the fine-tune anchor — missing cCREs raise errors rather than zero-fill.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L331-L360), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L467-L501), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L503-L568), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L570-L631), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L30-L116), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L25-L27)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph INIT["Tokenizer.__init__ — anchor from fine-tune cell line"]
        FT["cell_line_ft<br/>(.h5ad / AnnData)"] --> REF["input_genes_list / topk_ccres_list<br/>pert_genes_list"]
    end
    subgraph LOOP["tokenize() — per pretrain dataset"]
        PT["cell_line_pt[i]"] --> AL["UniformFeatureForAnnData:<br/>align to anchor features<br/>(zero-pad / drop / pool dups)"]
        AL --> ORD["normalize_total + log1p<br/>(order set by<br/>normalize_before_align_features)"]
        ORD --> PF["perturbation filter<br/>(apply_pert_gene_filter)"]
        PF --> DS["HF Dataset<br/>labels / pert_gene / celltype"]
        DS --> SAVE["save_dir / cell_line_name/"]
    end
    REF -.->|"feature space"| AL
    REF -.->|"perturbation universe"| PF
```

## Consuming Tokenized Datasets at Training Time

`HFBaseDataset` is the bridge between tokenized disk artifacts and the training loop, and its behavior explains *why* tokenization bakes in no control pairing. On construction it validates the three-feature schema, scans `pert_gene` and `celltype` columns to build per-celltype index dictionaries of control and perturbed cells (raising `ValueError` if any celltype lacks control cells), loads ESM2 embeddings for every unique `pert_gene`, and switches the `labels` column to torch format.

At batch time (`__getitems__`), each perturbed cell is paired with a **randomly sampled control cell from the same celltype** — control-to-control rows map to themselves unless `RANDOM_MAPPING_CONTROL_TO_CONTROL` is enabled. The assembled batch contains: the control expression vector under the modality-specific `MAIN_INPUT_NAME` (`"ctrl_cell_expr"` for RNA, `"ctrl_cell_tf_idf"` for ATAC), the stacked `pert_gene_emb`, `labels` (perturbed expression), plus the raw `pert_gene`/`celltype` strings; an optional `mse_weights` tensor joins if a weights pickle is provided. Note that `valid_indices` excludes control rows by default (`INVOLVE_CONTROL_TO_CONTROL = False`), so `len(dataset)` counts perturbed cells only. This pairing-at-batch-time design keeps tokenized files compact (no duplicated control vectors) while preserving stochastic control diversity across epochs.

The older `BaseDataset`/`DatasetForATAC`/`DatasetForRNA` family is explicitly marked `# Slow | Deprecated`: it keeps a full AnnData in RAM and assembles items lazily, whereas the HF path leans on Arrow-backed storage and batched indexing.

| Concern | Legacy `BaseDataset` family | `HFBaseDataset` family |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | Whole AnnData in memory | Arrow-backed `datasets.Dataset` from disk |
| Control pairing | Per-item `__getitem__` | Batched `__getitems__` |
| Preprocessing | Re-run at construction | Frozen at tokenization time |
| Status | `Slow \| Deprecated` | Current |

Sources: [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L175-L224), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L237-L266), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L268-L313), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L322-L334), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L22-L23)

## Practical Guidance from the Tutorials

The RNA tutorial notebook demonstrates both production workflows. **Workflow 1 (fine-tuning)** tokenizes each cell line independently with `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_rna`, passing `perts_to_exclude=load_gene_names_engine("Test_Info_{c}.csv")` so the held-out test perturbations never enter the training set — the loader utility handles both single-column gene lists and CSVs with a `target_gene` header. **Workflow 2 (leave-one-out pretraining)** instantiates `TokenizerForRNA` on the held-out cell line as the anchor, then tokenizes the remaining cell lines into `save_dir=.../loo_{cellline_ft}`, with `apply_pert_gene_filter=False` and `duplicated_features_handling=DuplicatedFeatureHandling.max_pooling`.

Four gotchas are flagged directly in the notebook's tips:

| Pitfall | Rule | Consequence if ignored |
|---|---|---|
| Control naming | Control labels in `.obs[pert_col]` must be **identical across all h5ad files** in a pretraining run | Per-celltype control lookup fails or silently splits control pools |
| `skip_raw_counts_check` | Set `True` only when certain data are raw counts | Double normalization (or skipped normalization) corrupts `labels` |
| Multi-gene knockouts | Concatenate symbols with `+` (e.g., `"GeneA+GeneB"`) | ESM2 embedding lookup treats the string as one unknown gene |
| Gene symbol sources | Use `gene_names_col` when `.var_names` are not symbols | Alignment zero-pads almost everything against the anchor |

Sources: [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L7-L21), [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L48-L62), [tokenize.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/tokenize.ipynb#L79-L103), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L330-L375)

## Where to Go Next

Tokenization is stage one of the DeSCOPE data pipeline; the natural continuation is [Perturbation Filtering and Preprocessing](13-perturbation-filtering-and-preprocessing), which dissects the filtering and normalization utilities introduced above, followed by [Feature Alignment and Vocabulary Handling](14-feature-alignment-and-vocabulary-handling) for a deep dive into `UniformFeatureForAnndata` and the ESM2 embedding registry. To see these artifacts in action, [Tutorial Pipeline: Tokenize, Train, Evaluate](4-tutorial-pipeline-tokenize-train-evaluate) walks the full workflow, and [Trainer and Accelerate Integration](15-trainer-and-accelerate-introduction) explains how `HFDatasetForRNA`/`HFDatasetForATAC` objects are wired into the training loop. For acquiring the input `.h5ad` files themselves, start from [Datasets Zoo and Downloads](3-datasets-zoo-and-downloads).

# Perturbation Filtering and Preprocessing



DeSCOPE treats perturbation filtering and value preprocessing as a distinct stage that runs **after** raw AnnData ingestion and **before** HuggingFace tokenization. This page explains how perturbation labels are selected, how control cells are protected from accidental removal, how expression values are normalized per modality, and how drug–dose perturbations are assembled into the composite identities the model consumes. Throughout, two modality pipelines exist in parallel — an scRNA-seq path and an ATAC-seq path — with modality-specific defaults for label columns and control names.

## Where Filtering Lives in the Pipeline

The end-to-end flow is uniform across modalities: validate and normalize expression values first, then apply the perturbation filter, then tokenize. This ordering is deliberate — normalization and feature selection can remove cells (e.g., NaN-labeled perturbations), so filtering against a *final* label set prevents you from tracking perturbations that no longer have any cells. Both the one-shot tokenizers (`tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_rna` / `..._for_atac`) and the deprecated in-memory `BaseDataset` classes follow this same preprocess → filter → tokenize sequence.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["Raw AnnData (.h5ad)"] --> B{"Modality"}
    B -->|"scRNA-seq"| C["preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata<br/>1. Drop NaN perturbation labels<br/>2. normalize_total(1e4) + log1p<br/>(skipped if already log-normalized)"]
    B -->|"ATAC-seq"| D["preprocess_atac_perturbation_adata_...<br/>1. Validate 1,355,445 cCREs + float dtype<br/>2. Keep top-k cCREs (stable sort)<br/>3. Drop NaN perturbation labels"]
    C --> E["_filter_perturbations<br/>include / exclude lists,<br/>control always preserved"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset<br/>columns: labels / pert_gene / celltype"]
    F --> G["HF Dataset saved to save_dir"]
```

Sources: [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L192-L222), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L274-L305), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L52-L71)

## The `_filter_perturbations` Contract

All explicit perturbation selection funnels through a single private function, `_filter_perturbations`, which enforces three rules. First, `perts_to_include` and `perts_to_exclude` are **mutually exclusive** — passing both raises a `ValueError`, and passing neither keeps every perturbation. Second, the control condition is **always preserved**: when including, `ctrl_name` is appended to the include list if missing; when excluding, `ctrl_name` is removed from the exclusion list. Third, labels are normalized via `.str.strip()` before membership testing, so trailing whitespace in `.obs` cannot silently fragment a perturbation group.

| `perts_to_include` | `perts_to_exclude` | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| set | set | `ValueError` — cannot specify both |
| `None` | `None` | All perturbations retained (logged) |
| set | `None` | Keep listed perturbations; `ctrl_name` auto-appended |
| `None` | set | Drop listed perturbations; `ctrl_name` auto-removed from exclusion |

> [!TIP]
> The whitespace stripping happens twice by design — once in `_filter_perturbations` and again inside `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset` when labels are written to the HF Dataset. This redundancy means a label like `"GeneA "` never survives to training as a distinct perturbation, which would otherwise split one group into two and corrupt downstream leave-one-out evaluation.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L19-L47), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L127-L134)

## Modality-Specific Preprocessing: RNA vs ATAC

The RNA path (`preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata`) performs two steps. It first prunes cells whose perturbation column is null, logging how many cells were removed. It then applies library-size normalization (`sc.pp.normalize_total` with `target_sum=1e4` by default) followed by `log1p` — **unless** the `guess_is_lognorm` heuristic detects the data is already log-normalized, in which case transformation is skipped. Setting `skip_raw_counts_check=True` bypasses the heuristic and forces normalization unconditionally, intended only when you know the input holds raw integer counts.

The ATAC path (`preprocess_atac_perturbation_adata_consistent_with_epiagent`) assumes the input is already value-transformed and instead validates structure: the feature axis must contain exactly 1,355,445 cCREs with continuous (float) values, as required by the EpiAgent reference implementation. It then reduces dimensionality via `select_topk_ccres`, which keeps the top-k cCREs ranked by total signal across cells using a **stable sort** so identical inputs always yield identical peak selections (default `topk_ccres=50000`). Finally, cells with NaN perturbation labels are dropped, mirroring the RNA NaN-pruning step.

| Aspect | scRNA-seq | ATAC-seq |
|---|---|---|
| Default `pert_col` | `gene` (tokenizers) / `target_gene` (legacy) | `perturbation` |
| Default `ctrl_name` | `non-targeting` | `control` |
| Value normalization | `normalize_total(1e4)` + `log1p`, guarded by `guess_is_lognorm` | None — input must already be TF-IDF float |
| Feature reduction | None here (deferred to vocabulary alignment) | Top-k cCREs by column-sum, stable sort (default 50,000) |
| Structural check | Log-normalization heuristic | Exact 1,355,445 cCREs + float dtype |
| NaN label pruning | Yes, with before/after counts | Yes |

> [!TIP]
> The two normalization flags have asymmetric semantics: `guess_is_lognorm` returning `True` **skips** normalization even when `skip_raw_counts_check=False`, while `skip_raw_counts_check=True` **always** normalizes. When preparing zero-shot evaluation data, the pretraining value of `target_sum` must be reproduced exactly — Tahoe-100M models were trained with `normalize_total=1e4`, and the Sciplex3 tutorial explicitly warns against deviating from it.

Sources: [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L571-L637), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L467-L488), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L491-L520), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L523-L568), [1_prepare.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L62-L77)

## Filtering Across the Three Execution Contexts

Perturbation filtering executes in three distinct contexts, each layering additional constraints on top of the shared `_filter_perturbations` contract. The module-level interaction looks like this:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Context1["Legacy in-memory (deprecated)"]
        DS["BaseDataset.__init__"] --> PA["preprocess_adata<br/>(abstract, per modality)"]
        PA --> F1["_filter_perturbations"]
        F1 --> CI["ctrl_cell_indices<br/>ValueError if empty"]
    end
    subgraph Context2["One-shot tokenizers"]
        T1["tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_{rna,atac}"] --> F2["_filter_perturbations"]
    end
    subgraph Context3["Pretraining tokenizers"]
        FT["Finetune adata defines<br/>pert_genes_list"] --> PT["Pretrain adata filtered<br/>via apply_pert_gene_filter"]
    end
```

**Context 1 — legacy in-memory datasets.** `BaseDataset.__init__` reads (or accepts) an AnnData, densifies sparse `X`, runs the modality-specific `preprocess_adata`, then applies `_filter_perturbations`. After filtering it computes `ctrl_cell_indices` and raises `ValueError("No control cells found!")` if the control group was eliminated — a downstream guard that catches over-aggressive include/exclude lists. Each `__getitem__` then samples a random control cell as the basal input and pairs it with the perturbed cell as the label, unless the cell itself is a control (in which case basal = label). The concrete subclasses wire in the modality defaults: `DatasetForRNA` uses `pert_col="target_gene"`, `ctrl_name="non-targeting"`, and `target_sum=1e4`; `DatasetForATAC` uses `pert_col="perturbation"`, `ctrl_name="control"`, and `topk_ccres=50000`.

**Context 2 — one-shot tokenizers.** `tokenize_adata_to_hf_dataset_for_rna` and `..._for_atac` are self-contained functions that accept a path or AnnData, copy it defensively, run the modality preprocessing, apply `_filter_perturbations`, tokenize into a chunked HF Dataset (default `chunk_size=20000` to bound memory), and persist to `save_dir`. Both docstrings guarantee that the control condition survives any include/exclude filter.

**Context 3 — pretraining alignment.** `TokenizerForRNA` and `TokenizerForATAC` invert the responsibility: the *finetune* dataset defines the canonical perturbation vocabulary (`pert_genes_list`, extracted from its `.obs` after dropping nulls), and every pretraining dataset is filtered to match. The `apply_pert_gene_filter` flag controls strictness — when `False`, all pretraining perturbations are kept (ATAC still drops NaN labels), enabling the model to see a broader perturbation space during pretraining than at finetune time.

| `apply_pert_gene_filter` | ATAC pretraining behavior | RNA pretraining behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `True` (default) | Keep only perturbations in finetune's `pert_genes_list` | Same — strict intersection |
| `False` | Keep all perturbations, drop NaN-labeled cells | Keep all perturbations, no extra filter |

The RNA tokenizer also exposes `normalize_before_align_features`, which toggles whether normalization happens **before** vocabulary alignment (normalize → align) or **after** (align → normalize) — relevant when duplicated gene names must be pooled before counts are transformed.

Sources: [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L37-L99), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L104-L171), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L146-L305), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L349-L360), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L380-L386), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L494-L501), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L559-L568)

## Cross-Dataset Perturbation Intersection

For cell-type transfer experiments, `intersect_adatas_for_celltype_transfer` implements a set-theoretic filter across two AnnData objects. It computes the intersection of source and target perturbation sets — optionally further constrained by the keys of a gene-embeddings `.pt` file, so only perturbations that actually have embeddings are kept — and asserts the control condition survives the intersection. Each side is then feature-aligned via `UniformFeatureForAnnData`, cell-filtered with `.isin(perts_to_keep)`, and cross-checked so both outputs share identical `var_names` ordering. The function writes `source.h5ad`, `target.h5ad`, and a `target_info.csv` listing each retained perturbation with its cell count — a manifest that later feeds evaluation and leave-one-out splits. Complementing this, `load_gene_names_engine` reads perturbation gene lists from single-column files or `target_gene`-keyed CSVs (deduplicating on load), providing the file-based counterpart for supplying explicit perturbation lists.

Sources: [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L206-L283), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L285-L327), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L330-L375)

## Perturbation Identity Preprocessing: Embeddings and Zero-Vector Fallback

Filtering determines *which* perturbations remain; a parallel step determines *what each perturbation means numerically*. `load_gene_embs` loads a `{gene_name: tensor}` dictionary and guarantees coverage for every perturbation present in the filtered AnnData (the legacy `BaseDataset` passes `adata.obs[pert_col].unique()` as `perts_to_emb`). Missing perturbations are never dropped here — they degrade gracefully:

| Perturbation form | Embedding resolution |
|---|---|
| Known single gene | Looked up directly from the `.pt` file |
| Unknown single gene | Zero vector, logged with count |
| Multi-gene (`GeneA+GeneB`) | Mean pooling over constituents, missing genes contribute zeros |
| Alias (`TAFAZZIN`/`TAZ`) | Alias injected so both spellings resolve |

This fallback design pairs with the filtering system: if you want *hard* coverage enforcement (no zero-vector perturbations at all), you intersect against the embeddings file via `intersect_adatas_for_celltype_transfer`; if you accept soft coverage, filtering alone suffices and the zero vectors absorb the gap.

Sources: [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L378-L464), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L68-L71)

## Case Study: Drug–Dose Perturbations in Sciplex3

Drug perturbation studies add a second axis — dose — that gene knockouts lack. The Sciplex3 zero-shot preparation notebook demonstrates the full drug preprocessing protocol. After confirming normalization state with `guess_is_lognorm` and aligning genes to the pretrained Tahoe-100M vocabulary (pad missing genes with zeros; overlap with the vocabulary becomes the "reliably predicted genes" set), dose values are calibrated: control cells get dose 0, and all doses are rescaled by `/1000/5` to convert nM to a μM-scale unit consistent with pretraining. Each cell then receives a composite label `drug_dose` (e.g., `dexamethasone_10.0`), which becomes the perturbation identifier the rest of the pipeline consumes.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["Sciplex3 h5ad"] --> B{"guess_is_lognorm"}
    B -->|"raw counts"| C["normalize_total(1e4) + log1p"]
    B -->|"log-normalized"| D["Skip transformation"]
    C --> E["UniformFeatureForAnnData<br/>align to pretrained vocabulary"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["Control dose ← 0<br/>dose_norm = dose / 1000 / 5"]
    F --> G["Composite label:<br/>condition + '_' + dose_norm"]
    G --> H["Uni-Mol2 CLS repr<br/>+ dose scalar appended<br/>→ drug_dose_embed.pt"]
```

The embedding step encodes the dose axis structurally: drugs receive a Uni-Mol2 CLS-token representation, and the normalized dose is **concatenated as an extra scalar** onto the embedding vector. The construction enforces dose-label discipline — non-control drugs never get a zero-dose entry and control never gets a non-zero one. Finally, ground-truth evaluation AnnData are assembled per cell type by concatenating non-control cells from the `ood` split with control cells drawn from the `test` split, and a `test_info` CSV template is generated listing each `drug_and_dose` target with cell counts (mirroring the biolord convention). This composite-label pattern is why the earlier whitespace stripping and control-preservation guarantees matter: every downstream consumer treats `drug_dose` strings exactly like gene perturbation labels.

Sources: [1_prepare.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L62-L127), [1_prepare.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L134-L157), [1_prepare.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L184-L198), [1_prepare.ipynb](/tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/1_prepare.ipynb#L206-L244)

## Parameter Quick Reference

| Parameter | Default | Defined in | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pert_col` | `gene` (RNA tokenizers), `perturbation` (ATAC), `target_gene` (legacy RNA) | tokenizer / dataset constructors | `.obs` column holding perturbation labels |
| `ctrl_name` | `non-targeting` (RNA), `control` (ATAC) | `_filter_perturbations`, datasets | Control label, always preserved by filters |
| `perts_to_include` / `perts_to_exclude` | `None` | `_filter_perturbations` | Mutually exclusive selection lists |
| `target_sum` | `1e4` | RNA preprocessing | Library-size normalization target; must match pretraining |
| `skip_raw_counts_check` | `False` | RNA preprocessing | `True` forces normalization, bypassing the log-norm heuristic |
| `topk_ccres` | `50000` | ATAC preprocessing | Number of highest-signal cCREs retained (stable sort) |
| `apply_pert_gene_filter` | `True` | Pretraining tokenizers | Restrict pretraining perturbations to finetune vocabulary |
| `normalize_before_align_features` | `False` | `TokenizerForRNA` | Normalize before vs. after vocabulary alignment |
| `chunk_size` | `20000` | All tokenizers | Cells per HF Dataset construction chunk |

Sources: [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L146-L305), [tokenizer.py](/src/descope/tokenizer.py#L570-L631), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L113-L171), [utils.py](/src/descope/utils.py#L523-L637)

## Where to Go Next

The filter output — a cleaned AnnData or a persisted HF Dataset with `labels` / `pert_gene` / `celltype` columns — is exactly what the tokenization machinery consumes; the chunked conversion mechanics are covered in [Tokenization: AnnData to HuggingFace Datasets](12-tokenization-anndata-to-huggingface-datasets), and the zero-padding / duplicate-gene-pooling details of `UniformFeatureForAnnData` belong to [Feature Alignment and Vocabulary Handling](14-feature-alignment-and-vocabulary-handling). To see how the surviving perturbation set is split for benchmarking, continue to [Leave-One-Out Evaluation Protocol](21-leave-one-out-evaluation-protocol); for how the filtered labels map to model-side perturbation conditioning, see [PertGene Encoder and ESM2 Embeddings](8-pertgene-encoder-and-esm2-embeddings).

# Feature Alignment and Vocabulary Handling



DeSCOPE must guarantee that every expression vector fed into the conditional VAE has an identical, positionally meaningful layout — column *i* must always refer to the same gene or cCRE, regardless of which dataset a cell originated from. This page dissects the machinery that enforces that contract: the **vocabulary anchor principle** (the fine-tune cell line defines the canonical feature space), the **alignment engine** that reindexes and zero-pads arbitrary AnnData objects into that space, the **duplicate-symbol resolution** strategies, modality-specific (RNA vs ATAC) alignment behavior, and the parallel **perturbation vocabulary** that maps target gene names to ESM2 embeddings.

Two distinct vocabularies operate simultaneously, and conflating them is the most common integration error:

| Vocabulary | Contents | Built by | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Input feature vocabulary** | Ordered gene symbols (RNA) or cCRE identifiers (ATAC) | `TokenizerForRNA` / `TokenizerForATAC` anchors | `UniformFeatureForAnnData` alignment → `labels` column → model `input_length` |
| **Perturbation vocabulary** | Target gene names (including `"GeneA+GeneB"` combos) | `ESM2_pert_features.pt` + `load_gene_embs` | `pert_gene_emb` column → model `input_pert_gene_embedding_size` |

Sources: [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L346-L347), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L378-L401), [train.py](tutorials/RNA_Gene/train.py#L52-L64)

## The Vocabulary Anchor Principle

DeSCOPE does not maintain a global vocabulary registry. Instead, the **fine-tune cell line** passed to a tokenizer's constructor becomes the single source of truth: its feature names and perturbation labels are frozen into anchor lists, and every pretraining dataset is subsequently projected onto them. The source code states this invariant explicitly: *"Other cell lines used for pretraining should retain the same topk-ccres and perturbation genes as cell line (finetune)"*.

Each tokenizer class extracts its anchors in `__init__` via `_get_inputs_and_perts_from_adata_ft`:

- **`TokenizerForATAC`** first routes the fine-tune AnnData through `preprocess_atac_perturbation_adata_consistent_with_epiagent` (format validation → top-k cCRE selection → NaN-perturbation removal), then records `topk_ccres_list` (the post-selection `var_names`) and `pert_genes_list` (unique values of the perturbation column).
- **`TokenizerForRNA`** drops cells with null perturbation labels, then records `input_genes_list` (the `var_names`) and `pert_genes_list`. Optionally, `gene_names_col` standardizes identifiers first, copying `cell_line_ft.var[gene_names_col]` over `var_names` so that alignment operates on gene symbols rather than Ensembl IDs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Anchor["Vocabulary Anchor — fine-tune cell line"]
        FT["AnnData (cell_line_ft)"]
        FT --> A1["input_genes_list / topk_ccres_list"]
        FT --> A2["pert_genes_list"]
    end

    subgraph Align["Per-pretraining-dataset alignment"]
        PT["AnnData (cell_line_pt)"]
        PT --> GN["gene_names_col → standardize var_names"]
        GN --> DUP{"Duplicated symbols?"}
        DUP -->|mean_pooling| MP["Average duplicate columns"]
        DUP -->|max_pooling| XP["Keep column with highest mean"]
        MP --> UF["UniformFeatureForAnnData"]
        XP --> UF
        UF --> AL["Reindex + zero-pad → aligned X"]
        AL --> RA["Re-attach obs perturbation column"]
        RA --> PGF{"apply_pert_gene_filter"}
        PGF -->|True| F1["Keep perts ∩ pert_genes_list"]
        PGF -->|False| F2["Keep all non-null perts"]
    end

    subgraph Emb["Perturbation vocabulary"]
        GE["ESM2_pert_features.pt"]
        GE --> LG["load_gene_embs"]
        A2 -. "requested perts" .-> LG
        LG --> Z["Zero-vector fallback"]
        LG --> MG["Mean-pool GeneA+GeneB"]
    end

    AL --> HF["HF Dataset: labels / pert_gene / celltype"]
    HF --> DS["HFDatasetForRNA / HFDatasetForATAC"]
    LG --> DS
    DS --> S0["train_ds[0]"]
    S0 --> CFG["DeSCOPEConfig: input_length = labels.shape[-1]<br/>input_pert_gene_embedding_size = pert_gene_emb.shape[-1]"]
    CFG --> MODEL["DeSCOPEForRNA / DeSCOPEForATAC"]
```

The downstream consequence is architectural: because alignment makes every tokenized dataset conform to the anchor, the model's input dimensions can be safely read off the **first training sample** at startup — `input_length` from `labels.shape[-1]` (the anchor vocabulary size) and `input_pert_gene_embedding_size` from `pert_gene_emb.shape[-1]` (the ESM2 dimension). There is no separate vocabulary checkpoint; the aligned data *is* the vocabulary contract.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L331-L360), [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L467-L501), [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L381-L386), [train.py](tutorials/RNA_Gene/train.py#L52-L64)

## Alignment Engine: UniformFeatureForAnnData

`UniformFeatureForAnnData` is the class that physically performs feature-space projection. Its contract, stated in the docstring, is to transform an input AnnData so it has *exactly* the target feature space: features present in the target but missing from the input are **filled with zeros**, features in the input but absent from the target are **dropped**, and feature order is rewritten to match the target list exactly. The class docstring includes a worked example: a 3-gene AnnData `['A','B','C']` aligned to target `['B','C','D']` yields column `'A'` dropped, `'B'`/`'C'` reordered into place, and `'D'` appended as an all-zero column.

The implementation is a vectorized gather, not a per-feature loop. In `__call__`:

1. `adata.var_names.get_indexer(target_feature_names)` resolves each target name to a source column position (or `-1` if missing).
2. A boolean `valid` mask filters out the `-1` positions.
3. A zero matrix of shape `(n_cells, len(target))` is allocated, and source columns are copied into the positions where `valid` is `True` — absent features remain zero by allocation.
4. The result is wrapped in a fresh `AnnData` whose `var_names` are the target names, and logging reports the overlap count and the number of zero-padded features.

Two operational caveats follow directly from the code. First, sparse matrices are densified at construction time (`X.toarray()`), so alignment on large datasets is memory-bound, not compute-bound. Second, the returned AnnData **contains only `X` and `var_names`** — the docstring warns that *all other attributes are cleared* — which has a direct consequence for the tokenizer pipeline described below. A `save()` method persists the aligned output, optionally converting to CSR sparse format to shrink file size.

> [!TIP]
> Because `UniformFeatureForAnnData` wipes `obs` and `var` during alignment, `TokenizerForRNA._tokenize` caches the perturbation labels *before* calling the aligner (reading `.obs[pert_col]` even in backed mode via `sc.read_h5ad(..., backed='r')` to avoid loading the full matrix) and re-attaches them afterward with `cell_line_pt.obs[pert_col] = pert_genes`. If you write custom alignment code, replicate this cache-and-restore pattern or your perturbation labels will silently vanish.

Sources: [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L30-L65), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L145-L184), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L186-L203), [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L516-L521), [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L541-L549)

## Resolving Duplicated Feature Names

Real-world genomics data routinely contains duplicated identifiers — multiple rows mapping to the same gene symbol, often from multi-mapping probes or per-transcript annotations. A `get_indexer`-based gather cannot tolerate duplicate source names, so `UniformFeatureForAnnData` resolves duplicates **eagerly, at construction time**, before any alignment occurs.

The `DuplicatedFeatureHandling` enum defines the two resolution strategies:

| Strategy | Mechanism (per duplicated name) | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| `mean_pooling` | Replace all duplicate columns with a single column containing the **per-cell mean** across them | Preserves aggregate signal; treats duplicates as redundant measurements of one locus |
| `max_pooling` *(default)* | Keep only the duplicate column with the **highest mean expression** across cells; discard the rest | Selects the dominant measurement; assumes other duplicates are lower-quality proxies |

> [!TIP]
> The duplicate resolution uses a subtle write-back trick: `var_names_make_unique()` renames duplicates to `feature-1`, `feature-2`, …, then `var_names.get_indexer(duplicated_features)` locates the first occurrence of each original name, and the pooled values are written into those first-occurrence columns. Note also the dtype guard: integer count matrices are promoted to `float32` when `mean_pooling` is selected, preventing silent integer truncation of fractional means.

The choice is plumbed through the full tokenizer stack: `TokenizerForRNA.__init__` and both `tokenize()` entry points accept a `duplicated_features_handling` parameter, and the class-level docstring example demonstrates `DuplicatedFeatureHandling.mean_pooling` for pretraining pipelines.

Sources: [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L25-L27), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L105-L143), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L72-L84), [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L455-L465)

## Modality-Specific Alignment: RNA vs ATAC

Although both tokenizers follow the anchor principle, the *mechanics* of alignment differ fundamentally between modalities, driven by the structure of each feature universe:

| Dimension | ATAC (`TokenizerForATAC`) | RNA (`TokenizerForRNA`) |
|---|---|---|
| Feature universe | Fixed: EpiAgent's 1,355,445 cCREs, validated before anything else runs | Open-ended: arbitrary gene symbol sets |
| Vocabulary reduction | Top-k cCREs by total column sum (`topk_ccres`, default 50,000) with **stable sort** for determinism | None — anchor vocabulary is whatever the fine-tune cell line has |
| Alignment operation | **Reorder-only** column subset: `cell_line_pt[:, self.topk_ccres_list]` | Full **reindex + zero-pad** via `UniformFeatureForAnnData` |
| Symbol standardization | Not applicable (cCRE IDs are shared) | `gene_names_col` rewrites `var_names` from a `var` column |
| Duplicate handling | Not required | `DuplicatedFeatureHandling` enum |
| Extra precondition guard | `check_adata_format_consistent_with_epiagent`: exact 1,355,445 columns, float dtype (TF-IDF applied) | Raw-counts heuristic via `guess_is_lognorm` during preprocessing |

The ATAC shortcut is deliberate and safe: since every ATAC dataset must pass the EpiAgent format check — which asserts *exactly* 1,355,445 float-valued columns — all pretraining and fine-tuning inputs draw from the same cCRE universe. No feature can be genuinely "missing"; only ordering can differ, so a reorder suffices and zero-padding never triggers. The top-k selection itself is deterministic by construction: `np.argsort(peak_sum, kind="stable")` descending, then a positional slice, ensuring identical cCRE sets across runs and datasets.

RNA, by contrast, has no shared feature universe — one dataset may use Ensembl IDs, another HGNC symbols, and a third may simply lack genes the anchor requires. Hence the full `UniformFeatureForAnnData` treatment with symbol standardization, duplicate pooling, and zero-padding, plus the perturbation-side filter (`apply_pert_gene_filter`) that intersects each pretraining dataset's target genes with `pert_genes_list`.

Sources: [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L467-L488), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L491-L519), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L523-L568), [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L379-L386), [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L535-L548)

## Normalization Ordering in the RNA Tokenizer

For RNA, the tokenizer exposes a flag that controls whether library-size normalization happens **before or after** feature alignment: `normalize_before_align_features` (default `False`). Both branches end in the same state — aligned features, normalized values, preserved perturbation labels — but the intermediate semantics differ:

| Branch | Order of operations | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `normalize_before_align_features=True` | `preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata` (normalize_total + log1p) **→** align features | Normalization denominators computed over the dataset's *full* gene space; missing genes zero-padded *after* normalization |
| `normalize_before_align_features=False` *(default)* | Align features on raw counts **→** normalize_total + log1p | Normalization denominators computed over the *aligned* (anchor) gene space; zero-padded columns participate in normalization |

The relevant preprocessor, `preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata`, removes NaN-perturbation cells and then applies `sc.pp.normalize_total(target_sum)` + `sc.pp.log1p` — skipping normalization only if the heuristic `guess_is_lognorm` detects already-log-normalized data (unless `skip_raw_counts_check=True` forces unconditional normalization). This means both ordering branches still require count-like input, and the flag is purely about *which columns are present* when per-cell sums are computed — a decision that materially changes expression magnitudes for cells with substantial expression outside the anchor vocabulary.

Sources: [tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L523-L557), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L571-L637)

## Perturbation Vocabulary: ESM2 Embedding Lookup

The second vocabulary maps perturbation labels to dense conditioning vectors. The canonical store is a `.pt` file of `{gene_name: embedding_tensor}` (ESM2 protein embeddings), loaded by `load_gene_embs` with a specific set of requested perturbations. The function enforces **total coverage**: every requested perturbation gets an entry in the returned dict, using fallback logic for gaps:

| Requested perturbation case | Resolution |
|---|---|
| Present in the embedding file | Returned as-is |
| Single gene, absent from file | **Zero vector** (dimension taken from any existing embedding) |
| Multi-gene combo `"GeneA+GeneB"`, some constituents missing | Per-gene vectors (zero for missing constituents) **mean-pooled** into one embedding |
| Alias gap (`TAZ` missing, `TAFAZZIN` present) | `TAZ` seeded by copying the `TAFAZZIN` tensor |

Every fallback is logged with exact counts — how many single-gene perturbations were zero-filled, and for which multi-gene combos which constituents were missing — so silent degradation of conditioning signal is at least *observable* degradation. The multi-gene convention (`+` separator, mean pooling over constituent embeddings including zeros) means combo perturbations are supported without schema changes.

The perturbation vocabulary flows into training through two hops. First, `HFBaseDataset.__init__` calls `load_gene_embs` with `perts_to_emb=self.ds.unique("pert_gene")` — the set of labels actually present in the tokenized data — guaranteeing no `KeyError` at sample time. Second, each batch fetch re-stacks per-sample embeddings: `batch["pert_gene_emb"] = torch.stack([self.gene_embs[g] for g in batch["pert_gene"]])`. For constructing custom perturbation vocabularies or lists, `load_gene_names_engine` provides tolerant file loading (single-column TXT/CSV, or multi-column CSV keyed by a `target_gene` header, with deduplication).

Sources: [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L378-L464), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L198-L205), [dataset.py](src/descope/dataset.py#L277-L286), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L330-L375)

## Vocabulary Intersection for Cell-Type Transfer

A third alignment scenario arises when transferring a model between two datasets (e.g., predicting perturbation responses in a new cell type): **both** sides must land on a shared vocabulary. `intersect_adatas_for_celltype_transfer` computes the joint intersection and produces mutually aligned artifacts:

1. **Perturbation intersection**: `source_perts ∩ target_perts`, optionally further constrained to `set(gene_embs.keys()) ∪ {ctrl_name}` if an embedding file is supplied — preventing the transfer from including perturbations that would silently become zero-vector conditions.
2. **Feature intersection**: `source_features ∩ target_features`, using `feature_names_col` if identifiers live in a `var` column.
3. Each AnnData is aligned to `features_to_keep` via `UniformFeatureForAnnData`, perturbation labels are re-attached, then cells and columns are filtered to the intersections.
4. A hard assertion verifies `source.var_names == target.var_names` element-wise before anything is written.
5. Outputs: `source.h5ad`, `target.h5ad`, and `target_info.csv` (per-perturbation cell counts for the target), with an assertion that control cells survived the intersection.

This utility is the eval-side counterpart of the anchor principle: instead of one dataset projecting onto another's vocabulary, two datasets negotiate a common one.

Sources: [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L206-L283), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L285-L327)

## Key Invariants Summary

Across all alignment paths, five invariants hold and are directly enforced in code:

1. **Positional identity** — after alignment, `var_names` equal the target list in order; feature position ⟺ feature identity ([utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L174-L179)).
2. **Zero-padding for gaps** — absent features are zeros, never dropped silently or resampled ([utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L172-L177)).
3. **Determinism** — ATAC top-k uses stable sorting; alignment ordering is exactly the anchor list ([utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L515-L519)).
4. **Perturbation label preservation** — labels are cached before alignment and restored after, since aligners clear `obs` ([tokenizer.py](src/descope/tokenizer.py#L541-L549)).
5. **Dimensions derived from data** — model `input_length` and `input_pert_gene_embedding_size` are read from the first aligned sample, making alignment errors surface immediately as shape mismatches rather than silent corruption ([train.py](tutorials/RNA_Gene/train.py#L54-L64)).

## Where to Go Next

- For how the aligned `labels` vectors become HF Dataset columns and get chunked into memory-safe batches, see [Tokenization: AnnData to HuggingFace Datasets](12-tokenization-anndata-to-huggingface-datasets).
- For the normalization and perturbation-filtering steps that surround alignment, see [Perturbation Filtering and Preprocessing](13-perturbation-filtering-and-preprocessing).
- For how `pert_gene_emb` is encoded inside the model, see [PertGene Encoder and ESM2 Embeddings](8-pertgene-encoder-and-esm2-embeddings).
- For how the derived `input_length` interacts with architecture hyperparameters, see [Model Configuration Reference](7-model-configuration-reference).
- For applying alignment when adapting pretrained checkpoints to new datasets, see [Zero-Shot and Fine-Tuning Workflows](22-zero-shot-and-fine-tuning-workflows).
- For adding a new modality with its own vocabulary rules, see [Extending DeSCOPE to New Modalities](24-extending-descope-to-new-modalities).


# Trainer and Accelerate Integration



DeSCOPE's training system does not reinvent distributed training — it delegates hardware orchestration to **HuggingFace Accelerate** through a thin, domain-specific trainer layer. This page explains how `DeSCOPETrainer` composes with the external `wppkg` trainer library and the Accelerator runtime to deliver a single code path that runs identically on one GPU, multi-GPU DDP, and DeepSpeed. You will learn the inheritance contract, the launch chain, the training-step mechanics under gradient accumulation, and the distributed control signals (loss reduction, early stopping, checkpoint/resume) that make it all work.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L1-L47), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L20-L26)

## Architectural Role: Where the Trainer Sits

The training stack is layered so that each tier owns exactly one concern. The `accelerate launch` CLI spawns the tutorial script with a distributed topology; `train.py` parses arguments and builds the dataset and model; `DeSCOPETrainer` implements the *domain* training loop (ELBO bookkeeping, evaluation cadence, early stopping); and the inherited base `Trainer` from `wppkg` performs the *mechanical* Accelerate work — preparing the model, dataloaders, optimizer, and scheduler. Everything below that line is Accelerate's responsibility.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Launcher["Process Launcher"]
        AL["accelerate launch<br/>--config_file accelerate_config.yaml<br/>--num_processes N"]
    end
    subgraph Script["Tutorial Script — train.py"]
        HP["HfArgumentParser<br/>(Data + Model + Training args)"]
        DS["HFDatasetForATAC"]
        MD["DeSCOPEForATAC model"]
    end
    subgraph Domain["Domain Layer — descope.trainer"]
        DT["DeSCOPETrainer<br/>train() / evaluate()"]
    end
    subgraph Infra["Infrastructure Layer — wppkg.dl"]
        BT["Trainer (base)<br/>prepare() model, loaders,<br/>optimizer, scheduler"]
    end
    subgraph Runtime["Acceleration Runtime"]
        AC["Accelerator<br/>device · backward · reduce<br/>save_state · log"]
    end
    subgraph Backend["Execution Backends"]
        SP["Single GPU"]
        MG["MULTI_GPU (DDP)"]
        DSPEED["DEEPSPEED"]
    end
    AL --> HP --> DS --> MD --> DT --> BT --> AC
    AC --> SP
    AC --> MG
    AC --> DSPEED
```

The backend selection is entirely declarative: the tutorial's `accelerate_config.yaml` flips a single `distributed_type` field between `MULTI_GPU` and `DEEPSPEED`, and the trainer code itself never changes.

Sources: [train.py](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L17-L91), [accelerate_config.yaml](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/accelerate_config.yaml#L1-L3), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L52-L58)

## The Inheritance Contract: DeSCOPETrainer over wppkg's Trainer

`DeSCOPETrainer` subclasses `wppkg.dl.Trainer`, and its constructor does exactly one thing before handing control back: it inspects the **unwrapped** model's forward signature. This produces `model_forward_keys`, the canonical list of keyword arguments the model actually accepts — a fact that becomes crucial later when filtering batches (see [Batch Key Filtering](#batch-key-filtering-the-model_forward_keys-mechanism)). Because the base `Trainer` is an external library (pinned at `wppkg==0.1.4`), the base class's internals live outside this repository — but its observable contract is fully inferable from how `DeSCOPETrainer` consumes it:

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class TrainingArguments {
        <<wppkg.dl>>
        +output_dir
        +mixed_precision
        +with_tracking
        +checkpointing_steps
    }
    class DeSCOPETrainingArguments {
        +alpha_mse_loss: float
        +alpha_kl_loss: float
        +pretrained_model_name_or_path
    }
    TrainingArguments <|-- DeSCOPETrainingArguments
    class Trainer {
        <<wppkg.dl>>
        +accelerator: Accelerator
        +model: prepared model
        +train_dataloader
        +eval_dataloader
        +optimizer
        +lr_scheduler
        +earlystop_callback
        +_save(path)
    }
    class DeSCOPETrainer {
        +model_forward_keys: list
        +train()
        +evaluate()
    }
    Trainer <|-- DeSCOPETrainer
    Trainer o-- Accelerator : owns
    DeSCOPETrainingArguments ..> DeSCOPETrainer : args=
```

The verifiable base-class contract, as consumed by `DeSCOPETrainer`, is summarized below. This table is the effective "API" your custom loops can rely on:

| Member | Type | Role in DeSCOPE's loop |
|---|---|---|
| `self.accelerator` | `Accelerator` | Every distributed operation: device, backward, reduce, save/load, logging |
| `self.model` | Prepared model | Already wrapped for the active backend; trained with `.train()` / `.eval()` |
| `self.train_dataloader` | Prepared loader | Sharded across processes by Accelerate |
| `self.eval_dataloader` | Prepared loader (optional) | Drives epoch-end evaluation when present |
| `self.optimizer` / `self.lr_scheduler` | Prepared objects | Stepped once per optimization step in the loop |
| `self.earlystop_callback` | Callback (optional) | Queried after each evaluation |
| `self.num_update_steps_per_epoch` | `int` | Used to reconstruct `completed_steps` on resume |
| `self._save(path)` | Method | Serializes the model artifact next to Accelerate state |
| `self.logger` | `Logger` | File-based, rank-aware logging (see below) |

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L35-L47), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L80-L200), [arguments.py](src/descope/arguments.py#L7-L22), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L23)

## Distributed-Aware Logging via Monkey Patching

One subtle integration detail: DeSCOPE patches the base Trainer's logger initialization at import time (`Trainer._init_logger = _init_logger`). The patched logger directs all training output to `run.log` inside `output_dir`, and it partitions verbosity by rank — the **main process** logs at `INFO` while **other processes** log only at `WARN`, keyed off `self.accelerator.local_process_index`. Console handlers are then silenced so the terminal stays clean even with many workers writing concurrently.

This is why every log line in the training loop can be written unconditionally: rank partitioning happens inside the logger, not at each call site. The progress bar, by contrast, is guarded explicitly with `disable=not self.accelerator.is_local_main_process`, so only one tqdm instance animates per machine.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L11-L32), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L62)

## The Launch Chain: From CLI to TrainingArguments

Configuration flows through three independent layers, each with a distinct scope. `HfArgumentParser` consumes the three dataclass groups in `train.py`; `DeSCOPETrainingArguments` merely **extends** `wppkg.dl.TrainingArguments` with three ELBO-specific fields, inheriting the full training surface (batch size, mixed precision, tracking, checkpointing, dataloader tuning) from the base library.

| Layer | File(s) | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| Distributed topology | `accelerate_config.yaml` | `distributed_type` (`MULTI_GPU` / `DEEPSPEED`), process count |
| Training behavior | `DeSCOPETrainingArguments` (via `wppkg`) | Precision, LR schedule, accumulation, tracking, checkpoint cadence |
| Model & data | `DeSCOPEModelArguments`, `DeSCOPEDataArguments` | Architecture dims, dataset paths, control-cell name, ESM2 embeddings |

The shell launcher wires these together — note how mixed precision (`--mixed_precision=bf16`) and experiment tracking (`--with_tracking=True --report_to=tensorboard`) are ordinary training-argument flags, not backend-specific settings. This is the Accelerate design philosophy: backend strategy lives in the config file, behavior lives in arguments.

Sources: [arguments.py](src/descope/arguments.py#L6-L22), [train.py](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L18-L22), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L27-L48), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L52-L58)

## The Training Step: Gradient Accumulation and Synchronization

The heart of the integration is the per-step sequence inside `train()`. Each micro-batch runs inside Accelerate's `accumulate(model)` context manager, which transparently suppresses gradient synchronization until the last micro-batch of the accumulation window. Every raw-PyTorch idiom has been replaced with its Accelerate counterpart:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant L as Training loop
    participant AC as Accelerator
    participant MD as Model (wrapped)
    participant OPT as Optimizer + Scheduler

    L->>AC: accumulate(model) — enter context
    L->>L: filter batch → model_forward_keys
    L->>MD: model(**filtered_batch)
    MD-->>L: loss, mse_loss, kl_loss
    L->>AC: backward(loss)
    Note over L,AC: sync_gradients = False while accumulating
    Note over L,AC: On final micro-batch: sync_gradients = True
    L->>AC: clip_grad_norm_(params, max_grad_norm)
    L->>OPT: step() → lr_scheduler.step() → zero_grad()
    L->>AC: reduce(loss/mse/kl, "mean") for logging
```

| Concern | Plain PyTorch | DeSCOPE (Accelerate API) |
|---|---|---|
| Device placement | `.to("cuda")` | `k.to(self.accelerator.device)` |
| Backpropagation | `loss.backward()` | `self.accelerator.backward(loss)` |
| Accumulation window | Manual micro-step counting | `with self.accelerator.accumulate(self.model)` |
| Gradient clipping | Unconditional | `clip_grad_norm_` **only when `sync_gradients`** |
| Cross-process loss averaging | Manual all-reduce | `accelerator.reduce(loss, "mean")` |
| Step counting | Manual | `completed_steps` incremented only when `sync_gradients` |

> [!TIP]
> The gradient-clipping guard at `if self.accelerator.sync_gradients` is not decorative — clipping per micro-batch would clip *unsynchronized* partial gradients with the wrong norm scale. Gating on `sync_gradients` guarantees clipping fires exactly once per optimization step, on the fully reduced gradient. The same gate drives progress-bar updates and checkpoint cadence, giving a single source of truth for "an optimization step occurred."

The logged total batch size makes the math explicit: `per_device_train_batch_size × accelerator.num_processes × gradient_accumulation_steps` — three independently tunable dimensions reported in the startup banner so you can verify effective batch scaling before the first step runs.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L49-L134), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L51-L58)

## Batch Key Filtering: The `model_forward_keys` Mechanism

Dataloaders carry keys the model must not see — dataset metadata, collation artifacts, auxiliary fields. Rather than hard-coding a key whitelist, `DeSCOPETrainer.__init__` reflects over the unwrapped model's forward signature:

```python
unwrapped_model = self.accelerator.unwrap_model(self.model)
self.model_forward_keys = list(inspect.signature(unwrapped_model.forward).parameters.keys())
```

Then in both `train()` and `evaluate()`, each batch is filtered: `{k: v.to(device) for k, v in batch.items() if k in self.model_forward_keys}`. This makes the trainer forward-compatible with any `DeSCOPE*` model variant — the batch contract is discovered, not declared.

> [!TIP]
> The `unwrap_model()` call matters: under DDP or DeepSpeed the trainer holds an Accelerate-wrapped model whose signature does not match the raw forward. Inspecting the *unwrapped* model guarantees the filter matches what `model(**kwargs)` ultimately dispatches to, regardless of backend. This is also why moving tensors to `accelerator.device` happens during filtering — one pass does key selection and device placement.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L44-L47), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L110-L116), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L208-L213)

## Distributed Loss Accounting: Reduce vs. Gather

DeSCOPE uses two distinct Accelerate aggregation primitives, chosen by purpose. During **training**, per-step losses are aggregated with `accelerator.reduce(loss.detach().clone(), "mean")` immediately at each step, then averaged over `logging_steps` by an `Accumulator` and enriched with `grad_norm` and the current learning rate before hitting the logger (and `accelerator.log` for TensorBoard when `with_tracking` is enabled). During **evaluation**, losses are accumulated per-process and joined with `accelerator.gather_for_metrics`, which handles the classic DDP pitfall of uneven final batches before the cross-process `torch.mean(torch.cat(...))`.

| Phase | Primitive | When | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Training logging | `accelerator.reduce(x, "mean")` | Every step | Rank-mean of current micro-batch losses |
| Evaluation metrics | `accelerator.gather_for_metrics(x)` | End of epoch | Uniformly gathered, drop-corrected metric set |
| Experiment tracking | `accelerator.log(dict, step=…)` | On `logging_steps` / epoch end | Forwards to TensorBoard etc. |

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L129-L153), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L205-L226)

## Early Stopping as a Distributed Control Signal

Early stopping is the one place where control flow itself must reach consensus across processes. After each evaluation, `earlystop_callback.check_early_stopping(eval_loss)` runs on every rank; if the metric has not improved, the local process calls `accelerator.set_trigger()`. Every rank then consults `accelerator.check_trigger()` — Accelerate's internally synchronized flag — so **all processes break out of the epoch loop together**, preventing the deadlock scenario where some ranks keep iterating a sharded dataloader while others have exited.

Note the documented caveat in the class docstring: early stopping is not resume-aware (a resumed run reinitializes the callback), and enabling it requires `eval_every_n_epochs` and `checkpointing_steps` to be aligned since the trainer does not auto-save the best model. The final `last_model` is always saved even when stopping triggers early.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L36-L43), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L166-L182), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L199-L203)

## Checkpoint Hooks and Resume Mechanics

Checkpointing is delegated to Accelerate's state system: interval checkpoints call `accelerator.save_state(dir)` for optimizer/scheduler/RNG state, followed by `self._save(os.path.join(dir, "model"))` for the model artifact. Two cadences coexist: integer `checkpointing_steps` fire per optimization step, while string values like `"epoch-10"` fire every N epochs (parsed at [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L184-L197)).

Resume reconstructs progress by parsing the checkpoint folder name — `epoch_{i}` or `step_{i}` — then calling `accelerator.load_state()`. For step-based resumes, the tricky part is intra-epoch position: `resume_step` is converted back through `gradient_accumulation_steps`, and the dataloader is advanced with `accelerator.skip_first_batches(train_dataloader, resume_step)` so sharded sampling continues exactly where it stopped. Deep checkpointing semantics and the best-model trade-offs are covered on the dedicated page.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L66-L96), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L102-L106), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L155-L161)

## Launch Configuration Reference

The full single-GPU launch recipe from the ATAC tutorial, grouped by concern. Swap `distributed_type` to `DEEPSPEED` in the YAML and add a DeepSpeed config file to scale out (details on the DeepSpeed page):

| Group | Flag | Example | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Precision & tracking** | `--mixed_precision` | `bf16` | Accelerate autocast policy |
| | `--with_tracking` / `--report_to` | `True` / `tensorboard` | Routes `accelerator.log` calls |
| **Optimization** | `--learning_rate` / `--lr_scheduler_type` | `1e-4` / `cosine` | Scheduler construction |
| | `--num_warmup_ratio` / `--weight_decay` | `0.1` / `1e-2` | Schedule shape & regularization |
| | `--max_grad_norm` | `1.0` | Clipping ceiling (sync-gated) |
| | `--gradient_accumulation_steps` | `1` | Micro-batches per optimization step |
| **Throughput** | `--per_device_train_batch_size` | `64` | Per-process batch size |
| | `--dataloader_num_workers` / `--dataloader_prefetch_factor` | `16` / `2` | Loader parallelism |
| | `--dataloader_pin_memory` / `--dataloader_persistent_workers` | `True` / `True` | H2D transfer & worker reuse |
| **Cadence** | `--logging_steps` / `--checkpointing_steps` | `50` / `epoch-10` | Log & checkpoint intervals |
| | `--eval_every_n_epochs` | — | Epoch-end evaluation frequency |
| **Loss weighting** | `--alpha_mse_loss` / `--alpha_kl_loss` | `1.0` / `1.0` | ELBO term coefficients |

Launch command shape:

```bash
accelerate launch \
    --config_file="./accelerate_config.yaml" \
    --num_processes=1 \
    train.py \
    $TRAINPARAMS $DATAPARAMS $MODELPARAMS
```
