Sources: [train_descope.sh](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L10-L58), [accelerate_config.yaml](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/accelerate_config.yaml#L1-L3)

## Summary and Reading Progression

The integration philosophy is strict separation of concerns: **wppkg's `Trainer`** owns Accelerate preparation, **`DeSCOPETrainer`** owns domain logic (ELBO accounting, evaluation cadence, distributed early stopping), and **Accelerate** owns all hardware semantics. Because every hardware-dependent operation routes through `self.accelerator`, the identical loop serves single-GPU, DDP, and DeepSpeed backends with zero code branching in `descope/trainer.py` itself.

Where to go next in the Training System track:

- Understand what `loss`, `mse_loss`, and `kl_loss` actually compute: [ELBO Loss: MSE and KL Composition](16-elbo-loss-mse-and-kl-composition)
- Master the save/resume/early-stop lifecycle you just saw summarized: [Checkpointing, Resuming, Early Stopping](17-checkpointing-resuming-early-stopping)
- Scale this loop across nodes with ZeRO: [Distributed Training with DeepSpeed](18-distributed-training-with-deepspeed)
- For the model whose forward signature drives `model_forward_keys`: [Model Configuration Reference](7-model-configuration-reference)
- To see this trainer inside an end-to-end workflow: [Tutorial Pipeline: Tokenize, Train, Evaluate](4-tutorial-pipeline-tokenize-train-evaluate)


# ELBO Loss: MSE and KL Composition



This page dissects how DeSCOPE turns its conditional VAE's probabilistic objective into concrete tensor operations: an **α-weighted sum of an MSE reconstruction term and an analytic KL divergence term**, computed inside the model forward pass and observed term-by-term by the trainer. We cover the mathematical form of each branch, the exact reduction semantics (including a subtle ATAC/RNA asymmetry), the float32 enforcement that protects the KL branch under mixed precision, the `ModelOutput` contract that carries all three losses to the training loop, and the configuration surface for tuning the balance. Architectural background for the encoders and decoder themselves is intentionally out of scope here — see [Prior and Posterior Variational Encoders](9-prior-and-posterior-variational-encoders) and [Decoder and Softplus Output Design](10-decoder-and-softplus-output-design).

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L155-L169), [models/utils.py](/src/descope/models/utils.py#L28-L41)

## The ELBO Objective, As Implemented

DeSCOPE trains a *conditional* VAE whose latent prior is not a fixed standard Gaussian but a learned, perturbation-aware distribution. Both the prior `p(z | ctrl, pert)` and the posterior `q(z | labels, pert)` are produced by twin `VariationalEncoder` modules fed with the same perturbation embedding but different expression contexts: the prior sees the control cell profile (`ctrl_cell_expr` / `ctrl_cell_tf_idf`), while the posterior sees the perturbed ground-truth `labels`. The variational encoders output `(z, mean, logvar)` via the reparameterization trick, and the decoder reconstructs predictions from the posterior sample.

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L145-L153), [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L231-L239)

Because both distributions are diagonal Gaussians, the KL term is computed in **closed analytical form** from the four moment tensors — no Monte Carlo sampling is involved in the KL branch, so its gradient estimator is deterministic given the moments. The reconstruction term is an MSE between softplus-activated predictions and `labels`, which corresponds to a Gaussian likelihood `p(x|z) = N(x̂, I)` with unit variance, up to constants absorbed by `α_mse`. The full training objective minimized by the optimizer is:

```
loss = α_mse · MSE(x̂, x)  +  α_kl · KL( q(z | x, e) ‖ p(z | c, e) )
```

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L162-L168), [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L248-L254)

The following concept map shows how data flows into the two loss branches — both terms share the perturbation embedding `e` as conditioning input, which is what makes the divergence a *conditional* KL:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs["Batch Inputs"]
        C["ctrl_cell_expr / ctrl_cell_tf_idf"]
        X["labels (perturbed profile)"]
        E["pert_gene_emb (ESM2)"]
    end

    subgraph Latent["Latent Space"]
        P["Prior moments (μ_p, logvar_p)"]
        Q["Posterior moments (μ_q, logvar_q)"]
        Z["z ~ q (reparameterize)"]
    end

    D["Decoder + softplus"] --> XH["x̂ predictions"]
    XH --> MSE["MSE branch"]
    X --> MSE
    P --> KL["Analytic KL branch"]
    Q --> KL

    E --> P & Q
    C --> P
    X --> Q
    Q -->|sample| Z
    Z & E --> D

    MSE & KL --> L["loss = α_mse·MSE + α_kl·KL"]
```

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L138-L169)

## MSE Reconstruction Term: Elementwise Errors and Gene-Level Weighting

Both model variants begin the loss computation identically: `nn.functional.mse_loss(preds, labels, reduction="none")` produces an **elementwise** error tensor of shape `(batch_size, input_length)`, deferring all reduction decisions to the following lines. This is deliberate — it leaves room for optional **gene-level weighting**, where the dataset can supply a `mse_weights` tensor that is multiplied onto the elementwise errors before reduction. Weighted and unweighted paths are selected at runtime by a simple `is not None` check.

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L155-L160), [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L241-L246)

The two modalities reduce the weighted tensor differently, and this is the one place where the loss composition is not perfectly symmetric between `DeSCOPEForATAC` and `DeSCOPEForRNA`. Note that the dataset fallback weight (`ones_weight`) is normalized by gene count, so under the fallback both weighted paths collapse to magnitudes comparable to the plain mean:

| Path | Reduction code | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| ATAC weighted | `(mse_weights * mse_loss_elementwise).sum(dim=-1).mean()` | Per-cell weighted **sum** over genes, then batch mean |
| ATAC unweighted | `mse_loss_elementwise.mean()` | Flat mean over batch × genes |
| RNA weighted | `(mse_weights * mse_loss_elementwise).mean()` | Gene-weighted flat mean over batch × genes |
| RNA unweighted | `mse_loss_elementwise.mean()` | Flat mean over batch × genes |

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L157-L158), [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L243-L244)

The weights themselves are optional and produced upstream in the data pipeline: `HFBaseDataset` accepts a `mse_weights_pkl_file` pickle mapping `(celltype, perturbation)` pairs to per-gene weight arrays, converts them to tensors at load time, and injects a stacked `mse_weights` batch entry inside `__getitems__`, falling back to the normalized ones tensor for pairs missing from the mapping. The tutorial scripts construct `HFDatasetForRNA` without this argument, so **default training runs the unweighted path** — but the hook is wired end-to-end: the trainer forwards only keys matching the model's forward signature (`model_forward_keys`), so `mse_weights` reaches `forward` automatically when the dataset produces it, and is silently dropped otherwise.

Sources: [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L207-L214), [dataset.py](/src/descope/dataset.py#L288-L293), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L44-L47)

## KL Divergence: Closed-Form, Float32, Latent-Wide Scale

The KL branch is implemented as a standalone function `kl_loss_func` shared by both model variants. It receives the four moment tensors and computes the standard closed-form divergence between diagonal Gaussians:

```
KL(q ‖ p) = ½ · Σⱼ [ logvar_p,ⱼ − logvar_q,ⱼ + (σ²_q,ⱼ + (μ_q,ⱼ − μ_p,ⱼ)²) / σ²_p,ⱼ − 1 ]
```

which is exactly what the code expresses as `-0.5 * torch.sum(1 + posterior_logvar - prior_logvar - (posterior_logvar.exp() + (posterior_mean - prior_mean).pow(2)) / prior_logvar.exp(), dim=-1)`, followed by a batch mean. Because it operates on moments rather than samples, this KL estimate has **zero estimator variance** — in contrast to sampling-based approaches that would re-introduce noise through the reparameterization trick a second time.

Sources: [models/utils.py](/src/descope/models/utils.py#L28-L41)

> [!TIP]
> The KL call is wrapped in `torch.amp.autocast(enabled=False, device_type="cuda")` with explicit `.float()` casts on all four moments. Under mixed-precision training, `logvar` and its exponential are numerically fragile in bfloat16/float16 — small logvar errors explode through `exp()`. This block forces the entire divergence computation into float32 regardless of the surrounding autocast policy.

The reduction structure of the KL term deserves attention when reading training logs: it **sums over the latent dimension** (`dim=-1`, width = `hidden_size`, default 672) and then averages over the batch. The MSE term, by contrast, is a flat per-element mean over batch × genes. The two branches therefore live on structurally different scales — KL grows with latent width while MSE dilutes across the gene dimension — and the `α` coefficients are the sole mechanism for rebalancing them. Tracking `mse_loss` and `kl_loss` separately (as the trainer does, below) is what makes this imbalance diagnosable rather than invisible.

Sources: [models/utils.py](/src/descope/models/utils.py#L34-L41), [arguments.py](/src/descope/arguments.py#L56-L60)

The KL gradient flows back into **both** variational encoders — the prior encoder's moments are not frozen targets but learned parameters of a conditional prior `p(z | ctrl, pert)`. This is what separates DeSCOPE from a vanilla VAE with a fixed `N(0, I)` prior: the model simultaneously shapes where the posterior should encode perturbed profiles and where the prior expects them given only control context. At inference time, `labels` are unavailable, so the forward loss path cannot execute at all — the `@torch.no_grad()` `inference` methods sample `z` directly from the prior and return `ModelOutput` instances with all three loss fields set to `None`.

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L146-L148), [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L178-L196), [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L264-L282)

## Composition Contract: α-Weighted Sum and the ModelOutput Trio

The single composition line `loss = self.alpha_mse_loss * mse_loss + self.alpha_kl_loss * kl_loss` is the entirety of the ELBO assembly — no annealing schedule, no β-warmup, no gradient surgery between terms. Both coefficients default to `1.0` and are stored as plain instance attributes on the model, set at construction time. Only the composite `loss` is backpropagated; `mse_loss` and `kl_loss` ride along as detached telemetry.

Sources: [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L132-L133), [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L169), [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L255)

The three scalars leave the model through typed `ModelOutput` dataclasses — `DeSCOPEForATACOutput` and `DeSCOPEForRNAOutput`, each carrying `loss`, `mse_loss`, `kl_loss`, and `logits`. This trio is a deliberate **contract between model and trainer**: the model owns loss mathematics and reduction policy; the trainer owns aggregation, backward, and observability, and never recomputes any loss itself. The end-to-end interaction looks like this:

Sources: [models/utils.py](/src/descope/models/utils.py#L12-L25), [modeling_descope.py](/src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L171-L176)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant DS as HFDatasetForRNA / HFDatasetForATAC
    participant TR as DeSCOPETrainer
    participant M as DeSCOPEForRNA / DeSCOPEForATAC
    participant KLF as kl_loss_func
    participant AC as Accelerator

    DS->>TR: batch {ctrl_*, pert_gene_emb, labels, mse_weights?}
    TR->>TR: filter keys by model forward signature
    TR->>M: forward(**filtered_batch)
    M->>M: softplus preds → elementwise MSE → reduction
    M->>KLF: prior/posterior moments (cast to float32, autocast off)
    KLF-->>M: kl_loss (latent-sum, batch mean)
    M-->>TR: ModelOutput{loss, mse_loss, kl_loss, logits}
    TR->>AC: backward(loss) — composite only
    TR->>AC: reduce each term, "mean" across processes
    TR->>TR: log all three keys at logging_steps
```

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L110-L117)

## Downstream Telemetry: How the Trainer Observes Each Term

During training, the trainer unpacks all three fields from the model output (L113–116) but backpropagates **only** the composite `loss` (L117). Every step, all three detached scalars are `accelerator.reduce(..., "mean")`-aggregated across processes into a three-slot `Accumulator`, which emits running means for `loss`, `mse_loss`, and `kl_loss` every `logging_steps` — alongside `grad_norm` and `lr` — to the file logger and optionally to the tracking backend. This per-term accounting is what lets a practitioner distinguish "reconstruction stalled" from "KL collapsed the posterior."

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L113-L117), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L130-L134), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L137-L153)

Evaluation mirrors the same decomposition. `evaluate()` runs the model under `torch.no_grad()`, gathers each term with `accelerator.gather_for_metrics` (with `.repeat(per_device_eval_batch_size)` to preserve sample weighting on the final partial batch), concatenates across devices, and returns `{eval_loss, eval_mse_loss, eval_kl_loss}`. The early-stopping callback consults **only `eval_loss`** — the composite — so the KL weight indirectly influences stopping behavior through the objective it balances.

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L205-L226), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L175-L182)

| Key | Phase | Aggregation chain | Consumer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `loss` / `mse_loss` / `kl_loss` | train | per-process value → `accelerator.reduce("mean")` → running mean over logging window | `run.log`, `accelerator.log` |
| `eval_loss` / `eval_mse_loss` / `eval_kl_loss` | eval | `gather_for_metrics` → `torch.cat` → global `torch.mean` | log dict; early stopping reads `eval_loss` |

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L98), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L222-L226)

## Tuning the Balance: Configuration Surface

Both loss coefficients are declared on `DeSCOPETrainingArguments` as HfArgumentParser fields, making them ordinary CLI flags. The tutorial entry scripts thread them into the model twice — once for scratch construction via the explicit constructor, once for fine-tuning via `from_pretrained` — so the balance is preserved across checkpoint reloads regardless of which path you take. Because `Trainer`/`Accelerate` handles the rest, no other code needs to know the split exists.

| Argument | Default | Plumbing path | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `alpha_mse_loss` | 1.0 | CLI → `train_args` → `DeSCOPEForRNA/ATAC(...)` or `from_pretrained(...)` → `self.alpha_mse_loss` | Scales reconstruction branch |
| `alpha_kl_loss` | 1.0 | Same path → `self.alpha_kl_loss` | Scales KL branch |
| `mse_weights_pkl_file` (dataset kwarg) | `None` | `HFBaseDataset` → `batch["mse_weights"]` → forward signature filter → weighted reduction | Per-gene error weighting by (celltype, perturbation) |

Sources: [arguments.py](/src/descope/arguments.py#L6-L17), [train.py](/tutorials/RNA_Gene/train.py#L60-L71)

> [!TIP]
> When tuning, remember the structural scale mismatch documented above: KL is summed over the 672-wide latent dimension while MSE averages over thousands of genes per cell. If logs show `kl_loss` dominating `loss`, raising `alpha_mse_loss` and lowering `alpha_kl_loss` are not symmetric interventions — the former rescales a diluted mean, the latter rescales a latent-wide sum — so adjust `alpha_kl_loss` in smaller increments and watch `eval_kl_loss` for posterior collapse (trending toward the prior's own entropy floor).

## Where to Go Next

The loss composition sits at the confluence of the model and training subsystems. To understand *where* the moments fed into `kl_loss_func` come from — and why the prior is conditional on control context — continue with [Prior and Posterior Variational Encoders](9-prior-and-posterior-variational-encoders). For the softplus activation applied to `preds` before the MSE is ever computed (and why a non-negative output matters for count-like data), see [Decoder and Softplus Output Design](10-decoder-and-softplus-output-design). For the machinery surrounding the loss telemetry — accumulators, early stopping, checkpoint resumption semantics — proceed to [Checkpointing, Resuming, Early Stopping](17-checkpointing-resuming-early-stopping), and for the distributed aspects of `accelerator.reduce` and `gather_for_metrics`, [Trainer and Accelerate Integration](15-trainer-and-accelerate-integration).


# Checkpointing, Resuming, Early Stopping



This page explains how DeSCOPE persists training state, how to resume an interrupted run bit-for-bit, and how evaluation-driven early stopping halts distributed sessions. All of this machinery lives in `DeSCOPETrainer.train()`, a single override of the training loop inherited from the external `wppkg` base trainer (pinned to `wppkg==0.1.4` in `pyproject.toml#L20-L26`). The tunable flags — `checkpointing_steps`, `resume_from_checkpoint`, `eval_every_n_epochs`, `earlystop_patience` — come from that base `TrainingArguments` dataclass; DeSCOPE itself only adds loss weights and a pretrained-model path ([arguments.py](/src/descope/arguments.py#L6-L22)).

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L35-L43), [arguments.py](/src/descope/arguments.py#L6-L22), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L20-L26)

## Persistence Architecture: Two Layers of State

DeSCOPE deliberately separates checkpointing into two independent layers. The first layer is **full resumable state**, written by `self.accelerator.save_state(output_dir)` — this captures everything Accelerate knows about the run (model, optimizer, LR scheduler, RNG state across all ranks) so a later run can pick up exactly where it stopped. The second layer is an **inference-ready model snapshot**, written by `self._save(...)` into a `model/` subdirectory, loadable through the standard `from_pretrained` pathway. Every periodic checkpoint directory therefore contains both layers side by side, while the terminal snapshot `last_model/` contains only the second layer.

```
output_dir/
├── step_1000/            # step-based checkpoint (int config)
│   ├── <accelerate state>  # save_state: model + optimizer + scheduler + RNG, per-rank
│   └── model/            # _save: inference-ready weights
├── epoch_9/              # epoch-based checkpoint ("epoch" / "epoch-N" config)
│   ├── <accelerate state>
│   └── model/
├── last_model/           # always written when train() exits — model only
└── run.log               # file logger target ([logging.py wiring])
```

This split maps directly onto the two consumption scenarios: `step_N/` or `epoch_E/` directories feed `accelerator.load_state()` for crash recovery, while `model/` and `last_model/` feed downstream inference — the shipped tutorial notebook points `pretrained_model_name_or_path` straight at `./trainer_output/GM12878/last_model` ([test.ipynb](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb#L29-L35)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph trainloop["DeSCOPETrainer.train()"]
        B["Batch loop<br/>(sync_gradients points)"] --> SV["accelerator.save_state()"]
        E["End-of-epoch hook"] --> EV["evaluate() → eval_loss"]
        EV --> ES["earlystop_callback<br/>set_trigger / check_trigger"]
    end
    SV --> CK["step_N/ or epoch_E/<br/>resumable + model/"]
    SV --> MS["self._save(...) → model/"]
    FIN["train() exit"] --> LM["last_model/<br/>inference-ready only"]
    trainloop --> FIN
    CK -. resume via .-> LS["accelerator.load_state()"]
```

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L155-L161), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L184-L197), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L199-L203)

## Checkpointing: Intervals, Formats, and the Final Snapshot

The `checkpointing_steps` argument is polymorphic: an `int` selects **step-based** checkpointing, while a `str` selects **epoch-based** checkpointing. These two paths execute at different points in the training loop and produce differently named directories, so the format you choose determines both the granularity and the recovery semantics of your run.

| Format | Example | Emission point | Directory created |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `int` | `500` | Inside the batch loop, every time `completed_steps % 500 == 0` on a real optimizer step (guarded by `sync_gradients`) | `output_dir/step_{completed_steps}/` |
| `"epoch"` | `"epoch"` | End of every epoch, after evaluation and the early-stop check | `output_dir/epoch_{epoch}/` |
| `"epoch-N"` | `"epoch-10"` | End of every Nth epoch — parsed via `split("-")[-1]` | `output_dir/epoch_{epoch}/` |

Two ordering facts matter for practitioners. First, step-based saves fire *before* the `max_train_steps` bail-out check in the batch loop, but epoch-based saves execute *after* the early-stop block — so when early stopping halts training at the end of epoch E, the `epoch_E/` checkpoint is **never written**; the only artifact from that epoch is `last_model/`. Second, the epoch directory name uses the 0-based epoch index from the `for epoch in range(...)` loop, so `epoch_9` means "state captured after the 10th epoch." Whatever you choose, `train()` unconditionally finishes with `self._save(output_dir/last_model)` followed by `wait_for_everyone()` and `end_training()` — even when early stopping triggered the exit.

> [!TIP]
> When early stopping fires at the end of an epoch, the `break` exits the epoch loop *before* the epoch-based checkpointing block runs. A `checkpointing_steps="epoch-N"` config plus active early stopping means the final epoch's resumable state is lost — only `last_model/` (weights, no optimizer state) survives from that epoch. If you need to resume near the stopping point, use step-based checkpointing.

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L155-L164), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L166-L197), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L199-L203), [train_descope.sh](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L32)

## Resuming: Exact Reconstruction of Training Progress

Resuming is driven entirely by the `--resume_from_checkpoint` flag pointing at an existing checkpoint directory. The trainer calls `accelerator.load_state(checkpoint_path)` first — restoring model, optimizer, scheduler, and RNG state — and then performs a small piece of string surgery on the directory's basename to reconstruct the loop counters. If the basename contains `epoch`, resumption starts at the *next* epoch (`starting_epoch = N + 1`, so `epoch_9` resumes at epoch index 10) with `completed_steps` rebuilt as `starting_epoch × num_update_steps_per_epoch`. If it contains `step`, the trainer multiplies by `gradient_accumulation_steps` to convert to real dataloader batches, derives `starting_epoch` from `resume_step // len(train_dataloader)`, and keeps the intra-epoch remainder for batch skipping.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["--resume_from_checkpoint<br/>provided?"] -->|No| Z["Cold start<br/>starting_epoch = 0"]
    A -->|Yes| B["accelerator.load_state(path)<br/>model · optimizer · scheduler · RNG"]
    B --> C{"basename is<br/>epoch_N or step_N?"}
    C -->|"epoch_N"| D["starting_epoch = N + 1<br/>completed_steps = N × updates/epoch<br/>resume_step = None"]
    C -->|"step_N"| E["resume_step = N × grad_accum<br/>starting_epoch = resume_step ∥ dataloader_len<br/>completed_steps = N<br/>intra-epoch remainder retained"]
    D --> F["Epoch loop resumes<br/>progress_bar pre-advanced"]
    E --> G{"First resumed epoch?"}
    G -->|Yes| H["accelerator.skip_first_batches<br/>skips the consumed batches"]
    G -->|No| I["Full dataloader"]
    D --> I
    F --> E2["Normal training continues"]
    H --> E2
    I --> E2
```

The `skip_first_batches` call at the start of the resumed epoch is what makes step-based recovery *exact*: rather than replaying data the previous session already consumed, the dataloader is fast-forwarded past `resume_step` batches, and the restored RNG state keeps sampling and augmentations identical ([trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L102-L106)).

One code-level detail deserves attention: the branch that is supposed to auto-discover the most recent checkpoint by scanning the working directory ([trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L72-L77)) is unreachable — the outer guard `if self.args.resume_from_checkpoint:` only passes truthy values, and inside that block the secondary condition `is not None or != ""` is tautologically true, so the `else` fallback can never execute. In practice this means the empty/`None` value (which skips the whole block anyway) and the auto-scan path both do nothing useful.

> [!TIP]
> Always pass an explicit checkpoint directory to `--resume_from_checkpoint`. The auto-discovery fallback inherited from the upstream Accelerate example is dead code here — a falsy value (`None`/empty) never enters the resume block at all, and no directory scanning ever happens. Passing nothing simply means "train from scratch."

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L66-L96), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L102-L106)

## Early Stopping: Evaluation-Triggered Distributed Halt

Early stopping is coupled to the evaluation cadence. At the end of each epoch — and only when an `eval_dataloader` exists and `(epoch + 1) % eval_every_n_epochs == 0` — the trainer runs `evaluate()`, which computes a rank-reduced mean of `eval_loss` (along with `eval_mse_loss` and `eval_kl_loss`) via `gather_for_metrics` ([trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L205-L226)). That scalar is handed to `earlystop_callback.check_early_stopping()`, whose patience is governed by `--earlystop_patience`.

The halt mechanism is explicitly distributed-safe. On any process whose callback decides the patience budget is exhausted, the code calls `self.accelerator.set_trigger()`; immediately afterward, every process runs `self.accelerator.check_trigger()` and breaks *together*. This two-step dance avoids the classic multi-GPU failure mode where rank 0 stops training while rank 1 hangs waiting for a collective that will never arrive.

| Behavior | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Trigger signal | `eval_loss` evaluated at end-of-epoch, gated by `eval_every_n_epochs` |
| Patience | `--earlystop_patience` evaluations without improvement |
| Cross-rank synchronization | `accelerator.set_trigger()` (deciding rank) → `accelerator.check_trigger()` (all ranks break) |
| Epoch checkpoint on halt | **Skipped** — the `break` precedes the epoch-checkpointing block |
| Final artifact | `last_model/` is still saved |
| Best-model tracking | None — the trainer never auto-saves the best snapshot |
| Resume support | **Not supported** — the callback is re-initialized from scratch on resume |

These last three rows come straight from the class docstring, which documents that early stopping does not survive resumption (the callback re-initializes), that you must align `eval_every_n_epochs` with `checkpointing_steps` if you want a snapshot near the best epoch, and that the final model is always saved ([trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L37-L42)).

Note also a deployment reality: in the shipped tutorial scripts, `DeSCOPETrainer` is constructed without any evaluation dataset ([train.py](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L80-L87)), so `self.eval_dataloader is None` and the entire evaluation/early-stop path is skipped — training runs to `num_train_epochs` and relies purely on scheduled checkpoints plus `last_model/`. To activate early stopping, you must supply an eval dataloader and set the patience and cadence flags.

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L166-L182), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L205-L226), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L37-L43), [train.py](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L80-L87)

## What Survives a Restart — and What Doesn't

The resume machinery is asymmetric by design: everything needed to continue *optimization* is persisted, while bookkeeping that shapes *when to stop* is not. This table is the practical checklist before interrupting a long run:

| Aspect | Restored on resume? | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model weights | ✅ | `accelerator.load_state()` |
| Optimizer + LR scheduler state | ✅ | `accelerator.load_state()` |
| RNG state (sampling / dropout determinism) | ✅ | `accelerator.load_state()` |
| Dataloader position (step-based resume) | ✅ | `accelerator.skip_first_batches()` |
| Epoch / step counters | ✅ | Basename parsing of `epoch_N` / `step_N` |
| Early-stop counter and patience budget | ❌ | Callback re-initialized from zero |
| Best-epoch bookkeeping | ❌ | No best-model auto-save exists |
| Tracking (TensorBoard) continuity | ❌ | Not persisted; logs continue under a fresh session |

Sources: [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L66-L106), [trainer.py](/src/descope/trainer.py#L37-L43)

## Configuring in Practice

The flags relevant to this page, as exercised by the reference launch script (note the epoch-based format `epoch-10` saving twice across a 20-epoch run):

| Flag | Role in checkpoint/resume/early-stop |
| --- | --- |
| `--output_dir` | Root for all `step_N/`, `epoch_E/`, `last_model/` directories and `run.log` |
| `--num_train_epochs` | Upper bound of the epoch loop |
| `--max_train_steps` | Optional global optimizer-step cap; checked inside the batch loop |
| `--checkpointing_steps` | `int` → step-based; `"epoch"` / `"epoch-N"` → epoch-based |
| `--eval_every_n_epochs` | Cadence for `evaluate()` and the early-stop check |
| `--earlystop_patience` | Evaluations without `eval_loss` improvement before `set_trigger()` |
| `--resume_from_checkpoint` | Explicit path to a `step_N/` or `epoch_E/` directory |
| `--with_tracking` | Enables `accelerator.log()` for eval metrics at each epoch |

A minimal resume invocation reuses the original training script with one added flag:

```bash
# Original launch (tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh)
accelerate launch --config_file="./accelerate_config.yaml" \
    --num_processes=1 train.py $TRAINPARAMS $DATAPARAMS $MODELPARAMS

# Resume from the epoch-10 boundary checkpoint
accelerate launch --config_file="./accelerate_config.yaml" \
    --num_processes=1 train.py $TRAINPARAMS $DATAPARAMS $MODELPARAMS \
    --resume_from_checkpoint="./results/descope/trainer_output/GM12878/epoch_9"
```

Because all flags are parsed by `HfArgumentParser` from the `DeSCOPETrainingArguments` dataclass ([train.py](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L18-L19)), resumption replays the *same* argument set as the original run — model architecture and data paths must match the checkpoint, or `load_state` will fail on shape mismatches.

Sources: [train_descope.sh](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L27-L58), [train.py](/tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train.py#L18-L19), [arguments.py](/src/descope/arguments.py#L6-L22)

# Distributed Training with DeepSpeed



This page explains how DeSCOPE scales training across multiple GPUs, with DeepSpeed as an optional acceleration backend. The core architectural fact: **DeSCOPE contains no DeepSpeed-specific code**. Instead, the entire distributed layer is delegated to [HuggingFace Accelerate](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate), which treats DeepSpeed as a swappable `distributed_type` backend toggled by a single YAML field. This design means the identical `DeSCOPETrainer` code path executes unchanged whether you run DDP on one GPU or ZeRO sharding on many.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L61-L69), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L20-L26), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L35-L47)

## Architecture: Accelerate as the Distributed Abstraction

DeSCOPE's dependency stack is deliberately layered so that no component above Accelerate knows which distributed backend is active. The `deepspeed` package is an **optional dependency** — commented out in `pyproject.toml` and documented as "Install deepspeed (optional)" in the README's Step 3 — while the mandatory dependencies (`torch`, `wppkg`) carry no DeepSpeed awareness at all. `wppkg` (the author's own utility package) supplies the base `Trainer` and `TrainingArguments`, which DeSCOPE extends via `DeSCOPETrainer` and `DeSCOPETrainingArguments`. All launch orchestration flows through the `accelerate launch` CLI, which reads `accelerate_config.yaml` and decides whether to instantiate plain DDP or a DeepSpeed engine beneath the same `Accelerator` API.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L20-L26), [README.md](README.md#L61-L69), [arguments.py](src/descope/arguments.py#L2-L7), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L8)

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Shell["Launch Layer"]
        SH["train_descope.sh<br/>env vars + hyperparameters"]
        CLI["accelerate launch<br/>--config_file --num_processes"]
        YAML["accelerate_config.yaml<br/>distributed_type: MULTI_GPU / DEEPSPEED"]
    end
    subgraph Framework["Distributed Framework"]
        ACC["Accelerator instance<br/>backend selected by YAML"]
        subgraph Backend["Active Backend"]
            DDPOpt["DDP (MULTI_GPU)"]
            DSOpt["DeepSpeed Engine (DEEPSPEED)<br/>optional install"]
        end
    end
    subgraph DeSCOPE["DeSCOPE Training System (backend-agnostic)"]
        WT["wppkg.dl.Trainer<br/>base class"]
        DST["DeSCOPETrainer<br/>trainer.py"]
        ARGS["DeSCOPETrainingArguments<br/>extends wppkg TrainingArguments"]
        MODEL["DeSCOPEForATAC / DeSCOPEForRNA<br/>cVAE model"]
    end
    SH --> CLI
    YAML --> CLI
    CLI --> ACC
    ACC --> DDPOpt
    ACC --> DSOpt
    WT --> DST
    DST --> MODEL
    ACC -.->|wraps model, optimizer, dataloaders| DST
    ARGS --> WT
```

Every arrow crossing from the DeSCOPE layer into the Framework layer passes through the `Accelerator` object — never through a backend-specific import. This is the invariant that makes DeepSpeed a configuration decision rather than a code change.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L20-L26), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L8-L32)

## The Three-Point Integration Contract

DeepSpeed enters the system at exactly three points, none of which touch library code:

| # | Integration Point | Location | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Installation** (optional) | `pyproject.toml`, `README.md` Step 3 | `deepspeed` is commented out of dependencies; installed separately via `pip install deepspeed` with system-specific build requirements |
| 2 | **Backend selection** | `accelerate_config.yaml` (shipped in all 4 tutorial dirs) | `distributed_type: MULTI_GPU` (default) or `DEEPSPEED`, plus a config-file convention |
| 3 | **Execution** | `src/descope/trainer.py` | Every distributed operation routes through `self.accelerator.*` calls, which behave identically under DDP or DeepSpeed |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L22), [README.md](README.md#L61-L69), [accelerate_config.yaml](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/accelerate_config.yaml#L1-L3), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L111-L133)

The backend selector ships identically in all four tutorial directories (`ATAC_Gene`, `RNA_Gene`, `RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/fine-tune`, `RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain`), and its two comments encode the entire activation contract:

```yaml
# Specify distributed_type as `DEEPSPEED` or `MULTI_GPU`
# If you are using MULTI_GPU, please do not pass a DeepSpeed config file.
distributed_type: MULTI_GPU  # DEEPSPEED
```

The second comment is a warning about Accelerate's validation rules: a `MULTI_GPU` run must not receive a DeepSpeed config file, while a `DEEPSPEED` run requires one (supplied via Accelerate's `--deepspeed_config_file` launch flag or the YAML's `deepspeed_config` field). Notably, the repository ships **no** DeepSpeed JSON config — scaling memory via ZeRO stage 2/3 is left as an explicit operator choice, keeping the default footprint minimal.

Sources: [accelerate_config.yaml](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/accelerate_config.yaml#L1-L3), [accelerate_config.yaml](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/accelerate_config.yaml#L1-L3), [accelerate_config.yaml](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/fine-tune/accelerate_config.yaml#L1-L3), [get_repo_structure: tutorials](tutorials/)

## Accelerator-Mediated Training Loop

The `DeSCOPETrainer.train()` loop is the definitive proof of backend-agnosticism. Each step performs six distributed operations, all through the `Accelerator` facade:

| Accelerator Call | Line | Purpose | Behavior under DeepSpeed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `accelerator.accumulate(model)` | L111 | Gradient-accumulation context manager | Enables `sync_gradients` gating; engine defers all-reduce until accumulation completes |
| `batch.to(accelerator.device)` | L112 | Per-rank device placement | Resolves to the local GPU assigned by the launcher |
| `accelerator.backward(loss)` | L117 | Backward pass | Invokes the DeepSpeed engine's backward, triggering ZeRO gradient partitioning |
| `accelerator.sync_gradients` gate | L118 | Guard for reduction boundaries | `True` only on the final micro-step of an accumulation window |
| `accelerator.clip_grad_norm_(...)` | L119 | Global-norm clipping | Coordinates the norm computation across ZeRO-sharded gradients |
| `optimizer.step()` | L120 | Parameter update | Inside DeepSpeed, this is the engine's fused step; ZeRO stages perform the gradient all-reduce here |

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L110-L122)

The gradient-accumulation pattern is structurally significant: clipping is *conditionally skipped* on non-sync steps (only executed when `sync_gradients` is `True`), ensuring the global gradient norm is computed once per optimization step rather than per micro-batch. `optimizer.step()` and `lr_scheduler.step()` also fire unconditionally inside the `accumulate` context — Accelerate internally no-ops them until the accumulation window closes.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L111-L122)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Batch from DataLoader"] --> B["Move tensors to accelerator.device<br/>filtered by model_forward_keys"]
    B --> C["model forward - returns loss, mse_loss, kl_loss"]
    C --> D["accelerator.backward loss"]
    D --> E{"accelerator.sync_gradients?"}
    E -- "False - mid-accumulation" --> F["skip clip"]
    E -- "True - window complete" --> G["accelerator.clip_grad_norm_"]
    F --> H["optimizer.step + lr_scheduler.step + zero_grad"]
    G --> H
    H --> I["accelerator.reduce loss/mse/kl, mean across ranks"]
    I --> J{"sync_gradients?"}
    J -- "Yes" --> K["progress bar + checkpointing branch"]
    J -- "No" --> A
```

> [!TIP]
> The `DeSCOPETrainer.__init__` (L44-47) extracts `model_forward_keys` from `accelerator.unwrap_model(self.model)` — the *unwrapped* model. Under DeepSpeed the trainer's `self.model` is a `DeepSpeedEngine` wrapper, not the raw `nn.Module`, so introspecting its signature directly would fail. This unwrap-then-introspect pattern is what lets `filtered_batch = {k: v ... if k in self.model_forward_keys}` (L112) work identically under both backends: any fix you make to batch collation must preserve exactly these forward-argument names.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L44-L47), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L110-L113)

## Cross-Rank Metric Aggregation: Two Strategies

DeSCOPE uses two distinct Accelerate aggregation primitives, each suited to a different statistical context:

| Context | Primitive | Semantics | Why This Choice |
|---|---|---|---|
| Training metrics (`loss`, `mse_loss`, `kl_loss`) | `accelerator.reduce(tensor, "mean")` (L131-133) | Scalar reduction across ranks | Cheap; runs every micro-step without inflating communication |
| Evaluation metrics | `accelerator.gather_for_metrics(tensor)` (L214-216) | Full tensor gather with automatic drop-last trimming | Requires the *complete* per-batch loss distribution so the mean over concatenated tensors is unbiased across uneven rank batches |

The evaluation path uses `gather_for_metrics` because the eval set may not divide evenly across ranks — naive averaging of per-rank means would weight small final batches identically to full ones. Note the `loss.repeat(per_device_eval_batch_size)` before gathering: it restores each scalar to its batch weight so the post-gather `torch.mean` reproduces the true dataset-level average.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L129-L134), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L205-L226)

> [!TIP]
> Under any distributed backend — DDP or DeepSpeed — *every rank* must execute the same sequence of collective calls (`reduce`, `gather_for_metrics`, `backward`, `clip_grad_norm_`). Both call sites in `DeSCOPETrainer` are unconditional inside the loops precisely to avoid distributed deadlocks. If you subclass the trainer and add rank-conditional collectives (e.g., `if accelerator.is_main_process: accelerator.reduce(...)`), only the main rank enters the collective and all other ranks hang at the next barrier.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L129-L134), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L214-L216)

## Launch Topologies Shipped in the Repository

The three tutorial pipelines demonstrate two canonical topologies, all sharing the same `TRAINPARAMS` structure — only device selection, process count, and batch scale differ:

| Tutorial | `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` | `--num_processes` | `per_device_train_batch_size` | Scale Profile |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh` | `"0"` | 1 | 64 | Single-GPU reference run |
| `RNA_Gene/train_descope.sh` | `"0"` | 1 | 64 | Single-GPU reference run |
| `RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/train_descope.sh` | `"4,5,6,7"` | 4 | 256 | 4-GPU multi-node-capable pretraining (Tahoe-100M) |

The `total_batch_size` invariant is computed and logged at loop entry (L51): `per_device_train_batch_size × num_processes × gradient_accumulation_steps`. All shipped configs use `gradient_accumulation_steps=1`, so effective batch equals 64 (gene pipelines) or 1024 (Tahoe pretrain). Every script pins `--mixed_precision=bf16` — a `TrainingArguments` field that Accelerate applies regardless of backend, and which DeepSpeed honors through its own bf16 pathway.

Sources: [train_descope.sh](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L51-L58), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/RNA_Gene/train_descope.sh#L51-L58), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/train_descope.sh#L51-L58), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L51-L59)

## Checkpointing and Resume: Accelerate State Management

Checkpointing is where backend differences are most consequential, and again DeSCOPE handles them transparently. Each save event performs two writes:

1. **`accelerator.save_state(output_dir)`** (L159/L195) — the distributed-complete snapshot. Under DeepSpeed with ZeRO sharding, this writes per-rank optimizer/parameter shards plus the launcher metadata; under DDP it writes consolidated states from the main process. The directory is named `step_{n}` or `epoch_{n}`, and the trainer's resume logic (L67-96) parses these names to reconstruct `starting_epoch` and `resume_step`, then calls `accelerator.load_state(checkpoint_path)` and `skip_first_batches` to skip already-consumed micro-batches without changing the RNG/data schedule.
2. **`self._save(...model)`** (L161/L197) — the deployable model artifact, written into a `model` subdirectory of the same checkpoint.

Epoch-based checkpointing accepts a `"epoch-N"` string format (parsed at L185-190), used by all shipped scripts as `epoch-10` (or `epoch-2` for Tahoe).

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L66-L96), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L155-L161), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L184-L197)

The shutdown sequence is backend-relevant too: after saving the final model (L200), the trainer calls `accelerator.wait_for_everyone()` (L201) — a barrier ensuring no rank exits before the final `save_state` completes on any rank — followed by `accelerator.end_training()` (L202), which finalizes the tracking integrations (TensorBoard, given `--report_to=tensorboard`) and releases the distributed resources held by the active backend. The rank-aware logger (L11-32) completes the multi-process discipline: the main process logs at `INFO`, all other ranks at `WARN`, all writing to a single `run.log` without interleaved duplicates.

Sources: [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L199-L203), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L11-L29)

## DDP vs. DeepSpeed: Choosing Your Backend

Because the toggle is purely configuration, the decision reduces to workload characteristics:

| Dimension | `MULTI_GPU` (DDP, default) | `DEEPSPEED` |
|---|---|---|
| Memory footprint | Full optimizer states + parameters on every GPU | ZeRO stages shard optimizer states/parameters/gradients across GPUs |
| Dependency burden | None beyond PyTorch | Optional `deepspeed` install with system-specific build (README Step 3) |
| Config artifacts | YAML only — *must not* pass a DS config file | YAML + a DeepSpeed JSON config you supply |
| Code path changes | None | None — identical `trainer.py` |
| Best fit for DeSCOPE | The shipped model scale (hidden_size 672, ~9 encoder/decoder layers) fits comfortably on a single modern GPU; 4-GPU DDP suffices for Tahoe-100M pretraining | Very large `input_length` (ATAC cCRE dimensionality) or scaled-up variants where optimizer-state memory dominates |

Sources: [accelerate_config.yaml](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/accelerate_config.yaml#L1-L3), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L22), [README.md](README.md#L61-L69), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/RNA_Drug/tahoe100m_pretrain/train_descope.sh#L33-L34)

## Activating DeepSpeed: Step-by-Step

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1["1. pip install deepspeed<br/>README Step 3"] --> S2["2. Edit accelerate_config.yaml<br/>distributed_type: DEEPSPEED"]
    S2 --> S3["3. Author a DeepSpeed JSON config<br/>ZeRO stage, bf16, batch params"]
    S3 --> S4["4. Pass config to launcher<br/>--deepspeed_config_file or YAML deepspeed_config"]
    S4 --> S5["5. accelerate launch train_descope.sh<br/>unchanged TRAINPARAMS"]
    S5 --> S6{"Launch succeeds?"}
    S6 -- "No: MULTI_GPU + DS config detected" --> S7["Remove config file OR switch distributed_type<br/>they are mutually exclusive"]
    S7 --> S5
    S6 -- "No: deepspeed not importable" --> S1
    S6 -- "Yes" --> S8["Verify via run.log:<br/>total batch size formula"]
```

Common failure modes, all derivable from the shipped configuration:

| Symptom | Root Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Accelerate rejects launch: DS config present with `MULTI_GPU` | YAML left at `distributed_type: MULTI_GPU` while a config file is passed | Follow the YAML's own comment: switch to `DEEPSPEED` first |
| `ImportError: deepspeed` | Optional dependency not installed | Complete README Step 3; DeepSpeed often needs a local compiler toolchain |
| Different batch semantics after switching backends | DeepSpeed configs may re-declare `train_batch_size`/micro-batch | Keep DeepSpeed `train_micro_batch_size_per_gpu` equal to `per_device_train_batch_size` from `TRAINPARAMS` |
| bf16 errors on pre-Ampere hardware | `--mixed_precision=bf16` requires bf16-capable GPUs | Switch `TRAINPARAMS` to `fp16` (both backends honor this field) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L61-L69), [accelerate_config.yaml](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/accelerate_config.yaml#L1-L3), [train_descope.sh](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/train_descope.sh#L27-L48), [trainer.py](src/descope/trainer.py#L51-L59)

For the surrounding training-system context: the trainer's construction, callback wiring, and argument plumbing are covered in [Trainer and Accelerate Integration](15-trainer-and-accelerate-integration); checkpoint formats, resume semantics, and the early-stopping trigger (`accelerator.set_trigger` / `check_trigger`, L176-182) are detailed in [Checkpointing, Resuming, Early Stopping](17-checkpointing-resuming-early-stopping); the loss terms being reduced (`mse_loss`, `kl_loss`) are derived in [ELBO Loss: MSE and KL Composition](16-elbo-loss-mse-and-kl-composition); and the end-to-end execution recipe spanning tokenize → train → test lives in [Tutorial Pipeline: Tokenize, Train, Evaluate](4-tutorial-pipeline-tokenize-train-evaluate).

# Inference Pipeline Design



DeSCOPE's inference system answers a single question: *given a population of unperturbed control cells and a perturbation identity, what would the perturbed cells look like?* Rather than predicting a single bulk profile, the pipeline **generates** cell-level counterfactuals by decoding latent variables sampled from a learned conditional prior — one synthetic cell per requested quota, driven entirely by control cells and gene embeddings. This page explains how that generation machinery is designed: the class topology in `src/descope/inference.py`, the conditional sampling loop, modality-specific preprocessing contracts, gene embedding resolution, and the handoff to metric computation. Metric definitions themselves are covered in [Perturbation Metrics via Cell-Eval](20-perturbation-metrics-via-cell-eval), and evaluation protocols in [Leave-One-Out Evaluation Protocol](21-leave-one-out-evaluation-protocol) and [Zero-Shot and Fine-Tuning Workflows](22-zero-shot-and-fine-tuning-workflows).

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L286-L348), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L178-L196)

## End-to-End Architecture

The pipeline is staged into three phases — **initialization**, **generation**, and **evaluation handoff** — connected through four artifacts held on the inference object: `adata_ctrl` (the control cell pool), `adata_test_ground_truth` (real perturbed cells, when available), `adata_pred` (the generated cells), and the test CSV template (the per-perturbation generation quota). The initialization phase consumes a trained checkpoint, a raw AnnData file, and the CSV template; the generation phase consumes control cells plus ESM2 gene embeddings; the evaluation phase compares `adata_pred` against `adata_test_ground_truth` through cell-eval. This separation means a perturbation never needs to be present in the input AnnData to be generated — only its embedding must exist, which is what makes zero-shot evaluation structurally possible.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Inputs["Constructor Inputs"]
        CSV["Test CSV template<br/>columns: target_gene, n_cells"]
        H5AD["AnnData h5ad<br/>control + perturbed cells"]
        CKPT["Trained checkpoint<br/>e.g. last_model"]
        EMB["ESM2 gene embeddings<br/>pt file"]
    end

    subgraph Phase1["Phase 1 - Initialization"]
        INIT["Load template<br/>validate schema"]
        PRE["preprocess_adata<br/>modality-specific"]
        CTRL["adata_ctrl<br/>control cell pool"]
        GT["adata_test_ground_truth<br/>or None"]
        LM["load_model<br/>from_pretrained"]
    end

    subgraph Phase2["Phase 2 - Generation loop"]
        LGE["load_gene_embs<br/>multi-gene mean pooling"]
        S["Sample batch of control cells<br/>with replacement"]
        M["model.inference<br/>prior-conditional decode"]
        NAN["NaN guard<br/>discard batch on failure"]
        Q["Accumulate until<br/>n_cells reached"]
    end

    subgraph Phase3["Phase 3 - Evaluation handoff"]
        ORG["_organize_final_results<br/>swap in real control cells"]
        PRED["adata_pred"]
        EVAL["compute_metrics<br/>cell-eval"]
    end

    CSV --> INIT
    INIT --> PRE
    H5AD --> PRE
    PRE --> CTRL
    PRE --> GT
    CKPT --> LM

    INIT --> LGE
    EMB --> LGE
    CTRL --> S
    LGE --> M
    S --> M --> NAN --> Q
    Q --> ORG
    ORG --> PRED
    GT --> EVAL
    PRED --> EVAL
```

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L200-L241), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L286-L348), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L350-L370)

## Class Topology: Mixin and Template Method

The module is organized around two compositional patterns. **`CellEvalMixin`** is a standalone capability class that wraps the external `cell-eval` library — it exposes metric discovery (`all_metrics`, `all_de_metrics`), metric computation, and a registry of four DeSCOPE-specific extra metrics. **`BaseInference`** is an abstract base class that inherits `CellEvalMixin` and applies the *template method* pattern: it fixes the entire generation algorithm in `inference()` while deferring exactly two hooks to subclasses — `load_model()` and `preprocess_adata()`. The concrete classes `InferenceForRNA` and `InferenceForATAC` are therefore thin: each supplies only a HuggingFace-style `from_pretrained` call and a preprocessing function; everything else (sampling, quota enforcement, result assembly, evaluation) is shared. This design guarantees that RNA and ATAC evaluations execute byte-identical generation logic, eliminating a whole class of modality-specific inference bugs.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class CellEvalMixin {
        +extra_metrics_func
        +all_metrics
        +check_whether_skip_de_metrics(metrics)
        +compute_metrics(...)
        +_compute_metrics(...)
    }
    class BaseInference {
        <<abstract>>
        +adata_ctrl
        +adata_test_ground_truth
        +adata_pred
        +test_csv_template
        +test_genes
        +inference(gene_embs_file, device)
        +_organize_final_results(results)
        +load_model(path)*
        +preprocess_adata(adata)*
    }
    class InferenceForRNA {
        +target_sum
        +skip_raw_counts_check
        +load_model(path)
        +preprocess_adata(adata)
    }
    class InferenceForATAC {
        +load_model(path)
        +preprocess_adata(adata)
    }
    class DeSCOPEForRNA {
        +inference(ctrl_cell_expr, pert_gene_emb)
    }
    class DeSCOPEForATAC {
        +inference(ctrl_cell_tf_idf, pert_gene_emb)
    }
    CellEvalMixin <|-- BaseInference
    BaseInference <|-- InferenceForRNA
    BaseInference <|-- InferenceForATAC
    InferenceForRNA --> DeSCOPEForRNA : from_pretrained
    InferenceForATAC --> DeSCOPEForATAC : from_pretrained
```

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L70-L97), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L199-L206), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L372-L391), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L394-L424)

## Constructor Contract: Template, Data, and Model

`BaseInference.__init__` enforces a strict contract before any generation can run. The test CSV template must contain exactly two columns — `target_gene` and `n_cells` — validated by `_check_test_csv_template`, which raises on missing columns. The template drives both *what* is generated (each row's `target_gene` selects a gene embedding) and *how much* (each row's `n_cells` sets the generation quota). The unique target genes are extracted into `self.test_genes`, with the control name appended so control cells also receive an embedding. After loading the model and preprocessing the AnnData, the constructor splits the data two ways: `_prepare_control_adata` extracts all cells whose `obs[pert_col]` equals `ctrl_name` (raising if none exist — inference is impossible without a control pool), and `_prepare_test_adata` extracts cells for all test genes, downgrading to `None` with a warning if any test gene is absent from the data. Finally, if the template lacks a control row, one is appended with `n_cells = len(adata_ctrl)` so the control population is also counted in the generation pass. Notably, this `{"target_gene", "n_cells"}` schema matches exactly the `target_info.csv` emitted by `intersect_adatas_for_celltype_transfer`, which is how cross-dataset templates are produced upstream.

| Template column | Type | Role in pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| `target_gene` | str | Selects the perturbation gene embedding; drives `test_genes` |
| `n_cells` | int | Generation quota per perturbation; controls `adata_pred` size |

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L200-L241), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L249-L284), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L323-L327)

## The Generation Loop: Prior-Conditional Sampling

The heart of the pipeline is `BaseInference.inference()`, decorated with `@torch.no_grad()`. For each template row, the loop repeatedly samples `batch_size` control cells **with replacement** via `random.choices`, converts them to a dense float32 tensor, and tiles the target gene's embedding across the batch so each control cell is paired with the perturbation condition. It then calls the model's `inference()` method and reads back `.logits` — the generated expression vectors. Three robustness mechanisms shape the loop. First, a **NaN guard**: if any generated cell contains NaN, the entire batch is discarded and re-sampled, preventing a single numerical failure from contaminating the output. Second, a **quota loop**: batches accumulate until `n_cells` is reached, with the final batch trimmed to remove overshoot. Third, **seeded stochasticity**: `random.seed(seed)` fixes control-cell selection across runs, so the only run-to-run variation left is which cells are drawn — the latent sampling noise comes from torch's global RNG (`torch.randn_like` inside the reparameterization), not the Python seed.

> [!TIP]
> At the model level, inference deliberately routes through the **prior** encoder, not the posterior: `DeSCOPEForATAC.inference()` concatenates the control cell with the perturbation embedding and samples `z ~ N(prior_mean, prior_logvar)`, never touching the posterior encoder or ground-truth labels. This is what makes the model generative at test time — the posterior encoder exists purely for training-time ELBO computation (see [Prior and Posterior Variational Encoders](9-prior-and-posterior-variational-encoders)). Note also that the `seed` argument governs only control-cell selection via Python's `random` module; latent noise is drawn from torch's unseeded global RNG.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    E["pert_gene_emb<br/>batch x emb_dim"] --> PG["PertGeneEncoder"]
    PG --> H["pert_embeddings<br/>batch x hidden"]
    C["control cells<br/>batch x input_length"] --> CAT1["concat"]
    H --> CAT1
    CAT1 --> PE["prior_encoder<br/>VariationalEncoder"]
    PE --> Z["z ~ N mean, std<br/>reparameterize"]
    Z --> CAT2["concat"]
    H --> CAT2
    CAT2 --> D["decoder MLP"]
    D --> SP["softplus<br/>non-negative output"]
    SP --> OUT["logits<br/>batch x input_length"]
```

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L286-L348), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L55-L58), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L178-L196), [modeling_descope.py](src/descope/models/modeling_descope.py#L264-L282)

## Modality Preprocessing Contracts

The two subclasses attach fundamentally different preprocessing semantics to the same base algorithm, reflecting the different scales on which each modality is modeled. For **RNA**, `preprocess_rna_perturbation_adata` removes cells with missing perturbation labels, then decides adaptively whether to normalize: if `skip_raw_counts_check=False`, a heuristic (`guess_is_lognorm` from the `wppkg` package) detects already log-normalized data and skips re-normalization; if `True`, it unconditionally applies `normalize_total(target_sum=1e4)` followed by `log1p`. For **ATAC**, `preprocess_atac_perturbation_adata_consistent_with_epiagent` first validates EpiAgent compatibility — the AnnData must contain exactly 1,355,445 cCREs with floating-point (TF-IDF) values — then selects the top-k most active cCREs by total column signal (with a stable sort for deterministic selection, where k comes from `model.config.input_length`), and finally drops cells with NaN perturbation labels. The ATAC path receives no log-normalization because the model operates in TF-IDF space, a distinction that also propagates into evaluation as we will see below.

| Dimension | `InferenceForRNA` | `InferenceForATAC` |
|---|---|---|
| Model class | `DeSCOPEForRNA.from_pretrained` | `DeSCOPEForATAC.from_pretrained` |
| Input representation | log1p-normalized expression | TF-IDF values over top-k cCREs |
| `pert_col` default | `"target_gene"` | `"perturbation"` |
| `ctrl_name` default | `"non-targeting"` | `"control"` |
| Normalization | heuristic-detect `normalize_total` + `log1p` | none (TF-IDF required upstream) |
| Feature selection | full `var_names` of input adata | top-k cCREs by total signal (stable sort) |
| Extra constructor params | `target_sum=1e4`, `skip_raw_counts_check=False` | — |

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L381-L424), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L571-L637), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L491-L568)

## Gene Embedding Resolution

Before generation, `load_gene_embs` resolves the test perturbations into conditioning vectors from a `.pt` file containing a `{gene_name: tensor}` dictionary — in the tutorials, ESM2-derived protein embeddings. The loader handles three cases that matter for real-world perturbation panels. Gene aliases are patched explicitly (a `TAFAZZIN` entry is duplicated as `TAZ`). Single-gene perturbations absent from the file are substituted with **zero vectors** — the generation proceeds, but the perturbation conditioning is silently neutral, so the log listing missing perturbations deserves a careful read. Multi-gene combinatorial perturbations, denoted with `+` (e.g., `"GeneA+GeneB"`), are resolved by splitting on `+`, substituting zeros for any missing constituent, and **mean-pooling** the constituent embeddings into one vector. This design means combinatorial conditions are never blocked at inference time; they degrade gracefully toward the mean of the available constituents.

> [!TIP]
> Because missing single-gene perturbations are zero-filled rather than rejected, a typo in the CSV template produces *plausible-looking but condition-free* predictions — every generated cell reflects only the prior over control cells. When results look suspiciously uniform across perturbations, check the "missing perturbations" log emitted by `load_gene_embs` first.

Sources: [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L378-L464), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L303)

## From Tensors to AnnData: Result Assembly

The raw generation output is a flat NumPy array of shape `(total_cells, n_features)`, which `_organize_final_results` re-materializes into a valid `AnnData`. The `obs[pert_col]` column is reconstructed by expanding each template row's `target_gene` across its `n_cells`, preserving the exact per-perturbation quotas; `var_names` are inherited from the control AnnData, anchoring the feature axis to the model's expected gene order. One step is critical for metric validity: when `use_generated_control_cells=False` (the only permitted setting — the flag is guarded by a hard assertion declaring generated controls "internal debugging only"), the pipeline **discards** the generated control cells and concatenates the *real* control pool into `adata_pred` instead. This matters because cell-eval's bulk metrics compute perturbation effects as `Δ = bulk_perturbation − bulk_control`; substituting real controls guarantees that both sides of the comparison in [Perturbation Metrics via Cell-Eval](20-perturbation-metrics-via-cell-eval) use identical control baselines, isolating generation quality from control-cell noise.

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L295-L301), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L344-L370), [test.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Gene/test.ipynb#L44-L52)

## Evaluation Handoff: The CellEvalMixin

`CellEvalMixin` bridges generated AnnData to the external cell-eval library, with one deliberate deviation: `compute_metrics()` monkey-patches `cell_eval._evaluator._build_anndata_pair` with `_build_anndata_pair_NOCHECK`, bypassing cell-eval's default validation that expression matrices be log1p-normalized. This is a necessity, not an oversight — ATAC predictions live in TF-IDF space (format checks would fail), and RNA predictions come out of a softplus decoder as non-negative but *not* log1p-scale values (see [Decoder and Softplus Output Design](10-decoder-and-softplus-output-design)). The stricter, validating path remains available via `_compute_metrics()` for users whose data conforms. Under the hood, the mixin instantiates a `MetricsEvaluator`, computes only the requested subset of the metric registry (skipping differential-expression computation entirely when no DE metrics are selected, via `skip_de`), and returns two Polars DataFrames (per-perturbation and aggregated results) plus the evaluator itself — the latter is the gateway to the extra metrics, which operate on `evaluator.anndata_pair`.

| Metric source | Examples | Access pattern |
|---|---|---|
| cell-eval built-in | `pearson_delta`, `overlap_at_N`, `discrimination_score_l1`, `mae` | `compute_metrics(metrics_to_calculate=[...])` |
| DeSCOPE extra | `pearson`, `pearson_delta_on_topk_de`, `direction_match_on_topk_de`, `edistance` | `infer.extra_metrics_func.<name>(evaluator.anndata_pair, ...)` |

The extra metrics exploit the same cell-eval artifacts: `pearson_delta_on_topk_de` reads the DE CSV that cell-eval wrote to `outdir`, ranks genes by FDR, and correlates predicted vs. real perturbation effects (bulk differences) over the top-k genes; `direction_match_on_topk_de` measures sign agreement, optionally splitting up- from down-regulated genes. Their mathematical definitions and interpretation belong to [Perturbation Metrics via Cell-Eval](20-perturbation-metrics-via-cell-eval); here the architectural point is that all of them hang off the single evaluator object returned by `compute_metrics`.

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L35-L67), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L126-L196), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L640-L707), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L728-L757)

## Canonical Usage Pattern

Both tutorials (`tutorials/RNA_Gene/test.ipynb`, `tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb`) instantiate the pipeline identically in four steps, differing only in constructor parameters. Step 1 constructs the inference object with the CSV template, the H5AD data, and the trained checkpoint path (e.g., `./trainer_output/HEPG2/last_model`, produced by the training system described in [Checkpointing, Resuming, Early Stopping](17-checkpointing-resuming-early-stopping)). Step 2 calls `infer.inference(...)` with the gene embedding file, device, and `batch_size=256`, keeping `use_generated_control_cells=False` as both notebooks warn emphatically. Step 3 computes metrics: cell-eval built-ins through `compute_metrics`, then the extra metrics off the returned evaluator. Step 4 aggregates per-perturbation scores into a summary table by mapping the extra-metric dictionaries onto the results DataFrame. The complete walk-through with real datasets is in [Tutorial Pipeline: Tokenize, Train, Evaluate](4-tutorial-pipeline-tokenize-train-evaluate) and the drug-perturbation case studies in [Drug Perturbation Case Studies: Sciplex3, Tahoe-100M](5-drug-perturbation-case-studies-sciplex3-tahoe-100m).

```python
# Step 1 - Initialize (RNA example; ATAC uses pert_col="perturbation", ctrl_name="control")
infer = InferenceForRNA(
    test_csv_template_fp="Test_Info.csv",
    adata="HEPG2.h5ad",
    pretrained_model_name_or_path="./trainer_output/HEPG2/last_model",
    pert_col="target_gene",
    ctrl_name="non-targeting",
    target_sum=1e4,
    skip_raw_counts_check=True,
)

# Step 2 - Generate
infer.inference(
    gene_embs_file="ESM2_pert_features.pt",
    device=torch.device("cuda:0"),
    batch_size=256,
    use_generated_control_cells=False,   # always
)

# Step 3 - Evaluate (built-ins + extras off the shared evaluator)
results, agg_results, evaluator = infer.compute_metrics(
    adata_pred=infer.adata_pred,
    adata_real=infer.adata_test_ground_truth,
    metrics_to_calculate=["pearson_delta", "overlap_at_N", "discrimination_score_l1", "mae"],
    control_pert=infer.ctrl_name,
    pert_col=infer.pert_col,
    de_method="wilcoxon",
    num_threads=32,
    outdir="./cell-eval-outdir/HEPG2",
)
pearson_delta_on_topk_de, _ = infer.extra_metrics_func.pearson_delta_on_topk_de(
    data=evaluator.anndata_pair, de_real="./cell-eval-outdir/HEPG2/real_de.csv", topk=20
)
```

Sources: [test.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Gene/test.ipynb#L29-L119), [test.ipynb](tutorials/ATAC_Gene/test.ipynb#L29-L117), [test.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Gene/test.ipynb#L146-L183)

## Design Trade-offs

Several decisions in the loop trade statistical purity for robustness and scale, and it is worth reading them explicitly. The with-replacement control-cell sampling means a small control pool can still fill large quotas, but the generated population is a bootstrap sample of the pool rather than an exhaustive draw; the quota coming from the CSV template (rather than from actual perturbed-cell counts) deliberately decouples generation size from data availability — essential for zero-shot conditions that have no observed cells at all. The discard-and-retry NaN handling favors simplicity over gradient-clip-style repair, at the cost of a mild selection bias toward numerically stable latent draws. And the template-driven architecture means the same code path serves seen, unseen, and combinatorial perturbations uniformly — the only modality-specific logic lives behind the two abstract hooks. For extending these patterns to new modalities, see [Extending DeSCOPE to New Modalities](24-extending-descope-to-new-modalities).

| Decision | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| With-replacement control sampling | Works with any pool size; deterministic under seed | Bootstrap duplication in small pools |
| Template-driven quotas | Enables zero-shot generation; decouples from data | Quota realism depends on template authorship |
| NaN batch discard | Simple, prevents silent corruption | Mild bias toward stable latent regions |
| Real-control substitution in `adata_pred` | Identical baselines for `Δ` metrics | `adata_pred` is not purely model output |
| Zero-fill missing gene embeddings | Graceful degradation for novel perts | Silent neutral conditioning if unchecked |

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L286-L348), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L350-L370), [utils.py](src/descope/utils.py#L438-L449)

To go deeper on this pipeline's neighbors: [Perturbation Metrics via Cell-Eval](20-perturbation-metrics-via-cell-eval) details every metric surfaced by `CellEvalMixin`; [Leave-One-Out Evaluation Protocol](21-leave-one-out-evaluation-protocol) and [Zero-Shot and Fine-Tuning Workflows](22-zero-shot-and-fine-tuning-workflows) show how this inference machinery is orchestrated for benchmarking and transfer; and the conditioning inputs consumed here — ESM2 gene embeddings and the decoder's output transform — are dissected in [PertGene Encoder and ESM2 Embeddings](8-pertgene-encoder-and-esm2-embeddings) and [Decoder and Softplus Output Design](10-decoder-and-softplus-output-design). For the module-level inventory of everything discussed above, consult [API Reference and Module Layout](23-api-reference-and-module-layout).


# Perturbation Metrics via Cell-Eval



Evaluating a perturbation-prediction model requires more than a single loss value: it demands bulk-profile correlations, differential-expression (DE) agreement, and distributional distances computed across hundreds of perturbations. DeSCOPE delegates this to **cell-eval** (ArcInstitute's evaluation framework, pinned at version `0.6.6`) and layers a small set of domain-specific extra metrics on top. This page explains the integration architecture, why DeSCOPE bypasses cell-eval's input validation, how each metric is computed, and how the pieces assemble into the end-to-end evaluation workflow used in the Sciplex3 and Tahoe-100M case studies.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L15-L22), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L1-L30), [2_inference.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/2_inference.ipynb#L1-L10)

## Integration Architecture: The CellEvalMixin

DeSCOPE's evaluation layer is built on a single inheritance strategy: the `CellEvalMixin` class carries all metric-computation capability, and both concrete inference classes inherit it through `BaseInference(CellEvalMixin, ABC)`. This means any `InferenceForRNA` or `InferenceForATAC` instance — the same objects that generate predictions — is also a fully equipped metrics evaluator. The mixin wraps cell-eval's `MetricsEvaluator`, introspects the `metrics_registry` for available metrics, and exposes four DeSCOPE-specific "extra metrics" as an attribute-style dictionary.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class CellEvalMixin {
        +extra_metrics_func: edict
        +all_metrics: list
        +all_de_metrics: list
        +compute_metrics(...)
        +_compute_metrics(...)
    }
    class BaseInference {
        <<abstract>>
        +test_csv_template
        +adata_ctrl
        +adata_test_ground_truth
        +adata_pred
        +inference(...)
        load_model()* 
        preprocess_adata()*
    }
    class InferenceForRNA
    class InferenceForATAC
    class MetricsEvaluator {
        cell-eval
    }
    class PerturbationAnndataPair {
        cell-eval
    }
    class metrics_registry {
        cell-eval
    }
    CellEvalMixin <|-- BaseInference : inherits
    BaseInference <|-- InferenceForRNA
    BaseInference <|-- InferenceForATAC
    CellEvalMixin --> MetricsEvaluator : constructs
    MetricsEvaluator --> PerturbationAnndataPair : owns
    CellEvalMixin --> metrics_registry : introspects
    CellEvalMixin --> utils : extra metrics
```

The mixin's constructor registers exactly four extra metrics — `pearson`, `pearson_delta_on_topk_de`, `direction_match_on_topk_de`, and `edistance` — into an `EasyDict` so they can be called with attribute syntax (`infer.extra_metrics_func.pearson(...)`). Registry introspection properties (`all_metrics`, `all_de_metrics`, `all_anndata_pair_metrics`) proxy directly to cell-eval's `metrics_registry.list_metrics()`, letting users discover the available built-in metric names at runtime before committing to a selection.

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L70-L124), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L199-L232)

## The Validation Bypass: Why DeSCOPE Monkey-Patches Cell-Eval

Cell-eval enforces a strict contract by default: both `real` and `pred` AnnData objects must contain log1p-normalized expression. DeSCOPE deliberately violates this contract, and the reason is documented in the source itself. For **ATAC**, the prediction target is TF-IDF values, which are neither counts nor log-normalized. For **RNA**, the decoder can output negative values (an artifact of the regression-based VAE decoder), which is legal input for metrics but fails cell-eval's log-normalization heuristic check (`guess_is_lognorm`).

The bypass is implemented in two cooperating pieces. First, `_build_anndata_pair_NOCHECK` is a drop-in replacement for cell-eval's internal pair builder that skips the commented-out `_convert_to_normlog` validation calls. Second, the public `compute_metrics` method monkey-patches it into place:

```python
cell_eval._evaluator._build_anndata_pair = _build_anndata_pair_NOCHECK
```

This is process-global patching — it affects every subsequent `MetricsEvaluator` construction in the Python session, not just calls through this mixin. The docstring notes that users who *want* format validation should call the private `self._compute_metrics` instead, which constructs `MetricsEvaluator` without the patch. This is a deliberate API design: the validated path remains one attribute-access away, while the unvalidated path is the default for model evaluation.

> [!TIP]
> The monkey-patch means the expression scale of your `adata_pred` is passed to cell-eval *as-is*. If you hand-craft predictions outside the DeSCOPE inference pipeline (e.g., baseline methods), ensure they are on the same scale as your ground truth — nothing will warn you about scale mismatches, and metrics like `pearson` will silently degrade.

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L35-L67), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L160-L196), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L15-L22)

## Built-In vs. Extra Metrics: A Two-Tier System

DeSCOPE's metric surface splits cleanly into two tiers with different provenance, signatures, and lifecycles. Built-in metrics are cell-eval's own implementations, invoked in bulk through `evaluator.compute(profile="full", skip_metrics=...)`. Extra metrics are DeSCOPE-local functions in `utils.py` that consume `evaluator.anndata_pair` — the `PerturbationAnndataPair` the evaluator constructed — plus, for the top-k DE metrics, a DE results CSV that cell-eval writes to the output directory.

| Dimension | Built-in metrics (cell-eval) | Extra metrics (DeSCOPE) |
|---|---|---|
| Source | `metrics_registry` in cell-eval 0.6.6 | `src/descope/utils.py` |
| Invocation | `infer.compute_metrics(metrics_to_calculate=[...])` | `infer.extra_metrics_func.<name>(...)` |
| Input | `adata_pred`, `adata_real` → handled internally | `evaluator.anndata_pair` + optional `de_real` CSV |
| Return | Polars `results` (per-perturbation) + `agg_results` (aggregated) | `dict[str, float]` + mean float |
| DE dependency | Computed internally by `MetricsEvaluator` (or skipped via `skip_de`) | Reads precomputed `real_de.csv` from the outdir |
| Examples | `mse`, `mse_delta`, `overlap_at_100`, `precision_at_200`, `de_spearman_lfc_sig`, `pr_auc`, `roc_auc` | `pearson`, `pearson_delta_on_topk_de`, `direction_match_on_topk_de`, `edistance` |

The Sciplex3 tutorial illustrates the typical built-in selection: error metrics (`mse`, `mae`, and their `_delta` variants), rank-overlap and precision-at-N curves (N ∈ {50, 100, 200, 500}), DE-level agreement (`de_direction_match`, `de_spearman_lfc_sig`), and discrimination (`discrimination_score_l1`, `pr_auc`, `roc_auc`). Note that the notebook subsets both predicted and ground-truth AnnData to a precomputed list of "reliably predicted genes" *before* calling `compute_metrics` — performance is evaluated strictly on the gene subset the model can express.

Sources: [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L126-L158), [inference.py](src/descope/inference.py#L99-L116), [2_inference.ipynb](tutorials/RNA_Drug/sciplex3_evaluation/zero-shot/2_inference.ipynb#L44-L137)

## Extra Metric Reference

Each extra metric operates on the bulk (mean) expression profiles that cell-eval's `PerturbationAnndataPair` exposes via `iter_bulk_arrays()`. The key algorithmic distinctions lie in *what* is correlated and *over which genes*.

| Metric | Compares | Gene scope | Default topk | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pearson` | Bulk perturbed profile (pred vs. real) | All genes | — | per-pert. dict + mean |
| `pearson_delta_on_topk_de` | Perturbation effect Δ = bulk_pert − bulk_ctrl | Top-k DE genes (lowest FDR) | 20 | per-pert. dict + mean |
| `direction_match_on_topk_de` | Sign of Δ (pred vs. real) | Top-k DE genes, optionally split up/down by `percent_change` | 100 | up/down dicts + means |
| `edistance` | Perturbation group vs. control group | All genes (distance-based) | — | per-pert. dict |

`pearson_delta_on_topk_de` is the most statistically interesting: rather than correlating absolute expression (which is dominated by highly-expressed housekeeping genes), it correlates the *change* induced by the perturbation, restricted to the genes the perturbation most strongly affects.
